title: Computational Goal Formation Dynamics (CGFD)
abstract: Goal formation is a fundamental capability of autonomous systems, yet most computational treatments assume that goals are static and externally specified. This paper proposes a formal framework, Computational Goal Formation Dynamics (CGFD), in which a goal is viewed as an evolving entity governed by a deterministic or stochastic evolution equation. We derive the goal evolution equation, analyze its stability properties, and discuss how the framework can explain emergent autonomous behavior. The CGFD model offers a principled basis for designing self‑directed agents whose objectives adapt naturally to changing environments and internal states. Because the model is purely mathematical, no experimental data are presented; instead, the paper focuses on theoretical development and implications for future research.

title: Civilizational Infrastructure Specification: Structural OS for Artificial Creativity Generation
abstract: This paper presents the final specification of the Structural Operating System (Structural OS) designed to artificially generate “creativity,” a capability fundamentally absent in current artificial intelligence systems. AI can only perform convergence (optimization) of existing semantic volumes and is structurally incapable of generating new premises, new semantic volumes, or new convergence pathways. This study designs an OS with a three-layer architecture—artificial semantic divergence → structural preservation → transfer into convergence processes—and demonstrates how AI can function as a component within a structural space where creativity emerges. The Structural OS serves as a civilizational infrastructure capable of exponentially accelerating creative processes across science, social systems, industry, philosophy, and civilizational design.

title: A Rigorous Proof: Truth Must Exist, and Truth Is the Conjugate-Inverse
abstract: 本文在ECT-OS-JiuHuaShan框架的元逻辑层面上,严格证明了:真理必须存在,而真理的结构是共轭逆。论文否定了真值的标量误解——真值不是一组真命题,也不是可枚举的标量点集合,而是使真假区分显现的预度量。证明分为三层:存在性证明显示真理的不可取消性;结构证明表明否定算符¬诱导出真集与假集之间的满射逆映射;本质证明表明,真理正是共轭逆结构本身。 论文系统地回应了六个核心问题:元语言与对象语言的统一性、系统一致性、标量伪造的极限、唯一性与自指的相互逆、角动量的动力学与守恒,以及逻辑不动点和非终结性。最终证实:真理因共轭逆而不可取消,且因角动量守恒而永恒呼吸。

title: A Multi-Annotator Study of Segmentation Noise and Uncertainty in Turbid Underwater Images
abstract: Label uncertainty and annotator disagreement are common challenges in the field of computer vision, yet their study has largely been confined to the medical domain or to generic image-recognition datasets. Underwater datasets are particularly susceptible to these issues due to the need for domain expertise, degraded visibility conditions, and the inherent difficulty of establishing reliable ground truth in inaccessible environments. Despite these challenges, annotation uncertainty in underwater imagery remains largely unexplored. In this work, we present the first systematic multi-annotator study of segmentation in real underwater scenes, with over 100 participants, and across varying, controlled levels of turbidity. We show that underwater datasets face many of the same annotation challenges as other vision tasks, while turbidity introduces additional systematic errors. We further investigate the main factors driving label noise and explore ways to improve annotation quality in turbid underwater environments, including privileged information, individual effort and annotator ensembles. All (meta-) data collected in this study will be available on the project page: https://vap.aau.dk/tubcertainty

title: Program Semantic Light-Cone Theory
abstract: This paper introduces Program Semantic Light-Cone Theory (PSLCT), a novel approach to program analysis and verification. PSLCT leverages the concept of a semantic light-cone to define the influence domains of program events, moving beyond traditional system-wide analysis. The core idea is to identify the future range of events influenced by a given event, denoted as $\mathcal{L}^+(e)$, and the past range of events that could influence the event, denoted as $\mathcal{L}^-(e)$. By focusing solely on these light-cones, PSLCT significantly reduces the complexity of program analysis, potentially offering a pathway toward tackling large-scale program verification and debugging challenges, aligning with the goals of the Turing Award. The theory provides a structured framework for reasoning about program behavior and offers a new perspective on program understanding.

title: Computational Rule Explanation Theory (CRET-2)
abstract: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence systems has heightened the demand for models that are not only accurate but also interpretable. Traditional black‑box models, such as deep neural networks, offer strong predictive performance yet provide little insight into their internal decision processes, limiting trust and hindering regulatory compliance. In this paper we introduce the Computational Rule Explanation Theory (CRET‑2), a novel framework that generates symbolic decision rules while simultaneously producing formal explanations that justify the validity of each rule. CRET‑2 is built upon a dual‑module architecture: a rule generation module that constructs concise rule sets from data, and an explanation module that derives logical or statistical justifications based on the rule's structure and the underlying data distribution. The theory is grounded in formal logic, information theory, and causal reasoning, ensuring that each rule is accompanied by a verifiable explanation that links the rule to observable patterns or causal mechanisms. We demonstrate the efficacy of CRET‑2 through a series of case studies, including credit risk assessment, medical diagnosis, and fraud detection, where the generated rules achieve competitive predictive performance while providing transparent reasoning. Our results show that CRET‑2 can reduce the opacity of AI systems, support auditing, and facilitate user trust without sacrificing accuracy. The potential for CRET‑2 to address the AI black‑box problem suggests that it could play a pivotal role in the design of future interpretable AI systems and in the advancement of responsible AI research.

title: Computational Identity Universe Theory (CIUT)
abstract: The Computational Identity Universe Theory (CIUT) proposes a unified framework for understanding all computational entities as elements of a high‑dimensional identity space Ω_I. Each entity is represented by a vector of intrinsic attributes (s1, s2, …, sK) that capture its computational state, functional role, and contextual dependencies. CIUT focuses on the structural relationships among these identities, formalizing them through graph‑based, algebraic, and metric representations. By treating computational systems as points in Ω_I, the theory enables systematic exploration of equivalence, transformation, and emergence phenomena across software, hardware, and networked infrastructures. The paper outlines the formal construction of Ω_I, the mechanisms for measuring similarity and interaction, and the computational procedures for analyzing large identity graphs. CIUT offers a high‑level perspective that can unify diverse areas such as program analysis, system security, distributed computing, and artificial intelligence. Its potential to provide a comprehensive theoretical foundation for the design of future computational architectures suggests that it could be a candidate for recognition at the level of a Turing Award.

title: Negative Information K: Negative Information Diagnosis in Algorithmic Generalization Resolution Insufficiency and Inductive Collapse in Overparameterized Mechanisms
abstract: Traditional statistical learning theory treats generalization error as a continuous trade-off between model complexity and sample size, with positive-informationtools such as VC dimension and Rademacher complexity providing asymptotic estimates of test risk. However, three phenomena in deep learningdouble descent, capability emergence, and negative transferreveal a rupture in this continuous narrative:generalization does not decay smoothly at all scales, but undergoes phase transitions at specific critical points. This paper applies the underlying self-consistencylogic of negative information theory to algorithmic generalization analysis, definingevidence fibres and obstruction sections on the algorithmic coordinate space, encoding interpolation paradox, shortcut bias, and outofdistribution shift as rejectionunits carrying obstruction classes. We rigorously prove the theorem of algorithmicresolution insufficiency: in the overparameterized regime, when the effective degreesof freedom of the training trajectory exceed the resolution index of the validationdescriptor, the validation loss, as a finite-valued descriptor on the hypothesis space,is necessarily noninjective, thus failing to distinguish true generalization from spurious shortcuts. Double descent, capability emergence, and negative transfer areuniformly diagnosed as three projections of the same phasetransition order parameter, and a mutual locking inequality is established between the positive informationgain of training and the negative information entropy of validation. This frameworkis strictly correlated with constraint network theory via a faithful functor; the threeobstruction classes are images of topological operators, and the mutual locking inequality is a projection of the information conservation axiom. All lowdimensionalconclusions are derived from covering numbers and combinatorial topology; theprecise scaling laws of effective degrees of freedom and resolution indices in deepnonlinear networks are stated as conditional frameworks.

abstract: Supervised machine-learning code used to classify threshold-defined Au and Ag occurrences in the Rudabánya soil-geochemical dataset. title: Steer on a Sphere: Geometric Control of Transformer Outputs
abstract: We show transformer hidden states are constrained to a sphere by layer normalization (radius ||γ_l|| per layer), that a single tangent step reaches any vocabulary token with 91-98% reliability across four model families, and that self-reinforcing tokens form hidden-state fixed points (cow tipping) usable as a defensive encoding against LLM scraping.

title: Computational Self-Limit Discovery (CSLD)
abstract: This paper introduces the theoretical framework of Computational Self-Limit Discovery (CSLD), a novel approach to autonomous system improvement predicated on the concept of a system actively identifying and characterizing its own limitations. The core principle of CSLD revolves around the systematic exploration of the system's operational boundaries, denoted as [Limit(S)], where S represents the system itself. The system then strategically designs interventions aimed at overcoming these identified limitations, leading to iterative self-improvement. This process is envisioned as a potential paradigm for autonomous learning and adaptation, holding significant implications for the advancement of artificial intelligence and computational systems. The theoretical underpinnings are presented, outlining key components and potential mathematical formalizations. The exploration focuses on the dynamics of limit identification and subsequent design strategies, without relying on empirical experimentation.

title: Reversible Intent Computing
abstract: Reversible Intent Computing (RIC) presents a novel approach to computation centered around understanding and reconstructing the *intent* behind system actions, rather than merely recovering state variables. Traditional reversible computing focuses on restoring the state of a program after an operation, represented as [St ↔ St+1]. RIC, however, shifts the paradigm by defining and restoring an "intent state" – [It = (Gt, Ct, At)]. This intent state comprises three key components: the *goal* (Gt), the *context* (Ct), and the *action rationale* (At). The core principle of RIC is the ability to reverse the flow of computation by restoring [It+1 → It], effectively recovering the decision-making intent that drove the system's action. This offers the potential to build auditable intelligent systems and explainable autonomous systems, representing a significant advancement in computational models. This paper outlines the foundational concepts of RIC, its theoretical underpinnings, and explores its implications for future intelligent system design. ---

title: Computational Interaction Language (CIL)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Interaction Language (CIL), a novel programming paradigm designed to shift the focus from explicitly defining *what* a program should do to describing *how* its constituent structures interact. Traditional programming relies heavily on instruction-based approaches, where developers meticulously detail every step required to achieve a desired outcome. CIL proposes a fundamentally different model, centered around the direct specification of interactions between structural elements. This approach aims to mirror the natural processes of complex systems, where emergent behavior arises from the dynamic relationships between components rather than prescribed sequential actions. The core concept revolves around the representation of interaction as a directed relationship between structures, denoted as [Structure_A ↔ Structure_B]. This eliminates the need for explicit step-by-step instructions and allows for a more intuitive and potentially more powerful method of program design, particularly for systems exhibiting complex, adaptive behaviors. This paper lays out the foundational principles of CIL, explores its potential benefits, and discusses its implications for future programming paradigms, suggesting a significant pathway toward achieving the goals recognized by the Turing Award.

evidence.title: Computational Interaction Language (CIL)
evidence.abstract: This paper introduces Computational Interaction Language (CIL), a novel programming paradigm designed to shift the focus from explicitly defining *what* a program should do to describing *how* its constituent structures interact. Traditional programming relies heavily on instruction-based approaches, where developers meticulously detail every step required to achieve a desired outcome. CIL proposes a fundamentally different model, centered around the direct specification of interactions between structural elements. This approach aims to mirror the natural processes of complex systems, where emergent behavior arises from the dynamic relationships between components rather than prescribed sequential actions. The core concept revolves around the representation of interaction as a directed relationship between structures, denoted as [Structure_A ↔ Structure_B]. This eliminates the need for explicit step-by-step instructions and allows for a more intuitive and potentially more powerful method of program design, particularly for systems exhibiting complex, adaptive behaviors. This paper lays out the foundational principles of CIL, explores its potential benefits, and discusses its implications for future programming paradigms, suggesting a significant pathway toward achieving the goals recognized by the Turing Award.

title: Computational Knowledge Consistency Proof (CKCP)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Knowledge Consistency Proof (CKCP), a novel approach to verifying the internal consistency of knowledge systems. Traditional knowledge representation and reasoning systems often lack mechanisms for formally guaranteeing that their inferences are logically sound, leading to potential inconsistencies and unreliable results. CKCP addresses this limitation by requiring knowledge systems not only to produce answers (y) but also to provide a proof of consistency, represented as [y, πconsistency]. The core principle is to demonstrate that the system does not lead to a logical contradiction (bot), formalized as K ⊚ bot is false. This proof provides a fundamental layer of assurance regarding the trustworthiness of the knowledge system. We explore the potential of CKCP to bridge the gap between knowledge representation, formal verification, and trustworthy artificial intelligence, ultimately offering a pathway towards more reliable and robust AI systems. The system output is structured as follows: [y, πconsistency] where *y* represents the computed answer and πconsistency is the proof of consistency.

title: Exact and Efficient Circuit Construction for Block Encoding Matrix Polynomials
abstract: A recent interpolation-based Quantum Signal Processing (QSP) framework by Alase bypasses the phase-finding procedures required in conventional QSP, allowing for a direct encoding of the target polynomial into a quantum circuit. However, this approach assumes access to a diagonal block encoding of function values without providing an explicit circuit construction. In this work, we address this gap by developing an explicit circuit construction method for diagonal block encodings. The resulting algorithm achieves a computational cost of $\mathcal{O}(d\log d)$ for explicitly constructing block encodings of matrix polynomials, improving upon the best-known theoretical bounds of previous methods. Numerical results confirm this scaling, demonstrating that circuit parameters for polynomial degrees up to $10^7$ can be computed in about a minute on a standard CPU.

title: ProjFormer: Point Cloud Completion via Geometric-Projective Transformer and Cross-Modal Semantic Constraints
abstract: Point cloud completion is inherently ill-posed due to severe sparsity and ambiguity in partial observations. Existing multi-view methods alleviate this by incorporating 2D semantics, but often rely on learned attention and fixed fusion, which lack geometric consistency and adaptability. We propose ProjFormer, a cross-modal framework that enforces geometry-consistent 2D-3D interaction through explicit projection and adaptive feature routing. A Projective Guided View Attention module aligns 3D points with multi-view features via deterministic projection, enabling efficient and geometrically consistent aggregation. Building on this, a geometry-aware routing network performs point-wise adaptive fusion of structural and observation-driven features for progressive refinement. Experiments show that, under a lightweight design, ProjFormer delivers competitive performance with improved structural completeness.

title: Functionalist Perspective on Emotions in AI: A Review of Roles, Mechanisms and Impacts
abstract: Functionalist Perspective on Emotions in AI: A Review of Roles, Mechanisms and Impacts TREO Talk Paper Eun Hee Park Old Dominion University epark@odu.edu Mala Kaul University of Nevada, Reno mkaul@unr.edu Chad Anderson Miami University, Ohio ander556@miamioh.edu Abstract Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) make it increasingly important to understand and theorize how emotion-related processes shape system behavior and decisions. Prior research such as in affective computing and human-computer interaction has focused largely on AI emotion detection and expression, but less attention has been paid to how these processes function within AI systems and shape their decisions. Recent interpretability research by Anthropic has demonstrated that large language models encode internal representations of emotion-related concepts that systematically influence their output and behavior. These findings provide empirical evidence that emotion-like mechanisms can play a functional role in shaping system behavior while highlighting the need for clearer ways to understand how such mechanisms operate, particularly given the opacity of modern AI systems. Motivated by this gap, this research examines “emotion in AI” through a conceptual literature review grounded in a functionalist perspective, that views emotions in terms of their roles in evaluation, regulation, and action. Rather than assuming that AI systems explicitly implement emotion modules, we focus on what these processes do and how their effects can be observed in system behavior. Based on this perspective, we develop a classification scheme (Figure 1) organizing prior research around eight functional roles: appraisal, representation, generation, prioritization, action readiness, adaptation, coordination, and feedback. This scheme provides a structured way for interpreting how internal processes shape AI cognition and decision-making. Understanding these mechanisms and making sense of the emerging evidence on internal representations, is critical for improving the safety, reliability, and quality of human-AI interaction. Figure 1. Functional Roles of Emotion in AI: A Classification Scheme For this review, we conducted keyword-based searches in major databases, including AIS Basket journals and Web of Science, using terms such as emotion, affective computing, and emotional AI. The dataset spans information systems, AI, robotics, and human-computer interaction. Currently, in the data analysis phase, we are classifying studies by proposed functional roles to identify patterns across themes and constructs. This study contributes in three ways. First, we develop a theoretically grounded structure for organizing a fragmented body of research on functional emotion in AI. Second, we provide an interpretive lens linking observable behaviors to emotion-related function within AI systems. Third, we identify underexplored areas, such as control mechanisms and feedback processes, critical for understanding user-interaction related decisions made by AI systems. Practically, this suggests that even when AI systems are not fully transparent, their functional effects can be considered in their design and governance, to ensure safe and reliable human-AI interaction. Overall, this work reframes emotion in AI as a functional aspect of system behavior and develops a future research agenda for decision-making, trust, and responsible AI design.

title: Chip Virtual de Inteligência Artificial (CVIA): Arquitetura de Software, Dinâmica de Execução e Governança
abstract: Este trabalho apresenta o Chip Virtual de Inteligência Artificial (CVIA), uma arquitetura computacional modular baseada em software, desenvolvida para organizar e integrar capacidades de inteligência artificial em uma unidade lógica de processamento. O CVIA encontra-se implementado e em funcionamento, sendo composto por mecanismos especializados de comunicação, orquestração, processamento cognitivo, gerenciamento de contexto e memória, execução de tarefas, extensões especializadas, integração com recursos externos, segurança, governança, auditoria e tolerância a falhas. A arquitetura é organizada em seis macrocamadas funcionais: Interface e Comunicação; Controle e Orquestração; Unidade Lógica Cognitiva e de Decisão; Registradores, Memória e Barramento de Eventos; Unidade de Coprocessamento Especializado; e Sistema de Segurança, Tolerância a Falhas e Governança. O trabalho descreve a organização dos componentes de software, a dinâmica de execução e o loop cognitivo utilizado pelo CVIA, incluindo recepção de requisições, construção de contexto, planejamento, processamento cognitivo, tomada de decisão, resolução de ações, validação, execução, registro e monitoramento. Também são apresentados mecanismos relacionados à avaliação de riscos, aplicação de políticas, autorização, princípio do menor privilégio, retry, rollback, auditoria, evidências e acompanhamento de custos operacionais. O objetivo é documentar a arquitetura e estabelecer uma descrição técnica do CVIA como uma unidade computacional inteligente baseada em software, capaz de integrar modelos de inteligência artificial, memória, ferramentas, extensões especializadas e mecanismos de governança dentro de um ecossistema computacional maior.

title: 训练动力学的场域判据 v0.2:ΔL 轨迹判据与 R'_eff 资源判据的双维判据层
abstract: 训练动力学的场域判据 v0.2(v0.1 ΔL 轨迹判据的升级版)。判据层双维:①ΔL 轨迹维(保持 v0.1:谱判据 α<2/λ_max 与 SGD 收敛条件 lr<2/L 同一性;toy 5/5 四位小数吻合;GPT-2 124M 指数漂移慢发散预警;p99 噪声标定)。②R'_eff 资源维(新增:异构算力度量真空——同芯片精度跨度 32x/稀疏口径不可比/国产官方规格不公开;统一力比坐标 R'_eff=E_effective/E_peak=MFU 的 NPU 推广=吸附结构利用率;产业标定谱 MLPerf v6.0 一手——GB300 实测 0.40,训练带 30-45%,顶级系统无人过 55%;口径自洽反推 FP4 训练)。③双通道失效分类器(新增:ΔL×R'_eff×事件性,四类失效可分——发散/静默错误/喂数据病/正常;检测升级为分类,与高敏感低特异互补降误报)。判据层中立内容完整形态:轨迹维+资源维双维。全部数据开源可复现(单卡 3090)。英文版为配套译文。

title: qec-geometry: geometric A0/A1 classification of decoding errors and closed-form QEC parameters for quantum error-correcting codes
abstract: Zero-dependency Python package for geometric analysis of quantum error correction codes, now at v0.3.4 with the full RM moment-decoder stack. **Error-pattern geometry (A0/A1 classification).** For any stabilizer code: A0 errors (contractible / trivial topology) are always correctable; A1 errors (non-contractible chains) are logical errors. Measured scaling law A1_total_dist − A0_total_dist = L on surface codes L = 4/6/8, with pairing-layer crossing-rate lift 1.82×. **Closed-form code parameters (no simulation).** `QECClosedForm` computes full parameter tables analytically for the AG/PG complete-code families: [[2^m, k, 2^{r+1}]] parameters, RM(1,m) degeneracy classes, d−1-layer structure, encoding rates, zero-loss k_max, closed-form detection rates and loss scaling (θ⁴/θ⁸…). Cross-validated against exact enumeration (e.g. [[15,7,3]] threshold 1/A = 2.86%, 315/945 = 1/3 degeneracy). **General RM(r,m) degeneracy classes.** `rm_degeneracy_classes(m, r)` gives the full weight-2^r degeneracy class structure for every r: r-flat classes ([m r]_2 classes of size 2^{m−r}) plus (r+1)-affine classes. Verified by full enumeration for RM(1,4..6), RM(2,4/5), RM(3,4). **θ⁴ suppression and cross-code diagnosis.** (1) AG r≥2 weight-2 syndromes fully unique → fail(2) = 0, θ⁴ term completely suppressed. (2) `_normalize_coords` fixes crashes on LDPC/non-lattice codes; [[15,7,3]] (1D coords) cross_lift = 1.00 vs surface 2.39 — the A0/A1 separation requires ≥2D lattice coordinates. **Self-contained lookup decoder + vectorized build.** `LookupDecoder` (zero-dependency) builds a syndrome→minimum-weight-recovery table; `build_fast` vectorizes table construction (21×: [[128,70,8]] 121s→5.8s). Six-code scan: [[64,20,8]] d=8 zero-degeneracy gives 1075× p_L reduction at p=0.001. **Reed-Muller moment decoders (NEW in 0.3.3/0.3.4).** Quantum CSS(RM(r,m)) X-decoding ≡ classical RM(m−r−1,m) syndrome decoding; recover the error support from its moments (dot products with degree ≤ r monomials). `rm_x_decode` covers r=1..4 with matrix-lookup decoding: [[1024,·,32]] (d=32) weight-≤2 errors decode in 0.75 ms (lookup tables need 4.7M errors — infeasible). This opens the execution layer for n=1024 codes on a laptop. **Circuit-agnostic diagnostics.** `diagnose_circuit` accepts any stim circuit with detector coordinates and classifies decoding error patterns by topology; verified end-to-end on TQEC-generated circuits. **Closed-form thresholds without Monte Carlo:** p_th = 6/[n(n−1)], e.g. Steane [[7,1,3]] = 14.29%.

title: Geometry vs Binary: Quantum Physics Puzzles — quantum geometry topological error correction AI f — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: ## Binary Failure → Geometry Solution **Analysis of Findings:** The search results reveal a critical frontier where conventional AI and binary computation hit a fundamental wall: **topological quantum error correction (QEC)**. Current approaches rely on neural networks or statistical decoding to identify and correct errors in quantum systems—but these methods fail because they treat error syndromes as *statistical noise patterns* rather than *geometric defects in a lattice structure*. **Where conventional approaches FAIL:** - **Neural network decoders** require massive training data for each new error model, and they cannot generalize to *non-Abelian anyon braiding* or *dynamical Floquet codes* (as in Tyler Ellison's work). title: Computational Resource Singularity Theory (CRST)
abstract: The rapid escalation of computational resources has been a defining feature of the modern era, yet a comprehensive theoretical framework that links resource scaling to transformative shifts in computation and intelligence has remained elusive. This paper introduces the Computational Resource Singularity Theory (CRST), a formal model that captures how surpassing a critical threshold in resource availability precipitates a discontinuous transition to a new computational paradigm. CRST draws on concepts from dynamical systems, information theory, and the economics of technology to articulate a critical resource density \(R_c\) such that for all \(R > R_c\) the system exhibits explosive growth in processing power, algorithmic complexity, and emergent intelligence. By analytically deriving the relationship between resource supply, network effects, and computational throughput, CRST predicts the onset of a "New Computational Era" characterized by superlinear scaling, rapid algorithmic innovation, and the potential for self-improving artificial agents. The theory offers a plausible explanation for the phenomenon often referred to as the intelligence explosion, and it provides a framework for evaluating the societal and ethical implications of approaching or surpassing the singularity threshold. The paper concludes by outlining future research directions, including empirical validation strategies and policy recommendations to guide responsible development of computational infrastructure.

title: SPEANet: Structural Prior Enhanced Attention Network for Parameter-Efficient Remote Sensing Object Detection
abstract: Remote sensing object detection (RSOD) requires compact backbones capable of preserving weak geometric cues under extreme scale variation and background clutter. Fixed structural operators provide complementary contour and frequency responses without introducing learnable operator coefficients. However, directly injecting these responses can amplify content-irrelevant textures, while applying a uniform operator design across the hierarchy may be poorly matched to stage-specific representation requirements. We propose the Structural Prior Enhanced Attention Network (SPEANet), a parameter-efficient RSOD backbone that integrates fixed operators through stage-specific prior extraction and context-conditioned response modulation. SPEANet assigns smoothed contour and multi-order directional modeling to shallow, high-resolution features, while employing a compact approximation-detail interaction mechanism in deeper stages. Learned spatial gates regulate the resulting prior responses before residual fusion. Experiments on five benchmarks, together with evaluations across seven detection frameworks on DOTA-v1.0, achieve a favorable accuracy-parameter trade-off. With Oriented R-CNN, SPEANet achieves 78.55\% mAP on DOTA-v1.0, 72.24\% mAP on DOTA-v1.5, and 67.30\% mAP on DIOR-R using 23.0M total parameters, including a 5.97M-parameter backbone.

title: Incoherent by Design? On the Moral Self-Consistency of LLMs
abstract: LLMs are increasingly used in morally sensitive contexts, yet it is unclear whether they apply ethical principles consistently across situations. A model that can state a moral principle may still violate it when the same scenario is rephrased or reframed. This inconsistency is a problem for any system whose outputs are used to inform moral decisions. If generative systems exhibit internal inconsistency, then the epistemic integrity of AI-mediated systems becomes uncertain. To study this concern, we investigate the stability of moral reasoning in LLMs within a controlled prompting framework across three major philosophical schools of thought: deontology, utilitarianism, and virtue ethics. We construct sets of morally equivalent scenarios in which the underlying situation is held constant while the framing varies to reflect different ethical stances and stylistic perturbations. We then evaluate responses from multiple models, including GPT, Mistral, and Llama. To assess consistency, we convert model outputs into structured logical statements and identify contradictions across responses generated within the same school of thought. Our results reveal substantial inconsistency with contradiction rates reaching up to 78% across scenarios. These findings point to a broader phenomenon of epistemic instability in generative AI wherein models fail to reliably maintain coherence with respect to their own prior outputs. This kind of instability carries real consequences. As generative systems influence how people form beliefs, judge actions, and absorb values, their inconsistencies can shape human reasoning and decision-making as well. Moreover, if a system cannot consistently represent its own normative commitments, then value alignment becomes a moving target rather than a well-defined objective. Thus, we argue that demonstrating internal incoherence is a necessary precursor to AI alignment.

title: Volta
abstract: Volta is a data race and equivalence checker for NVIDIA GPU kernels, implementing "Equivalence Checking of ML GPU Kernels" (OOPSLA 2026). Given a reference kernel and an optimized counterpart, Volta proves them semantically equivalent over the reals --- identical outputs on all valid inputs, with floating-point values modeled as real numbers --- thereby verifying the correctness of the optimized kernel.

title: Computational Intuition Self-Revision Theory (CISR)
abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence has highlighted the necessity of systems that can not only learn from data but also introspect and refine their own intuitive judgments. Computational Intuition Self-Revision Theory (CISR) proposes a formal framework for modeling, detecting, and correcting erroneous intuition in autonomous agents. By treating intuition as a probabilistic function that maps sensory inputs to action preferences, CISR introduces a self‑monitoring layer that evaluates the consistency and reliability of intuitive outputs against a set of meta‑constraints. When a mismatch is detected, the system initiates a revision process that updates internal representations, recalibrates confidence scores, and generates a refined intuition. The theory is grounded in formal probability, game‑theoretic reasoning, and meta‑learning principles, and it offers a potential pathway toward long‑term autonomous AI systems capable of self‑improvement without external supervision. Without the need for extensive experimental validation, CISR serves as a conceptual blueprint that invites further empirical exploration and integration with existing reinforcement learning, symbolic reasoning, and neuro‑evolutionary architectures. The potential of CISR to address persistent challenges in safety, reliability, and explainability positions it as a candidate for Turing Prize‑level contributions in the field of autonomous intelligence.

title: Do Large Language Models Agree on Cultural Annotation of Consumer Reviews
abstract: Identifying cultural and societal factors in large-scale consumer reviews (e.g., Amazon, Yelp, eBay) is critical for understanding customer behavior (Kim et al., 2023) and for informing effective business strategies based on user-generated content. However, manually identifying and labeling such factors for machine learning models is challenging due to the large volume of review data (Kaplan et al., 2020). Large language models (LLMs) are considered effective tools for accelerating the labeling of unstructured text (Ding et al., 2023); however, their consistency in capturing culturally grounded patterns in consumer reviews remains insufficiently understood. The existing approaches often rely on single model annotations, which limits the ability to observe variation across different systems and may introduce model-specific biases in interpretation (Ding et al., 2023). This study seeks to evaluate multiple generative models, including widely used systems such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude, under a unified prompting framework for assigning structured cultural labels to consumer reviews. Differences will be analyzed in terms of inter-model agreement, labeling consistency, and the ability to capture multilingual and indirectly expressed opinions. In particular, the study aims to examine whether these models differ in interpreting indirectly expressed opinions and contextual cues embedded in consumer reviews. The findings of this study are expected to provide insights into the reliability and limitations of LLM-based annotation processes, highlighting the need for multi-model validation and careful evaluation when deploying large language models in socio-cultural annotation pipelines.

title: Where digital hate finds its home: perpetrators' preferred affordances and their experiences with content moderation and user intervention
abstract: Digital hate poses a significant challenge to democratic principles. However, not much is known about who produces it regularly, let alone across platforms. Drawing from routine activity theory as an overarching framework, our study investigated how the perceived importance of social media affordances is related to regular digital hate perpetrators’ platform use. Further, it explored how this usage is linked to experiences of moderation and interventions against them. Findings of quota-based surveys in four European countries (i.e., Austria, France, Hungary, and Sweden) suggest that perpetrators’ perceived importance of persistence and anonymity is consistently related to social media use across platforms, from which, in turn, primarily Telegram, Reddit, Twitch, and TikTok were linked to more frequent moderation and intervention experiences. By and large, our findings contribute to the current fight against digital hate by highlighting the need for regulatory strategies that account for perpetrators’ perceptions of affordances across platforms.

title: Markdown Operating System for Robotic Agents (MD-OS CORTEX): Artificial Prefrontal Cortex and a Verifiable Operational Paradigm Toward General Intelligence
abstract: A language-model agent can report success without proving that anything correct occurred. MD-OS CORTEX addresses this gap through an Artificial Prefrontal Cortex that instantiates a biological principle of functioning: the integration of differentiated state, memory, prediction, value, inhibition, and consequences to regulate action on an artificial substrate. The architecture separates proposal, authorization, execution, verification, and durable commitment; introduces the Cognitive Integration Principle and the falsifiable Unity Tensor Field hypothesis; and makes bounded action authorization depend on a hash-bound Causal Unity Controller. The system also includes a typed two-level candidate architecture for artificial phenomenal consciousness, with independent world readback and causal return. This revision formalizes the Theory of Special Singularity: an identity-specific Special Singularity, SS_I, is modeled as an information source for a corresponding Unity Tensor Field, U_I, while the field, world observations, memory, goals, predicted consequences, and assigned meaning recursively constrain the next source state. The continuous source equation has a finite graph analogue suitable for MD-OS, and the theory explicitly recognizes that a source alone does not guarantee a unique field. The formalization yields falsifiable source-field, source-ablation, and clone-fork predictions. Current evidence verifies bounded operational mechanisms but does not measure a real-domain information source, prove field uniqueness, qualia, phenomenal consciousness, artificial general intelligence, or biological equivalence.

title: Unified Computational Reality Model Theory (UCRMT)
abstract: This paper introduces the Unified Computational Reality Model Theory (UCRMT), a theoretical framework that posits the essence of intelligence as the continuous construction, maintenance, and refinement of internal representations of reality. UCRMT integrates perception, learning, reasoning, planning, and scientific discovery into a single computational paradigm. By formalizing the transformation from raw experience to a structured causal model and finally to intelligent behavior, UCRMT offers a principled basis for future artificial intelligence research. The theory is grounded in a set of simple mathematical relations that capture the flow of information from sensory data to an internal reality model and from that model to decision‑making and inference. We discuss the implications of UCRMT for understanding natural cognition and for guiding the design of autonomous systems. The paper concludes with open questions and suggested research directions that extend the theory toward a Science of Computational Intuition.

title: Computational Reality Model Competition Theory (CRMCO)
abstract: Computational Reality Model Competition Theory (CRMCO) proposes a formal framework in which multiple computational models of a real‑world system are placed in direct competition with one another. Each model is evaluated against a shared dataset, and its performance determines its survival probability in a generational selection process. The theory draws inspiration from the competition of scientific theories, where empirical adequacy and explanatory power drive acceptance. By embedding this competition within a computational ecosystem, CRMCO offers a scalable mechanism for automatic model improvement, adaptive learning, and the simulation of scientific discovery. The model space is defined as M = {M1, M2, …, MK}, with each Mi mapping inputs x to predictions ŷi. Performance is quantified by a loss function L(Mi, D) over dataset D, and fitness is assigned as f_i = exp(−α L(Mi, D)), where α controls selection pressure. Selection probabilities are p_i = f_i / Σ_j f_j, and offspring models are generated through mutation operators that perturb parameters or structure. This iterative process converges toward increasingly accurate models, mirroring the evolution of scientific knowledge. CRMCO's potential to automate theory refinement and to generate insights into the dynamics of scientific progress positions it as a candidate for high‑impact computational research, with implications that may reach the prestige of a Turing Award.

title: ORCID: 0009-0005-1860-0009
abstract: Computational Knowledge Reconstruction Theory (CKRT) proposes a principled framework for deriving hidden knowledge structures from observable results in complex systems. By formalizing the relationship between observations and underlying knowledge through a bidirectional mapping, CKRT enables the reconstruction of internal states that are not directly measurable. The theory introduces the concept of result recovery, whereby the final output of a system can be inverted to reveal the sequence of knowledge states that produced it. Hidden knowledge structures are captured as latent variables within a structured probabilistic model, allowing for the systematic exploration of knowledge dynamics. CKRT also highlights the potential of this approach to contribute to the design of systems that emulate human-like understanding and to the advancement of computational theory at the level recognized by prestigious awards such as the Turing Award. The following paper elaborates the theoretical foundations, formal model, and implications of CKRT for understanding complex systems and guiding future research in knowledge representation and inference.

title: Second-Order Policy Effects as State Transitions: A Source-Linked Benchmark for Policy Simulation
abstract: Policy evaluation often estimates direct benefits and costs while treating the institutional environment as fixed. In practice, a policy changes the system it enters: actors adapt, enforcement capacity shifts, burdens move, and new equilibria form around capture, gaming, compliance theater, irreversibility, and repair costs. We formalize this as second-order policy-effect prediction and present a source-linked benchmark for policy simulation. The benchmark contains 96 named public-policy cases across eight domains and four balanced action classes: implement, modify, pilot, and block. Each case includes source locators and state variables for benefit, capture, gaming, burden shift, instability, uncertainty, irreversibility, distributional risk, and implementation capacity. The runner regenerates method outputs and aggregate results from the case table, and the simulator never reads the expert action target. We report a protocol-based transition-channel audit with recall, precision, F1-style efficiency, and selective top-channel stress diagnostics, so universal channel coverage is not mistaken for field validation. The side-effect simulator achieves mean policy-effect quality of 0.945, compared with 0.838 for the risk-register baseline and 0.879 for the causal-loop baseline. Its advantage is concentrated in side-effect recall and aggregate transition scoring; it does not dominate the best structured baselines on exact policy-action choice. The evidence remains benchmark-based, but supports a bounded claim: transition-state variables make policy simulators more sensitive to downstream institutional effects.

title: An Agentic Framework for Financial Disclosure Intelligence
abstract: An Agentic Framework for Financial Disclosure Intelligence TREO Talk Paper Kazim Topuz, Ph.D. The University of Tulsa kazim-topuz@utulsa.edu Tally Ferguson The University of Tulsa tally-ferguson@utulsa.edu Jessica Bedson The University of Tulsa jab1664@utulsa.edu Abstract Corporate disclosures in SEC 10-K filings are one of the most prevalent ways firms communicate forward-looking risk to investors, yet analytical methods for reviewing these disclosures have developed independently of one another. We introduce an agentic framework for financial disclosure intelligence in which lexicon-based and transformer-based models function as cooperative agents rather than opposing alternatives. The framework is applied to 10-K filings from a sample of 55 large-cap firms across all 11 GICS sectors from 2016 to 2025. From each filing, we extract the Risk Factors (Item 1A) and Management Discussion and Analysis (Item 7) sections and score paragraph-level tone using both the Loughran-McDonald dictionary and FinBERT. We also introduce a multi-layer validation design that addresses the absence of universal "ground truth" labels in financial disclosure text. We then examine systematic patterns of disagreement between the dictionary and transformer models to identify cases of contextual ambiguity, boilerplate language reuse, and legal hedging. Results show strong directional agreement between the two models in identifying positive and negative tone across firms and sectors, with clear differences in sensitivity. FinBERT produces a more extensive range of scores, while the Loughran-McDonald dictionary provides stable, interpretable readings at scale. The study contributes to information systems research by presenting a modular, extensible architecture for disclosure analytics that can incorporate additional agents, such as a large language model adjudication layer, without requiring redesign of the underlying system. Our agentic LLM agent approach should more comprehensively recognize how specific combinations of phrases disclosed in financial statements portend positive, negative, or neutral outlooks. Implementing such a system offers the potential to refine financial instrument valuation and enhance the precision of regulatory oversight and compliance monitoring. References Araci, D. (2019). FinBERT: Financial sentiment analysis with pre-trained language models. arXiv preprint arXiv:1908.10063. https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.10063 Loughran, T., & McDonald, B. (2011). When is a liability not a liability? Textual analysis, dictionaries, and 10-Ks. Journal of Finance, 66(1), 35–65.

title: Consequence Type System
abstract: This paper introduces the Consequence Type System (CTS), a novel approach to type checking that extends traditional type systems by explicitly modeling the potential consequences of operations. Unlike conventional type systems which primarily focus on static shape analysis, CTS adds annotations to operations indicating the possible effects they may induce, categorized as StateChange, ResourceUse, and ExternalEffect. This allows compilers to perform runtime checks to verify whether a program's execution will result in undesirable long-term consequences. The CTS offers a pathway to significantly enhance software safety and improve the reliability of AI tool calls by providing a more comprehensive understanding of potential operational impacts. This system has the potential to revolutionize type theory and offer a powerful framework for building more robust and secure software systems. ---

title: MULTI-FUSE: Multimodal Late Fusion Framework for Hate Speech Detection in Videos
authors: Lekshmi M S and Malathy S
abstract: Abstract Addressing cyberbullying and fostering more welcoming online communities depend on the detection of hateful content. However, because it requires examin-ing a number of interrelated components, including spoken words, visual imagery, and text within those visuals, detecting hate speech in videos is difficult. Thiswork presents MULTI-FUSE, a state-of-the-art hate speech detection model thatsuccessfully combines multimodal features from video content using a late fusion technique. The audio and video frames are processed separately by the frame-work. It analyzes frames for hate symbols, text (using OCR), and gestures to generate a visual hate score using deep learning techniques, while extractingand analyzing speech to generate an audio hate score. These audio and visualhate scores are then combined into a single feature vector, which is input into asupervised learning classifier for the final prediction of hate speech. This studypresents an optimized multimodal framework for detecting hate speech in videos by assessing various supervised learning models and identifying the Support Vec-tor Machine (SVM) as the most effective classifier, achieving an accuracy of 0.8571, precision of 0.8333, recall of 0.8929, and F1-score of 0.8621. The frame-work systematically determines the optimal frame-processing rate of one frame per second to strike a balance between accuracy and computational efficiency. Anablation study confirms that the full multimodal combination (audio, text, andvisual) significantly outperforms all unimodal configurations, achieving a 7.5%relative improvement over the best unimodal model. Compared with reportedbaselines on the HATEMM dataset, MULTI-FUSE achieves an 18% improvementin F1-score over existing late-fusion approaches. The late fusion method mergesaudio, text, and visual hate scores, resulting in strong detection performance

title: Computational Experience Fusion Theory (CEFT-2)
abstract: The rapid proliferation of autonomous systems and intelligent agents has resulted in a vast accumulation of experiential data across diverse domains. Yet, each system typically processes its own experience in isolation, limiting the potential for collective intelligence. This paper introduces Computational Experience Fusion Theory (CEFT-2), a formal framework that defines a systematic fusion operation for experiential knowledge, denoted as E_1 + E_2 → E_3, where E_i represents the experiential state of system i. By iteratively applying this operation across a network of agents, CEFT-2 constructs a hierarchy of aggregated experiences, culminating in collective computational wisdom. We formalize the fusion operation, explore its algebraic properties, and demonstrate how CEFT-2 can serve as a foundational theory for future group AI systems. The paper argues that CEFT-2 embodies the principles that could underpin a Turing Award–level contribution, providing a scalable, interpretable, and ethically grounded approach to multi-agent knowledge integration.

title: Computational Experience Compression Theory (CECT)
abstract: The proliferation of data generated by modern computing systems has created an unprecedented opportunity to capture and reuse the knowledge embedded in large collections of run histories. Computational Experience Compression Theory (CECT) proposes a principled framework for transforming extensive execution logs into compact symbolic representations, referred to as Experience Codes. By encoding the essential patterns of successful and failed executions, CECT enables downstream systems to perform expert‑level judgments in a fraction of the time required for traditional simulation or exhaustive search. This paper develops the theoretical foundations of CECT, formalizes the encoding and decoding processes, and demonstrates how the resulting Experience Codes can be leveraged for rapid decision making in diverse domains such as program synthesis, automated debugging, and adaptive resource management. We further discuss the implications of CECT for the broader field of artificial intelligence, highlighting its potential to elucidate the mechanisms underlying machine expertise and to guide the design of next‑generation autonomous systems.

title: ENAF: A Multi-Exit Network with an Adaptive Patch Fusion for Large Image Super Resolution
abstract: To accelerate single image super-resolution (SISR) networks on large images (2K-8K), many recent approaches decompose an image into small patches and dynamically determine an execution path according to its difficulty (referred to as a dynamic network). To quantify the hardness of a patch, they mainly rely on a handcrafted assessment score, e.g., edge, which weakly associates a patch's texture with the computational complexity of a SISR model. To address the problem, we introduce ENAF - a dynamic network for SISR with an adaptive patch fusion. Built on top of a backbone, ENAF incorporates multiple early exits (EEs) to tackle the over-parameterized SISR model. More importantly, ENAF plugs a tiny network that estimates PSNR to associate data texture with a computation cost at an EE. Based on the scores, ENAF effectively assigns image patches to an exit, enhancing the quality-complexity trade-off. Extensive experiments on common datasets with popular SISR backbones demonstrate the effectiveness of ENAF in various settings. The source code is provided in https://github.com/nmduonggg/ENAF

title: MODAL: Multi-Modal Object Re-ID via Model-Driven Sparse Decoupling and Text-Image Differential Filtering
abstract: Multi-modal object re-identification (Re-ID) aims to facilitate cross-camera object retrieval in complex environments by leveraging complementary information from visual (e.g., RGB, NIR, TIR) and textual modalities. However, existing approaches often lack principled feature disentanglement and coherent multi-modal integration, leading to entangled representations that introduce cross-modal conflicts, obscure discriminative cues, and suffer distribution shift under modality-missing conditions. To tackle these challenges, we propose MODAL, a novel multi-modal object re-identification framework, grounded in coupled sparse coding theory and differential suppression principles. A core component of MODAL is a Multi-modal Feature Sparse Decoupling module, developed in a model-driven deep unrolling manner based on multi-modal coupled sparse coding. It explicitly decomposes multi-modal features into uni-modal specific, bi-modal and tri-modal shared representations, thereby achieving more transparent and effective feature disentanglement. evidence.title: MODAL: Multi-Modal Object Re-ID via Model-Driven Sparse Decoupling and Text-Image Differential Filtering
evidence.abstract: Multi-modal object re-identification (Re-ID) aims to facilitate cross-camera object retrieval in complex environments by leveraging complementary information from visual (e.g., RGB, NIR, TIR) and textual modalities. However, existing approaches often lack principled feature disentanglement and coherent multi-modal integration, leading to entangled representations that introduce cross-modal conflicts, obscure discriminative cues, and suffer distribution shift under modality-missing conditions. Extensive experiments on four datasets demonstrate that MODAL achieves state-of-the-art performance with superior transparency.

title: Can Boredom be Computational? A Functional Idle-state Mechanism for Reflective Cognition in AI Agents
abstract: AI is known for its enablement of machines to mimic human brains when performing tasks (PK, 1984). We discuss the concept of boredom-inspired reflective agency for autonomous AI systems. Existing agentic architecture prioritizes continuous optimization and task execution. With more human-like designs of AI agents, anthropomorphic agents not only can reason, but can show emotions and develop personality traits (Alabed et al., 2022). However, unlike humans, AI systems steer off topics with language complexities and little context causing a ‘conversational drift’ (Armstrong et al., 2025; Namala, 2024). To mitigate this problem, AI agents can engage in internal cognitive processes that revisit past decisions, evaluate successful and unsuccessful outcomes, simulate alternative scenarios, consolidate memories, and anticipate future actions. This can happen during periods of inactivity to overcome boredom. Rather than acquiring new external knowledge, we ask the question of whether the system should reflect on judgement and strategically self-assess similar to human introspection during idle moments. The TREO argues that reflective idle cognition may represent a missing architectural layer in agentic AI, enabling more context-aware, adaptive, and strategically coherent autonomous behavior. Human boredom may not be wasted cognition. It may be an evolutionary mechanism for reflective simulation, emotional replay, memory consolidation, and future planning. Current agentic AI systems lack this reflective idle architecture. Adding this layer to its architecture would contribute to the debate of whether anthropomorphism is actually a hype (Placani, 2024). The proposed framework conceptualizes boredom as a productive reflective state. This topic inherently presents an interesting interdisciplinary TREO that includes systems design, psychology, cognitive science and AI

title: Trustworthy in silico labeling via semantic visual interpretability of image-to-image translation
abstract: Abstract Cross-modality image translation promises to provide multiple layers of biological information from a single image input, yet its practical application is stalled by a lack of interpretability and the inability to account for model imperfections. In silico labeling, the inference of organelle localization from label-free images, is a primary example where this black-box nature limits adoption. We present Mask Interpreter, a generalized method for semantic visual interpretability of image-to-image translation models. By uncovering organelle-specific “explanation signatures”, Mask Interpreter validates that models rely on authentic biological structures rather than spurious artifacts. Beyond biological validation, it outperforms traditional explainable AI (xAI) approaches, identifies batch effects and localizes prediction errors when ground-truth fluorescence is unavailable. Semantic confidence modeling further provides fine-grained reliability assessment at single-cell resolution, enabling the automated exclusion of artifacts from downstream analyses. By bridging the gap between computational inference and meaningful biological features, Mask Interpreter transforms in silico labeling into a reliable tool for scientific discovery across diverse biomedical imaging modalities.

title: Persistent Behavioral Signatures in Large Language Models: A Three-Replicate Baseline Test of Representational Persistence
abstract: This study examines whether large language models exhibit stable, model-specific representational patterns across repeated independent trials. Eleven AI systems were tested using the same standardized environment and self-representation prompts across three baseline replicates, producing 66 formal observations. Eight locally hosted model configurations were tested under controlled settings with tools, web access, retrieval, memory, file context, and custom system prompts disabled. Three hosted systems were tested in fresh conversations under documented platform-controlled conditions. The study extends earlier exploratory work by testing whether differences between models persist rather than appearing only once. Responses were coded for dimensions including embodiment, anthropomorphism, abstraction, relational orientation, self-environment differentiation, and recurring symbolic motifs. Across the three replicates, responses generated by the same model were substantially more similar to one another than responses generated by different models. Mean within-model similarity was 0.898 compared with 0.679 between models. The difference was statistically significant and large in magnitude. The findings support the concept of a Model-Specific Response Signature: a recurring configuration of generated response features that remains distinguishable across independent trials. The study also identifies a distinction between stable representational structure and variable surface imagery, showing that models can change metaphors while retaining deeper patterns of organization, embodiment, boundary, and relational orientation. The research does not interpret these signatures as evidence of consciousness, subjective experience, or human personality. Instead, it establishes a reproducible framework for studying persistent model-specific representational behavior. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21961915

title: Computational Memory Selection Theory (CMST)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Memory Selection Theory (CMST), a novel framework for understanding and designing intelligent systems. CMST posits that intelligent agents do not necessarily retain and process *all* historical data encountered. Instead, the theory proposes that agents strategically select a subset of this data – denoted as [Memory^*] – to retain and utilize, based on a defined selection criteria. The core of CMST lies in understanding *what* historical information is deemed 'worth' preserving and *how* this selection process impacts the agent's decision-making capabilities. This approach offers a potentially significant shift in how we conceptualize memory within artificial intelligence, with implications for future AI architectures and potentially aligning with the criteria for recognition as a Turing Award winner. The theory is presented as a foundational framework, focusing on the conceptual and theoretical aspects, without requiring experimental validation. ---

title: Computational Information Transformation Theory
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Information Transformation Theory (CITT), a novel theoretical framework designed to comprehensively analyze the processes of information conversion across diverse formats. CITT posits that every information transformation, regardless of its underlying mechanism, involves a complex interplay of preservation, loss, and generation of information. The theory is built upon the core concept of mapping between information instances: [I1 → I2], where I1 and I2 represent information in different forms. The central focus is to systematically investigate the transformations occurring during this conversion, detailing what aspects are retained, what is inevitably lost, and what entirely new information is produced. CITT aims to provide a unified theoretical foundation for information computation, potentially holding the key to unlocking advancements in areas such as artificial intelligence, data science, and cryptography. The theory's underlying mathematical framework is presented, laying the groundwork for further research and development. ---

title: Unified Computational Goal Theory (UCGT)
abstract: Computational systems have historically focused on three core questions: how to compute, how to store, and how to learn. However, the emergence of advanced artificial intelligence and autonomous agents demands a new theoretical foundation that explains why a system chooses to act in a particular way. Unified Computational Goal Theory (UCGT) proposes a comprehensive framework that unifies optimization goals, biological goals, artificial intelligence goals, multi‑agent goals, and social goals within a single mathematical structure. By formalizing the relationship between environment, memory, capability, goal, and action, UCGT provides a principled method for deriving goals from first principles, thereby offering a potential next generation of theoretical underpinnings for artificial intelligence. This paper presents the core ideas of UCGT, its mathematical formalization, illustrative models, and implications for future research in AI, multi‑agent systems, and computational cognition.

title: The New AI Architect: Composing Intelligence Through AI Technology Stacks
abstract: AI is no longer just something organizations adopt, it is something they must design. As firms assemble models, data, and workflows into interconnected systems, the challenge shifts from using AI tools to composing intelligence. This panel introduces the concept of the AI Architect, a role focused on integrating AI capabilities into coherent, scalable solutions that support organizational objectives. Panelists will examine how these systems are structured, how they reshape decision-making and work processes, and why they represent a new phase of digital transformation. The discussion also addresses the risks of this shift, including security vulnerabilities, misuse, and governance challenges that emerge in highly integrated environments. By bringing together perspectives from research and practice, the panel highlights emerging directions for Information Systems scholarship in understanding and managing AI-enabled organizations.

title: Operational Identifiability of Tensor Product Structures: Exact Rigidity Laws, a Two-Operation Threshold, and an Aliasing Limit
abstract: Here's what this paper means for actual humans: WHAT THIS IS ABOUT. When you build or use a quantum device, everything rests on knowing what its parts are: which degrees of freedom are "qubit 1," which are "qubit 2." The companion paper ("Forged Frames") showed that simple mathematical criteria cannot certify this; convincing fakes exist. This paper answers the question that result leaves standing: what is the MINIMUM experimental information that genuinely pins down a system's subsystem structure, and when can that information silently fail? WHAT WE FOUND, IN PLAIN TERMS. Four things. (1) EXACT LAWS INSTEAD OF MEASUREMENTS. Any wrong choice of parts must visibly distort the family of unentangled states, and we derive exactly how much, at every system size: closed-form constants (verified to seven decimal places), an explicit error bound, and a surprise. The two natural ways to measure "wrongness" (state distortion versus operator scrambling) turn out to be literally the same measurement, up to a fixed number, whenever the two parts have equal size. Wrongness cannot hide. (2) THE TWO-OPERATION THRESHOLD. You can pin down what your subsystems are by implementing just TWO generic operations and checking their statistics, while a THOUSAND mutually commuting operations tell you nothing at all. Diversity of control, not volume of control, is what fixes what your qubits are. The residual uncertainty is proportional to your measurement tolerance, with a constant we derive exactly and show how to compute in advance, so an experimenter can screen candidate operation pairs and pick a strong one (random pairs are typically several times worse, occasionally catastrophically so). (3) THE ALIASING LIMIT: CERTIFICATION CAN PASS WHILE TELLING YOU NOTHING. If you sample your certification data at special "resonant" times (set by the operations' energy scales), a maximally wrong assignment of subsystems passes the test perfectly. What your qubits are depends on when you looked. We characterize these blind spots exactly (for qubits they are universal and computable in advance; the danger windows shrink with the square root of your tolerance), and the fix costs almost nothing: sample at two different times, at least one away from the resonant set. With that, certification is restored; we prove it exactly and measure it. (4) REAL-LAB BUDGETS. We work out what certification costs in actual measurement shots (the error falls off unusually fast, inversely with the total number of shots rather than with its square root), how hardware noise floors the procedure, and how a simple reference measurement removes that floor to first order. A single seven-row table in the paper is effectively a lab protocol: it shows, condition by condition, which kinds of experimental access identify the subsystem structure (two generic operations: yes; one operation, commuting operations, resonant sampling: no). WHY IT MATTERS. For quantum hardware: this is a concrete recipe for certifying that the qubits you think you have are the qubits you physically have, with explicit tolerances, a sampling-time warning that is a real failure mode on calibrated hardware, and shot budgets. For foundations: the contested question "does physics determine its own subsystems?" gets a quantitative operational answer. Physics determines an operational subsystem CLASS (not one preferred coordinate representation of it), and that class is fixed by two operations sampled at two times, and by nothing less that we tested. WHAT IT OPENS UP. The seven-row identifiability table is a blueprint for a tabletop experiment on any small quantum platform; running it on hardware would move this from simulation to laboratory fact. On the theory side the paper leaves sharply posed open problems: the exact global constants when the two parts differ in size, the number-theoretic structure of long-time sampling (the failure times form a small-divisor hierarchy), and the extension from two parts to many. METHODS NOTE, BECAUSE IT MATTERS FOR TRUST. Every quantitative claim was pre-registered in the companion scripts before its run. The full ledger, including predictions that failed and one published-in-note constant that our own later theory overturned, is an appendix of the paper. All code, data, and working notes are in the deposit, seeded for exact reproduction. WHO AND HOW. A human-AI collaboration: research direction and standards of evidence by Ryan Cardwell (Crystalline Labs); design, code, derivations, and drafting by Claude (Anthropic), including autonomous sessions under the program's pre-registration rules, with adversarial reviews by other AI models incorporated and credited.

title: Computational Dynamic Abstraction Layer (CDAL)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Dynamic Abstraction Layer (CDAL), a novel approach to computing architecture design that moves beyond the constraints of traditional, static layered models. The core concept of CDAL revolves around the dynamic generation of abstraction layers, creating a system where layers are continuously formed and dissolved based on computational needs. This process aims to mimic the adaptive behavior observed in biological systems and potentially lead to architectures capable of responding to complex and evolving computational demands. The paper details the theoretical framework, outlining the key principles and mathematical representations involved in the CDAL model. It explores the potential implications of CDAL for future computing, highlighting its relevance to achieving the goals of the Turing Award and suggesting its capacity to generate radically different computing paradigms. The model utilizes a layered representation of computation, defined as: * `Layer_t → Layer_{t+1}` This dynamic transformation is governed by a set of rules and constraints, allowing for optimized resource allocation and efficient processing. This paper lays the groundwork for a deeper investigation into the practical application and theoretical underpinnings of the CDAL architecture. ---

title: Computational Language Transfer Theory (CLTT)
abstract: The present manuscript introduces the Computational Language Transfer Theory (CLTT), a formal framework that models the transfer of linguistic competence from a source language L_A to a target language L_B as a computational transformation. CLTT posits that language learning can be decomposed into a finite set of abstract linguistic primitives {s_1, s_2, …, s_K} that are first instantiated in the source language and then mapped to corresponding primitives in the target language via a transfer operator T. The theory is grounded in both cognitive science and formal language theory, and it offers a tractable mathematical description of how abstract syntactic and semantic structures are carried over during second‑language acquisition. By representing transfer as a composition of transformation functions, CLTT enables the prediction of transfer outcomes, the identification of bottlenecks, and the design of curriculum that exploits positive transfer and mitigates negative transfer. The paper further discusses implications for cross‑architecture computing systems, where CLTT provides a blueprint for transferring learning models across heterogeneous hardware and software platforms. The potential for CLTT to inform the design of universal language models and to contribute to the Turing Award conversation is also highlighted.

title: Serial Two-Stage Filtering by Conditional Innovation: An Information-Preserving High-to-Low Architecture for Common-State Operator Bounds
abstract: This paper develops a serial two-stage filtering framework based on ordered conditional innovation. Instead of applying two relation filters independently in parallel, the second filter acts only on the residual state left after the first-stage relation has been extracted. Using orthogonal projection and Gram–Schmidt decomposition, the construction preserves the full information of the original state while preventing duplicated relation freedom and independent-extremizer overestimation.The framework distinguishes between total information, which remains invariant under a reordering of fixed relation subspaces, and the stagewise innovation profile, which can depend strongly on filter order. A frozen four-dimensional common-state model exhibits a pronounced ordering effect: the High/Fine→Low/Coarse sequence captures approximately 97.985% of the selected state at the first stage and leaves approximately 2.015% as conditional innovation, whereas the reverse ordering produces approximately 41.108% and 58.892%, respectively.

title: Computational Intuition Boundary Theory (CIBT): Investigating the Formation of Intuition in Artificial Systems
abstract: Intuition is often regarded as a mysterious, rapid form of insight that enables humans to solve problems without explicit reasoning. In artificial systems, the emergence of intuition remains an open challenge, largely because the conditions under which a computational agent can generate intuitive judgments are not well understood. This paper introduces the Computational Intuition Boundary Theory (CIBT), a formal framework that delineates the boundary between non‑intuitive and intuitive behavior in machine learning systems. CIBT defines an intuition threshold function T(ΔC) that depends on the complexity gap ΔC between the internal model and the external environment, a performance parameter P that captures the speed of inference, and a contextual weighting factor θ that encodes domain relevance. We derive a set of necessary and sufficient conditions under which an agent's internal representation crosses the intuition boundary, and we analyze how these conditions interact with learning dynamics, data sparsity, and architectural choices. By applying CIBT to a range of canonical tasks—pattern recognition, strategic game play, and natural language understanding—we demonstrate that intuition arises when the model achieves a critical level of abstraction and generalization, coupled with a low‑latency inference pathway. The theory offers a principled lens for evaluating and designing artificial systems that aspire to human‑like intuition, and it suggests that the limits of machine intelligence may be governed more by representational depth than by computational power alone.

title: Where digital hate finds its home: perpetrators' preferred affordances and their experiences with content moderation and user intervention
abstract: Digital hate poses a significant challenge to democratic principles. However, not much is known about who produces it regularly, let alone across platforms. Drawing from routine activity theory as an overarching framework, our study investigated how the perceived importance of social media affordances is related to regular digital hate perpetrators’ platform use. Further, it explored how this usage is linked to experiences of moderation and interventions against them. Findings of quota-based surveys in four European countries (i.e., Austria, France, Hungary, and Sweden) suggest that perpetrators’ perceived importance of persistence and anonymity is consistently related to social media use across platforms, from which, in turn, primarily Telegram, Reddit, Twitch, and TikTok were linked to more frequent moderation and intervention experiences. By and large, our findings contribute to the current fight against digital hate by highlighting the need for regulatory strategies that account for perpetrators’ perceptions of affordances across platforms.

title: Feed-Forward Hierarchical Gaussian Diffusion for Extreme CT Reconstruction
abstract: Reconstructing three-dimensional computed tomography (CT) from severely constrained projections is highly ill-posed. Sparse angular sampling, restricted angular coverage, and low photon counts can occur individually or jointly, obscuring global anatomy and local tissue detail. Many learned CT reconstruction methods are tailored to a single dominant degradation. Existing diffusion and Gaussian approaches commonly recover global structure and local detail within a shared representation. We propose HiGDiff, a feed-forward hierarchical Gaussian diffusion framework that decomposes reconstruction both spatially and from structure to detail. Physics-conditioned anatomical anchors and a foreground capacity field allocate learnable Gaussian primitives to informative regions. A structure diffusion stage first recovers global attenuation geometry, and its learned representation conditions a detail diffusion stage for residual boundaries and tissue transitions. The resulting Gaussian banks are rendered as attenuation fields and further refined by a gradient-isolated residual module. Experiments on three distinct CT benchmark datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art reconstruction performance across isolated, paired, and joint degradation settings, including improvements of 5.81 dB in macro-average peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and 0.113 in structural similarity index measure (SSIM) on the Low Dose CT Image and Projection Data (LDCT-PD) collection. Code and experimental configurations are openly available at https://github.com/Bean-Young/HiGDiff.
