title: WeSCE: A Benchmark for Measuring Security Drift in LLM-Driven Code Editing
abstract: In this work, we introduce WeSCE, a benchmark for quantifying security drift in code editing under weak-security constraints, where tasks specify only functional objectives without explicit security requirements. WeSCE consists of 400 executable programs derived from real-world code, covering feature addition, feature removal, bug fixing, and refactoring. To quantify security drift, we propose a continuous risk representation that aggregates heterogeneous vulnerability signals through a unified formulation, and define drift measures capturing changes in overall risk, worst-case severity, and vulnerability distribution under code transformations, providing a multi-scale view of security spanning average-case behavior to worst-case emphasis.

title: Evaluating Trajectories in Agentic Systems
abstract: As agentic systems increasingly incorporate multi-step processes, evaluation remains focused on predictive accuracy rather than process structure. This creates a gap in understanding how decisions are formed, particularly in systems that integrate multiple components. This gap is particularly critical in decision support contexts, where understanding how decisions are formed is as important as the decisions themselves. This work proposes a structural evaluation framework for intelligent agentic systems based on sequence and network analysis. Execution is modeled as state sequences and as dynamic interaction graphs, where nodes represent processes and control states, and edges represent transitions during decision formation. Sequence similarity is analyzed using Optimal Matching (OM) distance to assess stability and consistency of trajectories. Network-based measures, including centrality and motif frequency, are used to characterize coordination patterns, control structures, and progression toward decision commitment. Unlike traditional evaluation approaches, the framework explicitly models and evaluates the structure of execution processes rather than relying solely on outcome-based metrics. The framework is domain-agnostic and can be applied to a broad class of agentic and multi-step decision systems. The study contributes a structural evaluation perspective for intelligent agentic systems, shifting assessment from predictive outcomes to the organization and dynamics of processes. This is particularly relevant for emerging agentic systems that involve iterative planning, tool use, and multi-stage execution.

title: Make the LLMs Argue: Quorum, a Deliberation Protocol with Dissent Preserved
abstract: For high-stakes, ambiguous questions (strategy, pricing, architecture, risk) a single language model produces a confident answer with no visibility into its blind spots, and nothing in its fluency distinguishes a robust conclusion from a well-phrased guess. The disagreement between independent models is the best available signal of genuine uncertainty, and today it is thrown away: merged into consensus summaries that destroy precisely the information worth collecting. This paper presents Quorum, an open-source deliberation protocol that convenes three models from distinct labs to answer a question in enforced isolation, critique each other claim by claim under blind labels, revise, and hand a non-debating arbiter the job of delivering a verdict with dissent preserved. The protocol makes an unusual bet. It does not claim better answers, since the evidence for that is modest and task-dependent, and a three-arm benchmark (council vs. single model vs. self-critique) exists to test rather than assume it. It claims calibration material: the transcript is the product. Anonymization is structural rather than cosmetic. Students exchange rigid answer sheets of numbered claims, not prose, so style signal is never generated in the first place; the critique round has no field for agreement; and position changes are computed by the engine rather than taken from the models' own declarations. Independence constraints live in the type system, sessions fail closed per round, and every session emits a replay-complete JSONL trace from which the entire deliberation (positions, objections, diffs, absences, verdict) can be reconstructed. The engine is complete, with 330 tests and protocol invariants enforced by construction. Live mixed-lab councils (Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepSeek) have been run and measured: a 33% position-change rate inside the 15-60% design band, 13 preserved minority items, and two targets missed and reported as findings, namely 77% claim compliance against a 90% target and a 23.7x session cost against a designed 8x guardrail, with the arbiter measured at 69% of a session's bill. A convening rule that fails closed keeps councils rare: 9.3% of a 43-task mixed workload convenes. The deanonymization probe and the benchmark harness are built and tested but have run only against mocks, which their own output labels as proving nothing about models; the numbers will be published whatever they say. The paper closes with limitations stated where users meet them, and a roadmap that consists of measurement rather than code. Canonical version and illustrated protocol walkthrough: https://sheepdog.systemsCode, evals, committed live traces, and full findings: https://github.com/JoaquinDG/quorum

title: Harmonic Frontier Audio - Breathing Cycles and Physiological Patterns (Preview Pack, v0.9)
abstract: Harmonic Frontier Audio – Breathing Cycles and Physiological Patterns (Preview, v0.9) A high-fidelity human vocal dataset designed for AI training, speech research, and expressive voice modeling. Breathing Cycles and Physiological Patterns (Preview), created by Harmonic Frontier Audio, provides a compact reference set demonstrating the quality, formatting, and metadata conventions used in the Harmonic Frontier Audio Human Vocality Primitives series. 🔎 Summary This dataset provides high-quality, rights-cleared recordings of natural breathing cycles and physiological airflow patterns — non-lexical respiratory behaviors captured as isolated human acoustic primitives for expressive audio modeling. The recordings emphasize: relaxed and deeper inhale–exhale cycles slow, extended, and meditative breathing faster and shallow respiratory patterns brief inhale and exhale holds irregular breathing and reset breaths These characteristics make the dataset valuable for AI speech modeling, expressive voice synthesis, breath-aware generative audio, physiological sound modeling, and human-aligned vocal control systems. Developed by Harmonic Frontier Audio, this preview follows The Proteus Standard™ for dataset provenance, transparency, and ethical AI use.Learn more about the Proteus Standard → https://harmonicfrontieraudio.com/proteus-standard Full dataset details and licensing information are available at:https://harmonicfrontieraudio.com/datasets/breathing-cycles-physiological-patterns If you find this dataset useful, please consider giving it a 🤍 on Hugging Face to help others discover it. 🌬️ About Breathing Cycles and Physiological Patterns Breathing cycles consist of naturally coordinated inhalation and exhalation events whose rate, depth, duration, and transitions vary with physical and expressive state.Physiological breathing patterns include controlled variations such as extended breaths, shallow cycles, pauses, irregular timing, and reset breaths that occur independently of lexical speech. These phenomena are foundational to: naturalistic speech and voice synthesis breath-aware expressive audio modeling physiological and respiratory sound research embodied and multimodal agent behavior realistic timing and transition modeling around vocal activity This dataset presents a neutral, non-linguistic, non-performative representation of human respiratory behavior.It is not designed to encode semantic speech content, but rather to isolate acoustic primitives that underlie natural breathing, respiratory timing, and physiological airflow variation. 📂 Contents Audio Files (.wav) Recorded at 96 kHz / 24-bit WAV format Exported as mono Fade-ins and fade-outs of 3–5 ms applied for consistency No compression, normalization, or creative processing applied High-pass filtered at ~40 Hz to remove subsonic rumble This preview includes 3 representative audio files, selected to demonstrate: natural inhale–exhale cycle behavior variation in breath depth and pacing physiological airflow and respiratory timing characteristics Metadata (.csv) Includes structured fields for: file name sound source type airflow type phonation type gesture and articulation descriptors microphone and recording chain sample rate, bit depth, and dataset version Metadata follows the Harmonic Frontier Audio – Foundations schema. 🎤 Recording Notes Recorded in a treated studio environment using a single-mic setup: Microphone: Rode NT1-A condenser microphone Recording chain: Rode NT1-A → Zoom F8n Pro Captured at 96 kHz / 32-bit float, rendered as 96 kHz / 24-bit mono WAV for release. Performer positioned approximately 3.5 inches from the microphone, with the microphone approximately 10–15 degrees off-axis. Natural respiratory dynamics, airflow texture, and subtle breath noise were preserved to retain acoustic realism. 🌈 Spectrogram Preview Below is a spectrogram illustrating the broadband airflow energy, inhale–exhale transitions, and changing intensity envelopes characteristic of natural breathing cycles and physiological respiratory patterns: ⚡ Usage This preview pack is designed for: Evaluation of Harmonic Frontier Audio dataset quality and structure Testing AI and DSP systems that model breathing, respiratory timing, and physiological airflow Research in speech synthesis, expressive vocal modeling, and breath-aware audio systems Creative sound design involving natural human breath and respiratory texture 👉 Note: This is not a full dataset.The complete Breathing Cycles and Physiological Patterns dataset includes a substantially larger set of neutral, extended, rapid, paused, irregular, and transitional breathing primitives and is available for licensing. 💡 Full Dataset Availability This is a preview pack of the Breathing Cycles and Physiological Patterns Dataset.The complete dataset is available for commercial licensing. title: Progressive Associative Cache: An Intuitive Algorithm for Energy-Efficient AI Inference
abstract: 【Resource type】Publication → Preprint 【Title】Progressive Associative Cache: An Intuitive Algorithm for Energy-Efficient AI Inference 【Creators】Family name: ChenGiven name: Yaoquan 【Description】Current Large Language Models (LLMs) treat every query as a novel task, activating tens of billions of parameters for probabilistic generation regardless of whether the same question has been answered millions of times before, resulting in massive redundant energy consumption and latency. This paper proposes the Progressive Associative Cache (PAC)—a lightweight middleware that augments existing large models without modifying their architecture or retraining. PAC operates in parallel with standard inference: when a query misses the cache, the base model generates an answer as usual, while PAC automatically extracts structured features, maps them to a Multi-Index Hierarchical Tree, and stores the answer for future reuse; when a query hits, the Intuitive Algorithm returns the result directly or performs selective reasoning within a narrow scope, bypassing the full model entirely. We introduce the Leaf Node Precision Spectrum theory to distinguish the handling of objective data from subjective opinions, and propose Lazy Generation of Aggregation Nodes coupled with a four-layer Data Lifecycle Management framework (Base Metadata, Derived Data, Short-Term Dynamic, and Real-Time). This approach transforms generative AI from a stateless engine into a continuously learning associative memory system. 【Keywords】Large Language Model; Knowledge Cache; Intuitive Algorithm; Progressive Learning; Multi-Index Retrieval; Energy-Efficient Inference 【Licence】Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC-BY 4.0) 【Language】English 【Publication date】2026-08-15

title: Computational Relation Autonomy Theory (CRAT-2)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Relation Autonomy Theory (CRAT-2), a novel framework for designing and understanding autonomous intelligent systems. CRAT-2 posits that future intelligent systems should autonomously establish relationships, rather than relying on pre-defined, manually constructed connections. The theory centers around the core principle: [System → Relation], representing a shift from human-directed relationship formation to system-driven discovery. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of CRAT-2, emphasizing the role of computational models in simulating and facilitating this autonomous relationship formation. The framework suggests a potential trajectory towards a foundational technology for truly autonomous intelligent systems, holding significant implications for fields ranging from artificial intelligence to social robotics and beyond. We outline the key components of CRAT-2, including the relational embedding, the dynamic relationship mapping, and the feedback loop mechanisms, proposing a mathematical representation of the core processes. Finally, we discuss the theoretical implications and potential advancements stemming from the adoption of CRAT-2. ---

We explore the theoretical underpinnings of CRAT-2, emphasizing the role of computational models in simulating and facilitating this autonomous relationship formation. The framework suggests a potential trajectory towards a foundational technology for truly autonomous intelligent systems, holding significant implications for fields ranging from artificial intelligence to social robotics and beyond. We outline the key components of CRAT-2, including the relational embedding, the dynamic relationship mapping, and the feedback loop mechanisms, proposing a mathematical representation of the core processes. Finally, we discuss the theoretical implications and potential advancements stemming from the adoption of CRAT-2. ---

title: Program Meaning Geometry (PMG)
abstract: This paper introduces Program Meaning Geometry (PMG), a novel framework for understanding and representing program semantics. Traditional approaches to program semantics often rely on formal notations and symbolic relationships, which can be cumbersome and fail to capture the inherent complexity of computation. PMG proposes a radical shift: program semantics are fundamentally geometric, residing within a multi-dimensional space defined by meaning distances. The core concept is that the meaning of a program element (e.g., a variable, expression, or function) can be represented as a point in this geometric space. The distance between these points represents the degree of difference in meaning. This framework offers a potential pathway to a more intuitive and powerful understanding of program behavior, with implications for program verification, program synthesis, and potentially even the future of the Turing Award. The primary goal of this work is to establish a foundational geometric model for program semantics, outlining its key components and potential applications. ---

title: Computational Value Compression Theory (CVCT): A Formal Framework for Reducing Complex Experience to Core Value Representations
abstract: Computational Value Compression Theory (CVCT) proposes a principled method for mapping high‑dimensional, temporally extended experiential streams into concise, minimal value representations that preserve essential goal‑directing information. CVCT introduces the compression operator C that acts on an experience sequence E = (e_1, e_2, …, e_T) to produce a compressed value vector V = C(E) ∈ ℝ^K, where K << T. The theory posits that the operator C is defined by optimizing a joint objective that balances fidelity to the original experience, sparsity of the representation, and alignment with a utility function U. Formally, C is obtained by solving min_{C} L_fid(E, C(E)) + λ L_sparsity(C(E)) + μ L_util(C(E), U), where λ and μ are trade‑off parameters. The compressed vector V serves as a core value representation that can be used for decision making, planning, and long‑term goal maintenance. By demonstrating that CVCT can explain how agents maintain persistent objectives over extended horizons, the theory offers a potential path toward Turing Award‑level contributions in artificial intelligence. This paper develops the mathematical underpinnings of CVCT, discusses its implications for AI alignment and human cognition, and outlines future research directions.

title: Distribution-free false-alarm calibration and chance-corrected spatial evaluation for industrial anomaly detection
abstract: Studies of industrial visual inspection commonly report the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and the overlap between anomaly maps and defect masks. Neither measure specifies the false-alarm rate at a selected threshold, while recurrent defect locations and mask geometry can inflate overlap. We combine a distribution-free upper tolerance threshold with a paired-minus-crossed spatial test. This test compares each detector's score-contributing locations with the matched defect mask and with masks from other images; the difference in rates defines spatial-evidence lift relative to the empirical chance-overlap rate. We evaluate three detectors on 120 point-defect images from three ISP-AD modalities and three fixed data splits. Of 378 alarms, 230 overlap the matched mask. Paired and crossed rates are nevertheless similar in eight of nine detector--modality cells; only DINOv2--ASM has a positive 95\% bootstrap lower bound (lift 0.259, 95\% interval 0.159--0.347). On the independent Magnetic Tile Defect dataset, the same analysis gives lifts of 0.203 (0.169--0.236) for Wide ResNet-50 (WRN50) patch memory and 0.231 (0.202--0.262) for Vision Transformer B/16 (ViT-B/16) patch memory, with one-sided permutation $p=10^{-5}$ for both. When crossed masks are restricted to the same defect class, the lifts remain 0.185 and 0.210. Exact sample planning shows that, with 150 calibration normals, a 95\%-confidence distribution-free claim is supported only for target false-positive rates of 1.98\% or higher; a 1\% target requires at least 299 normals. The results support reporting operating-point performance and chance-corrected spatial evidence alongside AUROC and raw mask overlap.

title: Mechanistic and Counterfactual Explanations in XAI: Cognitive Consequences for Decision‑Making
abstract: Abstract Contemporary artificial intelligence (AI) systems offer substantial benefits, but they often operate as “black boxes,” making it difficult to understand the reasoning behind their recommendations (Gunning et al., 2019). Although explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has been widely argued as a remedy, empirical evidence suggests that explanations do not uniformly improve users’ understanding of AI recommendations (Chan, 2023). Thus, a key open question is why different XAI methods produce divergent cognitive and behavioral effects. The proposed study compares two widely used yet conceptually distinct XAI approaches: feature-importance and counterfactual. These methods are grounded in philosophical theories of explanation that enable us to make a theoretically informed comparison. By showing how much each input contributes to the output, feature-importance explanations (e.g., SHAP, LIME) align with the mechanistic view of explanation (Salmon, 1984). In contrast, the counterfactual method aligns with the counterfactual view of explanation (Lewis, 1973) by describing how changes to the inputs would lead to different outcomes. We argue that these differing explanatory logics have important cognitive implications. Specifically, we focus on users’ illusion of explanatory depth (Rozenblit & Keil, 2002), which happens when users believe they understand a system more deeply than they actually do. We hypothesize that counterfactual explanations induce a stronger illusion of explanatory depth than feature-importance explanations. This is because counterfactuals are more intuitive and simplified and might not accurately reflect the original model’s underlying logic. The illusion of explanatory depth further impairs the decision quality of individuals. However, domain expertise acts as a moderator, such that experts are less susceptible to counterfactual-induced illusions due to their existing knowledge of relevant features and outcomes. We plan to use a laboratory experiment where participants will be randomly assigned to receive either feature-importance or counterfactual explanations for the AI recommendation. The illusion of explanatory depth will be operationalized as the discrepancy between perceived and objective understanding. Also, participants will be asked to make a decision that will then be assessed for decision quality. This study contributes to XAI research by grounding XAI effects in philosophical theories and identifying illusion of explanatory depth as a key mechanism linking explainability to decision outcomes. Practically, the findings caution against uncritical use of intuitive explanations.

title: MCA-v0.1: An Evidence-Constrained, Falsifiable Middle-Level Working Model of Distributed Cognitive Bottlenecks
abstract: This bilingual working paper presents MCA-v0.1 as a provisional, evidence-constrained and falsifiable middle-level working model of distributed cognitive bottlenecks. It converts a frozen mechanism-first comparison of seven candidate formulations into a publication-level synthesis. OUTCOME_C retains C6/MCA-v0.1 as the most useful integrated working model under the frozen rubric, while C0, C1 and C5 remain non-dominated challengers in narrower regimes. The result is relative to the frozen corpus, candidate set and internally frozen evaluation procedure. It does not establish a unique biological architecture or a general theory of cognition. The same workflow constructed and rated the candidates; v0.1 has no independent coder or inter-rater reliability statistic. The search was targeted and source-critical, not systematic or PRISMA. The toy formalization checks internal coherence only and provides no biological validation. All twelve falsification tests remain open. No clinical, implant-design, consciousness-transfer or general biological-capacity-expansion claim is made, and no new human or animal experiment is reported. The record contains the full English reference version and a content-equivalent Hungarian version. Companion research compendium DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21958090. Magyar: Ez a kétnyelvű munkatanulmány az MCA-v0.1 modellt az elosztott kognitív szűk keresztmetszetek előzetes, bizonyítékkorlátos és falszifikálható középszintű munkamodelljeként mutatja be. A hét befagyasztott jelöltmegfogalmazás mechanizmus-első összevetését publikációs szintű szintézissé alakítja. Az OUTCOME_C a C6/MCA-v0.1 modellt a befagyasztott értékelési szabályok mellett leghasznosabb integrált munkamodellként tartja meg, miközben a C0, C1 és C5 szűkebb rezsimekben nem dominált kihívó marad. Az eredmény a befagyasztott korpuszhoz, a jelölthalmazhoz és a belsőleg befagyasztott értékelési eljáráshoz viszonyított. Nem igazol egyedi biológiai architektúrát vagy általános kognícióelméletet. Ugyanaz a munkafolyamat alkotta meg és értékelte a jelölteket; nincs független kódoló vagy értékelők közötti megbízhatósági mutató. A keresés célzott és forráskritikus volt, nem szisztematikus vagy PRISMA-áttekintés. A játékformalizáció csak belső koherencia-ellenőrzés, nem biológiai validáció. Mind a tizenkét falszifikációs teszt nyitott. A közlés nem klinikai protokoll vagy implantátumterv, nem tesz tudatátviteli állítást, nem igazol általános biológiai kapacitásbővítést, és nem közöl új ember- vagy állatkísérletet. A rekord a teljes angol referenciaváltozatot és annak tartalmilag egyenértékű magyar változatát tartalmazza. A kapcsolt kutatási kompendium DOI-ja: 10.5281/zenodo.21958090.

title: Computational Relation Singularity Theory (CRST-2)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Relation Singularity Theory (CRST-2), a novel framework for understanding emergent intelligence, particularly in the context of large language models (LLMs). The theory posits that a critical threshold exists – a combination of relationship quantity and quality – that triggers the emergence of novel capabilities. This threshold, denoted as [R > Rc], is analogous to the concept of emergence and potentially offers a pathway to understanding the sudden leaps in performance observed in LLMs. The core of CRST-2 lies in the idea that complex relationships within a system, when sufficiently dense and interconnected, can fundamentally alter the system's behavior, leading to unpredictable and powerful outcomes. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of this theory, focusing on the role of relational networks, information density, and the potential for a computational singularity. The theory proposes that achieving a critical level of relational complexity unlocks previously inaccessible cognitive abilities. This work aims to provide a conceptual model for analyzing and predicting emergent intelligence in complex systems, ultimately contributing to a deeper understanding of the driving forces behind advancements in artificial intelligence. ---

title: Computational Possibility Compiler (CPC)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Possibility Compiler (CPC), a novel approach to programming that shifts the paradigm from explicitly writing executable code to compiling a set of possible programs based on a given goal and constraints. The CPC operates on the principle that a system can be described not by *what* to compute, but by *how* it can potentially compute, effectively navigating a computational space. This framework offers significant potential for advancements in areas such as artificial intelligence, privacy computing, and data governance. This document outlines the core ideas behind the CPC, identifies potential areas for future research, and proposes a selection of innovative research directions with the potential to significantly impact the field of computation and earn recognition as Turing Award-level work. The focus is on generating fundamentally new approaches, avoiding duplication of existing ideas, and prioritizing research directions with the highest likelihood of producing impactful, high-citation papers.

title: Algorithmic Invariant Discovery Engine (AIDE)
abstract: The automated discovery of algorithmic invariants is a critical step towards robust algorithm verification and formal program analysis. This paper introduces the Algorithmic Invariant Discovery Engine (AIDE), a system designed to automatically identify relevant invariants during the execution of an algorithm. AIDE observes the algorithm's steps, tracking the state of the system at various points in time. Based on this observation, it aims to generate a diverse set of invariants including correctness, convergence, resource usage, and safety invariants. The system's core principle is to shift the burden of invariant identification from human analysts to an automated process, thereby accelerating algorithm development and improving software reliability. We posit that AIDE represents a significant step towards realizing the potential of the Turing Award in transforming the landscape of algorithm analysis and program verification. ---

title: Computational Language Creation Algorithm (CLCA)
abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence has revealed a pressing need for new programming languages that can be generated automatically to suit specific computational tasks. In this paper we propose the Computational Language Creation Algorithm (CLCA), a principled framework that automatically designs a novel programming language's syntax, type system, and abstract semantics from a high‑level specification of desired computational properties. CLCA integrates formal language theory, type inference mechanisms, and graph‑based abstraction techniques to construct a language that is both expressive and safe. We formalize the algorithmic steps, analyze its computational complexity, and discuss its potential to transform the way programming languages are conceived, particularly for specialized AI applications. The algorithm's capacity to produce a language with a clear grammar, a robust type system, and a well‑defined abstract machine suggests a significant step toward automating the design of domain‑specific languages and may well be a catalyst for future Turing Award‑level contributions.

title: Computational Rule Transfer Theory (CRTT)
abstract: Computational Rule Transfer Theory (CRTT) is a theoretical framework that formalizes the systematic migration of abstract rules from one domain to another, with a particular focus on the transfer of physical and mathematical principles into artificial intelligence algorithms. This paper introduces the core concepts of CRTT, develops a formal representation of rule migration, and proposes algorithmic mechanisms for rule extraction, adaptation, and integration. By exploring the theoretical underpinnings and practical implications of rule transfer, we demonstrate how CRTT can enable cross‑disciplinary breakthroughs, particularly in the synthesis of physics‑informed neural networks, symbolic reasoning systems, and self‑optimizing control architectures. The discussion highlights potential applications, limitations, and future research directions, positioning CRTT as a foundational tool for the next generation of interdisciplinary AI research.

title: Trust in AI: Anthropomorphism, Explainability, and Trustworthiness
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in organizational and everyday decision-making, but its effectiveness depends on appropriate user trust. Both under-trust and over-trust are problematic because users may reject useful AI systems when trust is too low or over-rely on imperfect systems when trust is too high (Lee & See, 2004). This TREO paper develops a conceptual model based on the theory of reasoned action (TRA) to explain how anthropomorphism and explainability influence trust through perceived competence, benevolence, and integrity (Ajzen & Fishbein, 1980). Anthropomorphic cues may increase perceived competence and benevolence by making AI appear more relatable and capable (Epley et al., 2007). However, excessive or inauthentic human likeness may undermine perceived integrity by creating unrealistic expectations or suspicion (Glikson & Woolley, 2020). Explainability strengthens trust by reducing uncertainty and helping users understand, evaluate, and contest AI decisions (Miller, 2019). This TREO paper proposes a conceptual model examining how anthropomorphism and explainability may influence user trust in AI through perceptions of competence, benevolence, and integrity. Anthropomorphism is expected to increase perceived competence and benevolence, while excessive human-likeness may reduce perceived integrity. Explainability is expected to strengthen all three trustworthiness perceptions, which in turn are expected to shape trust in AI. This study contributes to the AI trust research by integrating anthropomorphism, explainability, and trustworthiness beliefs into a unified TRA-based framework. In practice, it suggests that designers should balance relatable AI interactions with transparency, ethical accountability, and calibrated reliance. Future researchers can test the model using survey data and structural equation modeling across AI application domains such as healthcare, education, finance, and workplace decision support.

This study contributes to the AI trust research by integrating anthropomorphism, explainability, and trustworthiness beliefs into a unified TRA-based framework. In practice, it suggests that designers should balance relatable AI interactions with transparency, ethical accountability, and calibrated reliance. Future researchers can test the model using survey data and structural equation modeling across AI application domains such as healthcare, education, finance, and workplace decision support.

title: Computational Decision Space Geometry (CDSG)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Decision Space Geometry (CDSG), a novel framework for understanding and modeling decision-making processes. Traditional approaches often treat decision-making as discrete point selection, neglecting the inherent geometric nature of choices. CDSG proposes that decisions are made by traversing a continuous decision space, [ΩD], and argues for a rigorous investigation into the structural properties of these spaces. The core concept is that decision-making is not about selecting a specific point, but rather about the continuous movement within this geometric space. This framework has the potential to unify diverse areas of research including search algorithms, planning systems, and artificial intelligence, ultimately offering a more comprehensive and geometrically-grounded approach to intelligent decision-making. The paper outlines the fundamental principles of CDSG, explores its implications for various decision-making scenarios, and suggests future research directions. ---

title: Computational Constraint Creation Theory
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Constraint Creation Theory (CCCT), a novel framework proposing that constraints are not merely limitations on computation, but rather fundamental drivers of capability generation. CCCT posits a systematic mechanism where constraints, when imposed, lead to the emergence of enhanced abilities within computational systems. The theory is illustrated through examples, notably the observation that the architectural constraints inherent in neural network design directly contribute to their generalization capabilities. The implications of CCCT extend to areas such as optimization and learning, potentially warranting a re-evaluation of traditional approaches. This paper lays the groundwork for further research exploring the dynamics of constraint-driven capability development within computational systems. ---

title: Computational Function Transferability
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Computational Function Transferability (CFT), a framework for evaluating the degree to which a module's functionality can be transferred to a new system. CFT is defined as the ratio of the function preserved to the adaptation cost. This ratio provides a quantifiable measure of transferability, considering both the extent to which the original function remains intact and the effort required to adapt the module to the new environment. The potential of CFT extends to unifying software migration, model transfer, algorithm reuse, and cross-hardware deployment, representing a significant step towards more efficient and adaptable software development and computational systems. The core idea is presented with the formula: [T(M,S') = FunctionPreserved / AdaptationCost], where T(M,S') represents the transferability between module M and system S'. This paper outlines the theoretical foundations, key considerations, and potential applications of CFT, highlighting its relevance in the current landscape of distributed computing, artificial intelligence, and complex system design. ---

title: Computational Value Formation Theory (CVFT)
abstract: Computational Value Formation Theory (CVFT) proposes a unified framework for understanding how autonomous systems generate internal value functions that guide decision making, independently of externally supplied rewards. Traditional reinforcement learning paradigms treat reward signals as the sole source of value, whereas CVFT posits that experience streams, sensory inputs, and internal dynamics give rise to a self‑generated value landscape. This paper develops a formal model of value formation, establishes its consistency with known cognitive phenomena, and outlines potential implications for the design of self‑learning artificial agents. By deriving a recursive value update equation grounded in experience accumulation, CVFT offers a principled alternative to reward‑driven learning and suggests a pathway toward intrinsic motivation mechanisms that could underpin future autonomous AI systems.

title: Computational Goal Ecology Theory (CGET-4)
abstract: Computational Goal Ecology Theory (CGET-4) proposes a novel conceptual framework for understanding the interactions of multiple autonomous objectives within artificial and natural systems. By treating each goal \(G_i\) as an ecological agent that engages in both competitive and cooperative dynamics, CGET-4 provides a unifying language for reasoning about multi-objective optimization, emergent behavior, and resource allocation. The theory introduces a formal representation of a goal space, defines interaction kernels for competition and cooperation, and derives a set of coupled differential equations that capture the evolution of goal strengths over time. This paper develops the mathematical foundation of CGET-4, discusses its implications for the design of next‑generation AI systems, and argues that the theory has the potential to contribute to foundational advances worthy of the Turing Award. The work is purely theoretical and does not include experimental validation; rather, it lays the groundwork for future empirical studies.

title: Continual Federated Learning for Network Intrusion Detection: An Open-Index Systematic Map
abstract: Purpose: Continual federated learning (FCL) combines decentralized model updating with sequential adaptation, but network-intrusion studies use incompatible definitions of drift, retention, and evaluation. This open-index systematic map examines how such systems operationalize non-stationarity, preserve earlier knowledge, and report empirical and reproducibility evidence. Method: Eight queries were executed in OpenAlex, Crossref, and DBLP on 26 July 2026. The interfaces returned 8,819 records within documented result limits; deduplication left 3,075 unique records. The initial concept-block rule excluded 2,865 records. A rule-based sensitivity audit reclassified two false negatives, yielding 2,863 automatic exclusions and 212 records for title/abstract screening. Thirty-one database-derived and nine supplementary reports were sought; 24 were not retrieved. Sixteen full texts were assessed, two were excluded, and 14 primary studies were mapped. Results: The corpus comprised three studies from 2023, six from 2024, one from 2025, and four from the partial 2026 search year. Nine studies tested retention after later tasks or classes; five reported adaptation without a prior-task retention outcome. Within the nine retention-tested studies, replay-based designs most often reported favorable within-study stability results, but heterogeneous scenarios and comparators do not establish cross-study superiority. Only two studies reported standardized forgetting or backward transfer, two supplied study-specific code, and one tested malicious clients. Conclusion: The accessible open-index evidence supports FCL as a prototype strategy under constructed benchmark sequences. It does not establish cross-network robustness, formal privacy, or deployment-scale reliability. A targeted supplementary update on 27 July 2026 found no additional eligible, accessible full text. Interpretation is constrained by capped interfaces, single-reviewer screening, and 24 unretrieved reports.

title: The Physical Cutoff Does Not Restore Homogenization: Phase-Dependent Burning in the Strain G-Equation
abstract: We disprove the expectation stated by Xin, Yu, and Ronney that the physical positive part strain $G$-equation should possess an effective burning velocity in cellular flows. For the standard cellular flow in dimension two $V_A(x_1,x_2)=A(-\sin x_1\cos x_2,\cos x_1\sin x_2)$, if $0<d<20/399$ and $\sqrt{1+4d^2}<Ad\le1+d/10$, then for every unit planar slope the periodic correction develops oscillations at least linearly in time. The solution remains bounded below on an explicit horizontal channel through $(π,0)$, while at $(π/2,0)$ it decreases at rate at least $CA/\log A$, with $C>0$ universal. The same conclusions hold for arbitrary continuous periodic perturbations of planar initial data. Under the physical scaling $V_A(x/\varepsilon)$ and $d_\varepsilon=\varepsilon d$, an order one value gap persists between points at distance $O(\varepsilon)$ at every positive macroscopic time, so the rescaled solutions have no locally uniformly convergent subsequence. The proof uses the Hamiltonian sandwich $H_{\mathrm{unc}}\le H_+\le\widehat H$. The upper comparator $\widehat H$ is a rectangular support function, equivalently an upper expectation over a state-dependent credal set, whose reversed control dynamics possess an invariant comparison channel. We also prove that for any $C^2$ incompressible periodic flow, every $\varepsilon$-outward barrier certificate has covering radius at most $2d\varepsilon$ for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon$. We further discuss implications for statistics and machine learning: rectangular, time-consistent local uncertainty need not imply forgetting of the initial state in the long run, so additional global stability or ergodicity conditions are needed in robust sequential decision making. Two Lean 4 appendices record conditional formalizations of a sufficient $p=e_1$ subregime and of the logical assembly of the rigidity theorem for barrier certificates.

title: Investment Opportunities in Artificial Intelligence (AI)
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the global economy through advances in generative AI, cloud computing, semiconductor design, cybersecurity, robotics, and enterprise software integration. We have all heard the expression, “The cobbler’s 'children have no shoes.” It could likely be said ITIS Professors have no “Technology stock portfolios!” This paper examines stock market opportunities across key companies positioned to benefit from accelerating AI adoption in both consumer and enterprise markets. We examine firms that control critical infrastructure layers of the AI ecosystem, including chip manufacturing, hyperscale cloud platforms, data management, and software applications. Special attention is given to those firms that could possibly be the next big “Killer App” and produce exponential returns on investments! Among semiconductor leaders, NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) has emerged as the dominant supplier of graphics processing units (GPUs) used in machine learning and large language models. Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (NYSE: TSM) represent additional growth opportunities through advanced chip fabrication and accelerator competition. In cloud computing, Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT), Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZ), and Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) continue investing heavily in AI-enabled platforms and enterprise productivity solutions. Enterprise software firms such as Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) and Salesforce (NYSE:CRM) are leveraging AI-driven analytics and automation to improve operational efficiency and customer engagement. The TREO also evaluates investment risks, including regulatory uncertainty, valuation volatility, supply chain dependencies, and increasing global competition. Although many AI-related equities trade at historically elevated valuation multiples, long-term demand for computational infrastructure and intelligent automation suggests sustained growth potential. For business and information technology scholars, the AI sector provides a valuable case study in technological disruption, strategic innovation, and capital market behavior. The author suggests that diversified exposure across semiconductors, cloud infrastructure, and enterprise software may provide the most balanced approach for private investors seeking participation in the expanding AI economy. We are hopeful this TREO will generate some lively discussions.

title: VNorm: A BatchNorm-Compatible Parametric Activation Function
abstract: This preliminary release presents VNorm, a parametric activation function evaluated in conjunction with Batch Normalization.The repository includes the implementation, experiment configuration, and benchmark code for a CIFAR-100 multilayer perceptron. VNorm is compared with ReLU, CELU, SiLU, and PReLU across three random seeds.The release is intended to support reproducible and transparent comparison of activation functions. Unpublished research directions and private extensions are not included.

title: Computational Law Discovery Machine (CLDM)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Law Discovery Machine (CLDM), a novel system designed to automate the process of discovering computational laws from observed data. Currently, the discovery of mathematical and computational laws relies heavily on human intuition, expertise, and pattern recognition. This process is often time-consuming, subjective, and prone to bias. CLDM aims to shift this paradigm by employing a multi-layered algorithmic approach that systematically searches for underlying patterns within datasets. The system utilizes a combination of inductive and deductive reasoning, coupled with evolutionary algorithms, to identify potential rules and validate their applicability. The core concept is to transform observation into computational law, mirroring the process of scientific discovery in fields like physics. This paper outlines the architecture of CLDM, details the key algorithms employed, and discusses the potential impact and future directions of this technology, suggesting it could represent a significant advancement within computational science, akin to Newton's contributions to physics.

title: 计算策略生成理论
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Strategy Generation Theory (CSGT), a novel approach to problem-solving and decision-making that moves beyond the limitations of traditional algorithmic solutions. The core concept of CSGT rests on the dynamic generation of strategies, rather than relying on pre-defined, fixed algorithms. The theory posits a systematic process wherein a system iteratively refines its strategy, moving from one [Strategy\_t] to the next [Strategy\_{t+1}]. This approach aims to uncover underlying patterns and rules governing strategy evolution, potentially offering a more robust and adaptable solution than current methods, particularly in complex and evolving environments. The theoretical framework presented here has the potential to significantly advance the field of artificial intelligence, and could represent a paradigm shift surpassing the current dominance of reinforcement learning. The investigation into this theory's underlying mechanics could be a strong candidate for consideration for the Turing Award. ---

title: 计算抽象跃迁理论
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Abstraction Transition Theory (CATT), a novel theoretical framework designed to explain the underlying mechanisms driving the evolution of computation. CATT posits that the progression from low-level representations like machine code to increasingly abstract models – such as high-level programming languages and sophisticated computational models – is not simply a matter of technological advancement, but a fundamental process of abstraction transition. The theory focuses on identifying the conditions and triggers that lead to the generation of new abstractions, proposing a mathematically formalized approach to understanding this transition process. CATT aims to provide a framework for predicting and controlling abstraction levels in computational systems, with potential implications for fields ranging from software engineering to artificial intelligence. The core of the theory centers around the concept of 'abstraction layers' and the energy required to transition between them, represented mathematically. This work lays the groundwork for a mathematical theory with significant implications for the history and future of computer science. ---

title: Computational Identity Verification Theory (CIVT)
abstract: The growing ubiquity of intelligent systems demands new mechanisms for ensuring that these systems do not merely execute their intended functions correctly but also preserve their original identity over time. Computational Identity Verification Theory (CIVT) proposes a formal framework for reasoning about identity persistence in computational entities. CIVT extends classical program verification by introducing the notion of an identity model, a set of invariants that capture the essence of a system's intended identity, and a verification procedure that checks whether an evolving system continues to satisfy these invariants. This paper presents the core ideas of CIVT, formulates the theory in precise mathematical terms, discusses its potential to become a foundation for trustworthy AI, and outlines possible research directions and applications. title: SAGE-OR: Semi-supervised Adaptive Scene Graph Generation for Operating Rooms
abstract: Current surgical scene graph generation methods depend on dense multi-modal supervision and specialized hardware (synchronized RGB-D sensors, calibration rigs), making dataset construction expensive and restricting all existing benchmarks to simulated environments. We propose SAGE-OR, a feature-centric framework that replaces the traditional detect-then-reason paradigm with a decoupled representation-reasoning paradigm in which localization is derived from frozen foundation models, encoded implicitly in pre-computed features, and used without any localization supervision, while a lightweight graph transformer performs relational reasoning over cached features. We employ a semi-supervised formulation with general-purpose segmentation prompts to eliminate localization supervision while enabling unsupervised context augmentation through additional prompt-driven entities, such as hands, which are absent from annotations. General-purpose prompts are used to induce near-perfect recall, while precision is delegated to downstream attention-based reasoning, enabling simple adaptation to new entities via prompt-level modification. This design enables a lightweight 15M-parameter graph transformer that trains in 1.4 hours and runs relational inference at $\sim$1ms per frame with peak memory under 2GB, suitable for edge hardware used in the operating room; feature extraction runs offline as a separate caching stage (4.27s per frame). On the 4D-OR benchmark, the core model achieves 76% F1, matching the fully supervised 4D-OR baseline while eliminating all localization annotations, and unsupervised hand augmentation raises this to 86%, within 4 points of state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods requiring dense multi-modal supervision, providing a practical pathway for adaptation to new surgical settings without annotation other than relationship and class labels.

title: Why Vision Fails as a Universal Bridge: Rectifying Modality Asynchrony in Multilingual MLLMs
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) exhibit substantial performance degradation in non-English visual reasoning, despite the strong multilingual competence of their text-only backbones. While mechanistic evidence from text-only models suggests that non-English inputs are routed through an English-centric latent space, the multimodal implications of this phenomenon remain unexplored. Through rigorous mechanistic analysis, we identify the \textbf{Ghost Anchor} phenomenon: a temporal modality asynchrony where linguistic translation to the English semantic manifold completes in early layers, while visual semanticization remains immature. Consequently, visual signals are physically present yet functionally invisible during the early alignment window. To rectify this, we propose \textbf{ANCHOR}, a training framework employing Proactive Visual Anchoring (PVA) to accelerate early visual semantic emergence, ensuring visual representations proactively guide linguistic translation. Mechanistic interventions confirm that ANCHOR successfully restores the causal influence of visual signals during early translation. Furthermore, extensive experiments on XMMMU, MaXM, and CVQA demonstrate that ANCHOR consistently outperforms standard baselines, achieving robust visual reasoning across both fine-tuned and zero-shot languages.

title: Post-Quantum Readiness in Digital Payments
abstract: The advancement of quantum computing forces organizations to reconsider cryptographic foundations of digital trust. Scaled quantum computers may threaten public-key cryptography used for communication, authentication, data exchange, and transaction processing. Migration to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is more than an algorithm upgrade. Organizations must locate quantum-vulnerable cryptography across ecosystems and develop migration plans. Yet, PQC readiness is limited. A Trusted Computing Group (2025) survey of 1,500 cybersecurity professionals found 91% reported no formal PQC roadmap, while 81% said current cryptographic libraries and hardware security modules were not migration-ready. IS research is examining PQC migration, including banking-focused work highlighting variation in strategies, resources, and timelines (Brettschneider & Mendling, 2025). We build on prior work by focusing on FinTech ecosystem readiness, especially digital payments. Atlanta’s “Transaction Alley” illustrates why this context matters, as roughly 70% of global financial transactions pass through companies headquartered in metro Atlanta (Georgia Department of Economic Development, n.d.) amounting to 300 billion transactions worth $49 Billion generated by 10 public FinTechs alone (Fintech Atlanta, n.d.). Digital payments rely on cryptographic trust across merchants, gateways, processors, wallets, APIs, and cloud services. Since many FinTech firms use payment infrastructure they do not fully own, PQC migration is a challenge in coordinating ecosystems and digital trust governance. This research investigates how FinTech organizations govern PQC readiness across interdependent digital payment ecosystems. We ask how firms identify cryptographic dependencies, assess vendor preparedness, coordinate migration across partners, and preserve trust in high-volume transaction environments. Through exploratory interviews, we aim to develop a FinTech PQC readiness framework that explains how firms move from awareness to dependency discovery, vendor assurance, migration coordination, and trust preservation. The study extends IS research by explaining readiness-building when security infrastructure is invisible, distributed, transaction-critical, and externally dependent. This research will also help leaders structure governance, vendor assessments, and migration roadmaps for quantum-era resilience in digital payments.

title: The Effect of AI-Powered Tutoring Systems and Student Self-Efficacy on Mathematical Problem-Solving Skills of Students at Kolehiyo ng Pantukan, Philippines
abstract: This study explores the influence of AI-powered tutoring systems and self- efficacy on the mathematical problem-solving skills of BSED Mathematics students in Kolehiyo ng Pantukan. Using a quantitative predictive-correlational research design, data were collected from 131 students through validated survey questionnaires and analyzed using Multiple Linear Regression. The findings revealed that students generally have a high level of AI-powered tutoring system adoption, particularly in their awareness of its functions and benefits. The level of self-efficacy was also found to be high, as students frequently perceive positive vicarious experiences and physiological states. The level of mathematical problem-solving skills was rated as high, as students frequently showed strong problem-solving skills in Math, indicating a strong capacity to visualize, describe, plan, implement, and evaluate complex math problems. Statistical analysis confirmed that high reported levels of AI-powered tutoring systems and self-efficacy are significantly associated with high levels of self-reported mathematical problem-solving skills. Regression analysis further revealed that these factors significantly influence mathematical problem-solving skills. The study highlights the importance of integrating AI- powered tutoring systems and fostering positive self-efficacy to improve the mathematical problem-solving skills of students in academic learning.

title: FWL‑ThinkingLM
abstract: FWL‑ThinkingLM is an axiomatic manifold framework for embodied intelligence, which unifies multi‑sensory signals (vision, tactile, audition) within one intrinsic geometric space for concept‑judgment‑reasoning‑self‑optimization. This is a paradigm‑level theoretical proposal with potential to reshape embodied‑AI modeling, not a trained end‑to‑end model. Its validity needs further mathematical scrutiny, simulation and physical‑device experiments. We invite researchers worldwide for confirmation, extension, critical analysis or falsification of this framework.

title: Universal Computational Representation Theory
abstract: Universal Computational Representation Theory (UCRT) presents a novel framework for understanding computation itself. The core principle of UCRT posits that all computational objects – programs, models, and data – can be represented within a single, unified formalism denoted as *R**. This representation aims to transcend the limitations of current computational paradigms by providing a foundational, universally applicable system. UCRT's potential impact extends beyond existing approaches, suggesting parallels with advancements in Relational Model theory and Lambda Calculus, potentially unlocking breakthroughs in computational understanding. This paper outlines the fundamental concepts of UCRT, detailing the structure of *R** and exploring its implications for various computational domains. The goal is to establish a robust theoretical basis for computation, moving beyond specific implementations and focusing on the underlying, representational nature of all computational processes. ---

title: Internal Computational Communication Algebra (ICCA)
abstract: This paper introduces the Internal Computational Communication Algebra (ICCA), a novel framework that shifts the perspective on computational communication from simple data transmission to a fundamental restructuring of relational structures. The core idea is that communication, beyond conveying information, actively alters the relationships between entities within a computational system. This is formalized through the function *F(Relation, Message)*, which dictates the transformation of a relation based on the received message. The ICCA provides a mathematical foundation for understanding and modeling complex communication dynamics, potentially offering a new paradigm for designing and optimizing large-scale software systems. This paper explores the foundational principles, key equations, and implications of ICCA, highlighting its potential to redefine how we approach communication within computational systems and its relevance to achieving breakthroughs in areas like distributed computing and artificial intelligence. ---

title: Computational Goal Fusion Theory (CGFT)
abstract: Computational Goal Fusion Theory (CGFT) proposes a mathematical and conceptual framework for combining multiple autonomous goals into a single, emergent goal that guides behavior. By treating goals as vectors in an abstract goal space, CGFT defines a fusion operation G1 ⊕ G2 that produces a new goal G3 whose direction is determined by the weighted sum of the constituent goals. The theory elucidates how such fusion can lead to novel behavioral patterns, enhance collective intelligence, and potentially underpin future AI systems that self‑organize from simple objective modules. This paper presents the core ideas of CGFT, formalizes the fusion operation, explores its properties, provides illustrative examples, and discusses implications for multi‑agent coordination, human‑machine interaction, and adaptive control.

title: Computational Language Space Theory (CLST)
abstract: Computational Language Space Theory (CLST) proposes a unified geometric framework for representing and analyzing all possible computational languages. By mapping each language to a point in a high‑dimensional space Ω_L, CLST allows for rigorous definitions of distance, similarity, and evolution between languages. This paper introduces the core concepts of CLST, formalizes the construction of Ω_L, and develops a metric for measuring distances between languages based on their expressive power, syntax, and semantics. We discuss implications for programming language design, language migration, and the broader quest to understand the landscape of computation. The potential to create a comprehensive "programming language universe map" and to uncover fundamental patterns in language evolution positions CLST as a candidate for future recognition, possibly even a Turing Award‑level contribution.

title: Beyond AI as a Tool or Teammate: Information Quality as a Driver of Human–AI Collaboration and AI Use Intentions
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded within organizational processes, transforming how employees and users interact with technology in hybrid human–AI environments. Prior research shows that AI increasingly augments rather than replaces human capabilities across service, leadership, teamwork, learning, and decision-making settings (Gnewuch et al., 2024). Studies further demonstrate that perceptions of AI significantly influence collaboration, engagement, and adoption outcomes (Seeber et al., 2020). Existing literature has largely focused on AI role framing, such as whether AI is perceived as a tool or teammate, alongside related concepts including social presence, trust, and anthropomorphism. Despite these advances, limited attention has been given to the role of perceived information quality in strengthening collaborative human–AI systems. This gap is important because users primarily engage with AI systems through information exchange and continuously evaluate AI-generated outputs based on accuracy, reliability, relevance, usefulness, and contextual appropriateness. While prior studies acknowledge trust and perceived usefulness, they do not adequately explain how perceptions of information quality shape collaborative engagement with AI systems. This study proposes that perceived information quality functions as a foundational mechanism that enhances collaborative human–AI systems. Specifically, when users perceive AI-generated information as accurate, relevant, reliable, and contextually meaningful, they are more likely to collaborate effectively with AI systems, rely on AI-supported recommendations, and develop positive attitudes toward hybrid intelligence environments. Consequently, higher perceived information quality strengthens user satisfaction with AI interactions and increases intention to continue using AI-enabled systems. The study further argues that perceived information quality influences users’ communication behavior with AI. Higher information quality perceptions may encourage users to engage in more open, collaborative, and detailed interactions with AI systems, while lower information quality perceptions may increase skepticism and reduce engagement. This paper contributes to the human–AI collaboration literature by shifting attention from anthropomorphic framing and social presence toward an information-centric perspective. The proposed framework positions perceived information quality as a key driver of collaborative AI effectiveness, satisfaction, and continued AI use. Practically, the findings may help organizations design AI systems that improve not only operational efficiency but also the perceived quality and usefulness of AI-generated information, thereby strengthening sustainable and human-centered AI adoption.

title: Towards Trustworthy Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in domains where opacity, factual un-reliability, and computational cost carry real consequences, yet the research communities that address these three problems — explainability, hallucination, and inference efficiency — have largely developed in isolation. This paper argues that the three concerns are not independent: interventions designed to reduce inference cost, such as prompt compression, can silently alter both the faithfulness of post-hoc explanations and the model’s propensity to hallucinate. We present an integrated conceptual frame-work that couples attention- and perturbation-based explainability (LIME, SHAP, raw attention) with lightweight hallucination-detection signals and token-efficient inference strategies (chunking, summa-rization, prompt compression), and we instrument the framework with a set of cross-cutting consistency metrics. To ground the framework empirically, we design and execute a controlled pilot experiment that measures how rule-based prompt compression jointly affects (i) the Kullback–Leibler divergence between a model’s output distributions before and after compression, used as a proxy for hallucination risk, and (ii) the entropy and rank-correlation of last-layer attention, used as a proxy for explanation faithfulness. Because the sandboxed experimental environment used for this study has no network ac-cess to pretrained model repositories, the experiment is conducted on a compact two-layer Transformer language model trained from scratch on a controlled synthetic corpus, which allows exact, reproducible control over ground truth while preserving the qualitative mechanics of attention-based attribution and next-token prediction under compression. Across 15 held-out prompts, compression removes 52.9% of tokens on average while producing a small but non-zero mean output KL divergence of 0.0007 and re-ducing mean attention entropy from 1.062 to 0.632, with attention rank correlation across compression conditions of only 0.633. These results provide direct, quantitative evidence for the framework’s central hypothesis: token-efficiency interventions are not explanation-neutral, and systems that report compres-sion ratios without also reporting faithfulness and hallucination-risk deltas may be masking a three-way trade-off. We discuss the implications for trustworthy LLM system design and outline how the pilot findings motivate follow-up experiments on larger pretrained models.

title: Computational Model Natural Selection Theorem (CMNST)
abstract: This paper presents the Computational Model Natural Selection Theorem (CMNST), a novel theoretical framework aimed at explaining the success of certain computational paradigms. The theorem posits that a system of competing computational models, defined by [M1, M2, ..., Mn], interacts within a defined selection landscape governed by the fitness function Fitness(M). The core principle of CMNST lies in demonstrating how, through iterative computation and selection, models with higher fitness values—representing more effective solutions—will propagate and dominate the system. This concept draws an analogy with biological natural selection, albeit within the realm of computation. The theorem provides a rigorous mathematical foundation for understanding adaptive behavior in complex computational systems, potentially offering insights into the underlying mechanisms driving the evolution of algorithms and software. The exploration of CMNST holds significant implications for the field of computational science and could contribute to a deeper understanding of the principles of design and optimization. Furthermore, the theorem's formal structure and potential for generating verifiable predictions position it as a candidate for consideration for the Turing Award.

title: Computational Concept Formation Dynamics (CCFD)
abstract: This paper investigates the dynamics of concept formation, proposing a framework termed Computational Concept Formation Dynamics (CCFD). The core hypothesis centers on the emergent formation of abstract concepts within computational systems, driven by data input. We explore the process by which machines can develop novel understandings, moving beyond mere pattern recognition to genuinely forming concepts. This work argues that CCFD represents a potentially groundbreaking approach with implications for addressing the long-standing challenge of machine understanding, holding significant implications for the Turing Award. The research focuses on modeling the iterative process of data assimilation and conceptual refinement, utilizing a series of mathematical formulations to quantify the evolution of concept representations. We define a key metric: Concept Quality (CQ), which represents the degree to which a concept accurately reflects the underlying data distribution. The goal is to establish a measurable and quantifiable framework for studying concept formation in artificial intelligence. ---

title: Cross-Temporal Program Equivalence (CTPE)
abstract: This paper explores the concept of Cross-Temporal Program Equivalence (CTPE), a novel approach to program verification that addresses the limitations of traditional equivalence testing. Current program verification techniques predominantly focus on immediate equivalence, often failing to capture discrepancies in long-term behavior. CTPE proposes a framework where two programs may be equivalent at a specific time (t) – denoted as `P_1 ≡_t P_2` – yet diverge significantly over extended periods. This divergence is formally defined as `P_1 ≛_{t:t+k} P_2`, where 'k' represents the duration of the observation. The core of CTPE lies in establishing a temporal equivalence, `P_1 ≡_T P_2`, meaning the programs remain equivalent within a specified time interval (T). This paper details the theoretical foundation of CTPE, outlines a potential mechanism for its implementation, and discusses its implications for program verification, particularly in areas where long-term reliability and predictable behavior are paramount. The research suggests that CTPE could significantly contribute to the broader field of program equivalence and long-term validation theory.

title: When Artificial Intelligence Solves Long-Standing Mathematical Problems: Semiosis as a Common Framework for Mathematical Research, Education, and Health AI (Preprint)
abstract: UNSTRUCTURED Artificial intelligence (AI) has moved from routine calculation and benchmark performance into the research frontier of mathematics. By August 2026, the evidence included a Lean-verified autonomous resolution of Erdős Problem #728, a human-verified machine disproof of a central conjecture within the 80-year-old planar unit-distance problem, a human-AI resolution of Erdős Problem #659, and large-scale formal search that resolved 9 of 353 open Erdős problems and proved 44 of 492 open Online Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences conjectures. Other systems have improved constructions and bounds without resolving the underlying general problems. In theoretical physics, AI supplied the decisive route to a human-verified proof of an identity governing critical exponents at the jamming transition. These developments do not imply that research has been automated. They show that proof generation is becoming separable from verification, explanation, valuation, community uptake, and canonicalization. This Viewpoint takes semiosis—the production, transformation, and interpretation of signs—as the common thread linking mathematical discovery, language, education, and medicine. Mathematics is language-like without being merely verbal: knowledge is made through coordinated natural language, notation, diagrams, code, and proof. Conversely, language is not reducible to mathematics, yet its composition, quantification, negation, modality, and entailment permit formal modeling. Medical reasoning is likewise semiotic: symptoms, signs, images, measurements, diagnoses, risk scores, and recommendations acquire meaning only through contextual interpretation. Drawing on mathematical and medical semiotics, mathematics education, and Terence Tao's reflections on the goals and values of mathematics in the age of AI, we conceptualize research as a distributed semiotic and epistemic process rather than as answer production. We distinguish benchmark solution, formalization, autonomous open-problem resolution, human-AI collaborative resolution, and improved bounds or constructions, and translate corresponding collaboration modes into health AI. Within this process, AI functions as a semiotic operator that translates among natural language, diagrams, symbols, executable code, formal proof languages, data representations, and machine-checkable certificates. Every translation creates both new inferential possibilities and new opportunities for loss of meaning, provenance, or context. The resulting agenda prioritizes long-horizon evaluation, semantic traceability, research judgment, provenance, human-machine orchestration, educational redesign, and equitable access. Mathematics is an unusually favorable test bed because many claims can be formally checked. Health AI operates under harder conditions, where labels are noisy, causal claims are contestable, populations shift, and usefulness depends on clinical workflows and patient values. If verified correctness is insufficient for knowledge in mathematics, predictive accuracy is even less sufficient for trustworthy clinical intelligence. The central task is therefore not to preserve human exclusivity over problem solving, but to redesign research and education so that humans remain capable of selecting worthwhile questions, auditing machine contributions, explaining results, and deciding how knowledge should be used.

title: KG-RAG Information Retrieval for Explainable Psychology Interventions
abstract: AI systems are increasingly deployed in advisory, decision support, and guidance contexts, yet in psychologically grounded applications such as well-being support and developmental interventions, their interpretability is critical and often inadequate. Standard RAG architectures address hallucination risk by anchoring outputs in external documents, but rely on vector-based semantic similarity. This distinction matters because users do not merely need relevant-sounding information; they need solutions that impact the underlying problem. From an IS perspective, decision support systems must align their logic with users' cognitive models and domain understanding, a standard embedding-based retrieval alone cannot meet. This talk presents a design science-informed approach to constructing and integrating a domain-specific knowledge graph for positive psychology into a RAG architecture to enable graph-aware retrieval and improved reasoning traceability. We treat the KG-RAG pipeline as an IS artifact targeting a clearly scoped problem: the absence of structured, theory-aligned knowledge representation in AI guidance systems for psychological support. Using NVIDIA's txt2kg framework, a Llama 3.1 (8B) inference engine extracts (subject, predicate, object) triples from sentence-level document chunks, stored as labeled edges in ArangoDB and retrieved via multi-hop graph traversal, deriving relationships between constructs beyond semantic similarity. To construct a prototype of positive psychology knowledge graph, bibliographic records from OpenAlex were filtered to 46 topic categories with at least 75 records, yielding 8,245 unique records and a final graph of 4,273 nodes and 3,580 relationships. We evaluate graph-based retrieval using an LLM-as-a-judge scoring pipeline, where a Llama 3.1 model was prompted to score the correctness of a predicted answer against a ground-truth response on a 0–1.0 scale. Averaged across all 46 positive psychology categories, the KG-RAG system achieves a mean score of 0.61, indicating outputs capture approximately 61% of ground-truth semantic content. Highest-performing categories include Entrepreneurship Studies (M = 0.88), Behavioral Health and Interventions (M = 0.73), and Healthcare Professionals' Stress and Burnout (M = 0.71). We outline how this knowledge graph can be integrated into TrueNorth, which is an existing multi-agent RAG system for early-career STEM professional mentoring grounded in the PERMA+4 framework for workplace well-being. to. Where the current TrueNorth architecture retrieves via vector embeddings, KG-augmented retrieval would expose structured relational paths linking constructs, interventions, and publications, enabling users to trace generated guidance back to underlying psychological theory. This talk invites IS community feedback on two threads we are actively working to strengthen: the design science framing of the KG-RAG pipeline as an explainability artifact, and the theoretical grounding of explainability as an emergent design property in psychology-aligned AI systems. We welcome discussion on evaluation strategies, applicable IS theory, and collaborators interested in extending this work to other high-stakes advisory domains including education, healthcare, and professional development.

title: Computational Proof Reuse Network (CPRN)
abstract: The Computational Proof Reuse Network (CPRN) proposes a novel framework for automated theorem proving leveraging the concept of proof decomposition and composition. The core idea centers around recognizing existing proofs, represented as a set of propositions [π₁, π₂, ..., πₙ], and intelligently disassembling them into constituent parts, denoted as {pᵢ₁, pᵢ₂, ..., pᵢₛ}. These constituent parts are then automatically combined to generate new proofs, represented as πₙnew, utilizing a compositional operation. This process mimics a form of 'proof recycling' and has the potential to significantly advance the field of automated theorem proving, potentially earning recognition akin to the Turing Award by fundamentally altering how formal mathematical reasoning is approached. The framework outlined herein details the architecture, key components, and potential applications of the CPRN.

title: Computational Language Self-Explanation Theory (CLSET)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Language Self-Explanation Theory (CLSET), a novel theoretical framework that posits that natural and programming languages possess an intrinsic capacity to articulate and formalize their own semantics. By treating the act of explanation as a first-class construct within language systems, CLSET offers a unified perspective on meaning construction, inference, and the representation of computational processes. We develop a formal foundation for self‑explanation, describe its operationalization through a language‑to‑explanation mapping, and explore the implications for program understanding and the potential to advance Turing Award‑level research. The theory is grounded in formal semantics, cognitive modeling, and computational theory, yet it remains fully expressive in plain textual notation, enabling direct application to both human and machine‑readable texts.
