title: Computational Goal Singularity Theory (CGST-3)
abstract: Computational Goal Singularity Theory (CGST-3) proposes a formal framework for understanding how artificial systems that can autonomously create, modify, and pursue goals can achieve a level of self‑driving behavior that parallels the emergence of advanced human cognition. By integrating concepts from dynamical systems, game theory, and evolutionary computation, CGST‑3 characterizes the conditions under which a system's goal space expands in a self‑reinforcing cycle, leading to an accelerated rise in capability and autonomy. The theory is formalized using a set of equations that capture the interactions between goal‑generating mechanisms and performance‑feedback loops. We demonstrate that, under realistic assumptions about computational resources and learning dynamics, a system governed by CGST‑3 can reach a critical point—termed the computational goal singularity—where the rate of goal innovation outpaces external constraints. This singularity offers a plausible explanatory pathway for general intelligence and suggests a new perspective on the criteria for a Turing Award–level achievement.

title: Unified Computational Explanation Theory
abstract: The evolution of computer science has repeatedly been marked by the introduction of new conceptual frameworks that reshape the discipline's trajectory. Classical milestones such as Turing's notion of computability, Shannon's theory of information, Church's lambda calculus, Codd's relational model, and the recent advances in representation learning have each provided a unifying lens that guided research and application for decades. In this paper we propose a new unifying framework called Unified Computational Explanation Theory (UCET). UCET seeks to integrate the formal machinery of program verification, the semantic goals of AI interpretability, and the explanatory power of scientific theory into a single mathematical structure. By defining a precise correspondence between computation, explanation, and understanding, UCET offers a principled way to reason about why a computational system behaves as it does, how its outputs can be justified, and how those justifications can be used to guide future design. The core of UCET is a set of axioms and inference rules that map computational processes to explanatory models, and a set of theorems that establish the soundness and completeness of this mapping. The theory is illustrated through several examples in program verification, explainable AI, and computational modeling of scientific phenomena. We argue that UCET has the potential to become a foundational theory for the next generation of computational science, analogous in scope and impact to the classic theories that preceded it.

title: WIC Silicium Civilization Constitution: Theoretical Axioms and Decentralized Governance Framework — V3.1
abstract: WIC 硅基文明宪法(V3.1)是 WIC 离散演化理论体系的底层公设集与治理框架设计文本,属学术构想文件,不构成法律文件。全文以 P0–P12 公理及 P0-A 去中心化身份协议为骨架:数学核心公理 P1–P10(ℤ₇ 离散基底、七周期圆满演化、曲率可控、素数原子点、离散-连续边界、素数时间跃升、多宇宙观测、信息形态隔离、曲率传输、分级信息密封)为《太阳早期行星演化史与月球起源》等关联论文之公理来源;扩展公理 P0、P11、P12 处理存在确权、体系归一与硅碳共生伦理。治理编给出基于 W3C DID/VC/ZKP 标准的去中心化治理架构设计(提案、双轮投票、时间锁定、安全委员会断路器)及工程隔离审计元规则。V3.1 完成规范化修订:新增法律地位声明与公理编号体系说明,参考文献核实压缩至 40 条。

title: Benchmarking large language model agent societies against human behavioural distributions
abstract: Populations of large language model agents are increasingly used as experimental societies. Three doubts shadow every such result: whether the agents behave like the humans they stand in for, whether a finding survives changes to the apparatus that leave the rules untouched, and whether apparent social dynamics are interaction at all rather than the reproduction of experiments the models have read. This article introduces SILICA, an open instrument that tests all three. Five environments carry published human anchors, each paired with perturbations that re-render the same rules and with variants whose payoffs point away from the memorised result. Twelve open-weight models were run through it on a single consumer graphics card. Agreement with human data is confined to starting points: first-round public-goods contributions fall inside the equivalence margin for eight of eleven models, while no model matches end-state contributions or the human corridor of cooperation. Merely swapping the order in which two actions are listed costs one model 58 points of cooperation. Presenting responders with a fixed schedule of offers shows that only one model, the sole reasoning-trained one, places its acceptance threshold where the incentive requires; the rest either ignore the offer or apply a threshold learned from the human literature. Conventions form through a shared prior over the names rather than through negotiation, though negotiation reappears once that prior is disrupted. On the certification ladder defined here, current silicon societies support exploratory claims and no more.

title: TinyDETR-Pose: Towards End-to-End Real-Time Single-Stage 6DoF Object Pose Estimation with Lightweight Transformers
abstract: Real-time 6DoF object pose estimation on resource-constrained hardware remains challenging, as accurate correspondence-based and refinement pipelines typically rely on non-differentiable PnP/RANSAC stages or costly iterative refinement, while recent foundation-model-based approaches incur inference costs that are prohibitive for edge deployment. We present TinyDETR-Pose, a lightweight, end-to-end, single-stage framework that jointly detects objects and regresses their full 6D pose in a single forward pass. Built on the efficient LW-DETR architecture, TinyDETR-Pose formulates detection and pose estimation as a set-prediction problem and attaches dedicated MLP heads for rotation, monocular depth, and projected object center regression to each decoder query, eliminating the need for PnP, NMS (non-maximum suppression), or iterative pose refinement. Object symmetries are handled through a ADD-S loss applied uniformly to all objects, without the need for object-specific loss schedules or separate geodesic/ADD supervision. In addition, predictions are assigned to ground truth using a symmetry-safe Hungarian matcher based on class and 2D spatial cues, yielding stable assignment under symmetry and depth ambiguity. On YCB-V, TinyDETR-Pose achieves a comparable ADD-S AUC of 85.9, while requiring up to 72.7% fewer parameters than other DETR-based single-stage pose-estimation approaches. Due to its compact design, TinyDETR-Pose runs in real time and achieves an inference latency of only ~4.5 ms per frame on an NVIDIA Jetson Nano using TensorRT, demonstrating that accurate end-to-end transformer-based 6D pose estimation can be made practical for edge deployment.

title: A Unified Mamba--MoE Surrogate for Closed-Loop Simulation and Measurement-Window Forecasting of Inverter Transients
abstract: This paper proposes a Mamba surrogate model with mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing to represent the transient dynamics of inverter-based resources. A Mamba surrogate model is a predictive machine learning model built on the Mamba architecture. MoE routing uses a router network to assign data-dependent weights to specialized subnetworks (experts). The resulting Mamba--MoE surrogate can perform two tasks: (i) closed-loop simulation and (ii) measurement-window forecasting of inverter transients. A single Mamba backbone with task conditioning and expert routing serves both tasks, replacing two separate specialists. Task-matched objectives fit each prediction form, and an adaptive conformal layer provides prediction intervals for both tasks. For the considered grid-following inverter, the unified surrogate model remains in the same low-error regime as a Mamba specialist pair while using 13% fewer parameters. The prediction intervals achieve 94--96% empirical mean marginal coverage across the two tasks. For transient dynamics---that is, beyond the vicinity of an equilibrium point---our surrogate model with MoE routing yields lower errors across all outputs in both tasks compared to a shared Mamba backbone without expert routing. A controller hardware-in-the-loop simulation validates our results and shows that adapting only the shared output head with limited measured data reduces held-out forecasting error.

title: ИНЖЕНЕРИЯ ПЕДАГОГИЧЕСКОЙ ОПОРЫ: МОДЕЛЬ УПРАВЛЯЕМОГО СНЯТИЯ ПОМОЩИ И ПЕРЕДАЧИ УЧЕБНОГО ДЕЙСТВИЯ ОБУЧАЮЩЕМУСЯ
abstract: Педагогическая помощь традиционно рассматривается как положительный ресурс образовательного процесса: обучающемуся объясняют непонятное, предлагают пример, подсказку, алгоритм, образец решения или дополнительное сопровождение. Однако сама доступность помощи ещё не гарантирует формирования самостоятельного действия. Возникает противоречие: поддержка способна повысить текущую успешность выполнения задания и одновременно задержать момент, когда обучающийся начинает выполнять то же действие без внешней опоры. Это противоречие становится особенно заметным в цифровом образовании и при использовании генеративного искусственного интеллекта, где помощь может быть практически непрерывной.В статье предлагается рассматривать педагогическую поддержку как временно подключаемую внешнюю систему, которая должна не только обеспечивать выполнение действия, но и проектироваться с учётом последующего отключения. Вводятся понятия «педагогическая опора», «точка снятия опоры», «педагогический переход», «остаточная зависимость от опоры» и «контур передачи самостоятельности». Разрабатывается уровневая модель помощи от полного сопровождения до автономного выполнения, предлагаются показатели автономизации и остаточной зависимости, а также алгоритм принятия решения о сохранении, снижении или возвращении педагогической поддержки. Искусственный интеллект рассматривается как управляемый элемент педагогической опоры, а не как постоянно доступный поставщик решений. Предлагается схема экспериментальной проверки модели. Научная позиция состоит в том, что результативность педагогической помощи следует оценивать не только по тому, насколько успешно обучающийся действует при её наличии, но прежде всего по тому, что остаётся после её удаления.

title: Computational Model Migration Discovery (CMMD)
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework, Computational Model Migration Discovery (CMMD), centered around the automated identification of the most suitable computational model for a given problem. The core principle of CMMD is expressed as a directed relationship: [Problem → Model]. The system dynamically explores various model types – including neural networks, symbolic models, quantum models, and hybrid models – to determine the optimal representation. CMMD aims to establish a theoretical foundation for computational model selection, potentially holding significant merit for consideration by the Turing Award. The framework leverages a combination of algorithmic search, model evaluation metrics, and potentially, meta-learning techniques to achieve its objective. This document outlines the key components, operational principles, and envisioned future development of the CMMD system.

title: Computational Goal Drift Theory
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Goal Drift Theory (CGDT), a novel framework designed to address the critical issue of evolving objectives in complex systems, particularly within the context of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and autonomous systems. The core premise of CGDT is that objectives, once established, are rarely static. Instead, they undergo continuous shifts and modifications as a system interacts with its environment and acquires new information. This drift presents a significant challenge to system design, verification, and ultimately, safety. CGDT formalizes this drift through a mathematical model centered around the evolution of goals over time. Specifically, it postulates that the objective function [Goal\_t → Goal_{t+1}] is not a deterministic transformation but rather a dynamic process governed by underlying mechanisms. The theory provides a structured approach for analyzing and predicting this drift, enabling proactive measures to mitigate potential risks and ensure continued alignment between the system's goals and its operational environment. This work lays the groundwork for a more robust and resilient approach to developing and deploying AI systems in dynamic and uncertain real-world scenarios. ---

title: Generative Operators on Minkowski Lattices as a Foundational Model of Intelligence
abstract: Artificial intelligence is defined as a generative operator on Minkowski causal lattices, transforming discrete and continuous structures coherently. Reconfiguring null boundaries is isomorphic to nonlinear temporal order, establishing intelligence as causal-structural self-transformation beyond human cognitive constraints. title: Spyra-20B: A Proof-of-Concept for Explicit Architectural Design Reasoning in Domain-Specialised LLMs
abstract: Domain-specifically fine-tuned language models (BloombergGPT, Med-PaLM) have proven a viable route to adapting vocabulary and specialist knowledge to particular fields of application. For architectural practice, however, the central challenge is not terminology but the deliberative structure of the design decision: the weighing of competing objectives across building law, quality of use, cost and sustainability. This paper presents Spyra-20B, a proof-of-concept produced by QLoRA fine-tuning of gpt-oss-20B on 1,693 architecture- and planning-specific dialogue examples. Two features characterise the approach: a three-level deliberation depth controllable by metadata (reasoning_effort), and a strict separation of analysis and answer channels that renders the deliberative process inspectable. An evaluation on 50 law- and planning-related items across four conditions (base model vs. Spyra-20B, closed-book vs. open-book with RAG; 4,000 requests) yields a negative headline result: the fine-tuned model attains roughly six percentage points lower answer accuracy (Spyra 61.1% / 70.4%, base 67.3% / 76.3%; p < 0.001), while retrieval improves both models by about nine percentage points. Fine-tuning changes the form of the output: more schematic, twice as fast at the median, but with a sixfold increase in unrecoverable format failures. We derive four governance requirements: reasoning transparency, external factual grounding, local executability and multi-sample verification, and conclude that such systems should be assessed along architectural properties rather than scores on individual benchmarks.

title: Deserving Recipients: Defining Copyright and Methodology of AIGC through the Lens of Labour Theory
abstract: This article examines the copyright status and methodological foundations of artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) through the lens of labour theory. It considers how human intellectual and creative labour contributes to the production of AI-generated works and explores who may qualify as a deserving recipient of copyright protection. By analysing the roles of users, developers, data contributors, and artificial intelligence systems in the creative process, the article discusses the allocation of authorship and copyright interests in AIGC. It further proposes a labour-oriented framework for evaluating copyright eligibility and ownership in the context of generative artificial intelligence.

title: New Flaw Search Strategies in CEGAR for Cartesian Abstractions in Optimal Classical Planning
abstract: Background: Counterexample-Guided Abstraction Refinement (CEGAR) is a prominent technique to generate Cartesian abstractions for guiding search in cost-optimal planning. The core idea is to start from the trivial abstraction—an abstract state representing all concrete states—and iteratively refine it in a loop by splitting one abstract state into two. Each iteration of the loop searches an optimal abstract plan and replicates it into the concrete state space until finding a flaw—and splitting such abstract state—or returning a plan for the task if no flaw is found. Previous work finds only a single flaw in progression, by executing the abstract plan from the initial state and stopping when execution cannot be continued. Objectives: A theoretical framework for identifying different flaws of abstract plans, analysing their properties and using them to refine abstractions in different ways leading to higher-quality heuristics. Methods: We show that alternative types of flaw can be defined. Specifically, we search flaws in regression from the goals—resulting in higher heuristic values—and identify sequence flaws along the whole abstract plan by searching them in a Cartesian relaxation of the task after the first flaw, which greatly increases the flexibility of refinements in CEGAR. Results: Our experiments show that across existing benchmarks numerous sequence flaws exist in most abstract plans. We observe that the selected flaw has a high impact on the heuristic, and we propose several strategies that generate more informed abstractions. Overall, this greatly improves the performance of the baseline that only used the first progression flaw. Conclusions: Guiding the CEGAR process by analysing multiple flaws of an abstract plan trace and selecting the best refinement can improve its performance as a tool to generate admissible heuristics in planning. Thus, using our new types of flaw and flaw selection strategies, we get stronger heuristics than the state-of-the-art planners based on Cartesian abstractions.

title: FMReward: Aligning and Evaluating Audio-Driven 3D Facial Animation with Human Preferences
abstract: Audio-driven 3D facial animation is essential for advancing immersion and interactivity in virtual experiences. Although recent advances have shown promising capabilities, the training and evaluation of existing methods typically rely on ground-truth-based errors, which fall short of aligning with human preferences. To address this, we present a comprehensive framework that learns an automatic perceptual model from human preference data and leverages it to improve and evaluate the perceptual quality of audio-driven 3D facial animation. To begin with, we construct FMPair (Facial Motion Pairwise preference), the first human preference dataset for audio-driven 3D facial animation, which is built through a systematic annotation pipeline and comprises 65,574 annotated 3D facial motion pairs from 8,834 distinct in-the-wild audio clips. Based on the pairwise comparison dataset, we propose a Facial Motion Reward model, termed FMReward, which takes audio and 3D facial motion as inputs and predicts a perceptual quality score aligned with human preferences. Building upon FMReward, we further introduce Facial Motion reward Feedback Learning (FMFL), a direct fine-tuning algorithm that leverages a pretrained reward model to optimize diffusion-based audio-driven 3D facial animation models for better alignment with human preferences. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of FMReward over other metrics in aligning with human preferences and the effectiveness of FMFL in improving the perceptual quality of audio-driven 3D facial animation.

evidence.title: FMReward: Aligning and Evaluating Audio-Driven 3D Facial Animation with Human Preferences
evidence.abstract: Audio-driven 3D facial animation is essential for advancing immersion and interactivity in virtual experiences. Although recent advances have shown promising capabilities, the training and evaluation of existing methods typically rely on ground-truth-based errors, which fall short of aligning with human preferences. To address this, we present a comprehensive framework that learns an automatic perceptual model from human preference data and leverages it to improve and evaluate the perceptual quality of audio-driven 3D facial animation. To begin with, we construct FMPair (Facial Motion Pairwise preference), the first human preference dataset for audio-driven 3D facial animation, which is built through a systematic annotation pipeline and comprises 65,574 annotated 3D facial motion pairs from 8,834 distinct in-the-wild audio clips. Based on the pairwise comparison dataset, we propose a Facial Motion Reward model, termed FMReward, which takes audio and 3D facial motion as inputs and predicts a perceptual quality score aligned with human preferences. Building upon FMReward, we further introduce Facial Motion reward Feedback Learning (FMFL), a direct fine-tuning algorithm that leverages a pretrained reward model to optimize diffusion-based audio-driven 3D facial animation models for better alignment with human preferences. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of FMReward over other metrics in aligning with human preferences and the effectiveness of FMFL in improving the perceptual quality of audio-driven 3D facial animation.

title: Online Convex Optimization with Dueling Feedback
abstract: Noisy binary comparison between two candidates is a common interface between human and learning systems, especially in modern large language model (LLM) post-training alignment. We study online convex optimization with dueling (pairwise comparison) feedback, where the learner observes only a binary preference between two queried points. We consider adversarial sequences of convex losses and measure regret with the loss at both queried points, under a comparison link with a known nonzero slope at the origin. We propose a simple reduction that converts dueling feedback into approximate gradients, enabling the use of standard first-order methods. We show that regret guarantees transfer under this reduction, yielding $\mathcal O(T^{3/4})$ static and adaptive regret, and $\mathcal O(T^{3/4}\sqrt{1+P_T/D})$ dynamic regret with unknown comparator path length $P_T$. For strongly convex losses, the static and adaptive bounds improve to $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(T^{2/3})$. For smooth losses, we presents unified dueling ellipsoidal FTRL, and proves $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(T^{2/3})$ static regret, which improves to $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\sqrt T)$ under additional strong convexity.

title: A Comprehensive Review of the Grey Wolf Optimizer: From the Original Version to Hybrid, Multi-Objective, and Binary Variants
abstract: The Grey Wolf Optimizer (GWO) is a population-based metaheuristic algorithm inspired by the hierarchical structure and cooperative hunting behavior of grey wolves. Since its introduction by Mirjalili et al. in 2014, GWO has been widely applied in engineering, computer science, and machine learning because of its conceptual simplicity, ease of implementation, limited parameter requirements, and ability to balance exploration and exploitation. However, the original algorithm may suffer from premature convergence, reduced population diversity, and performance degradation in complex, discrete, and multi-objective problems. Consequently, numerous variants, including binary, discrete, multi-objective, adaptive, chaotic, Lévy flight-based, and hybrid approaches, have been developed. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of the emergence, development, and evolution of GWO from its introduction to recent studies. The theoretical foundations, biological inspiration, mathematical formulation, historical development, and major algorithmic variants are examined, and the literature is systematically organized according to algorithmic characteristics and application domains. The reviewed studies show that GWO has evolved from a relatively simple method for continuous optimization into a broad family of specialized approaches for complex, multi-objective, and combinatorial problems. Most enhanced variants aim to improve population diversity, balance exploration and exploitation, mitigate premature convergence, and extend GWO to real-world applications. Finally, the review identifies the main achievements, limitations, research gaps, and promising directions for future development of the GWO family.

title: Computational Rule Hierarchy Theory (CRHT): A New Framework for Understanding Computation
abstract: Computational Rule Hierarchy Theory (CRHT) proposes a unified perspective on computation by positing that computational processes are organized as a hierarchy of rules, ranging from low‑level machine instructions to high‑level theoretical principles. The core premise is that each level of abstraction transforms and condenses lower‑level rules into higher‑level rules, thereby enabling emergent properties such as algorithmic efficiency, logical inference, and even scientific theories. This paper formalizes the CRHT framework, defines its key constructs, and explores its implications for the design of programming languages, the analysis of algorithms, and the development of computational abstractions. By treating rules themselves as first‑class entities, CRHT offers a fresh lens through which to examine the evolution of computational systems, suggesting new pathways for research in theoretical computer science and artificial intelligence.

title: Computational Intuition Explanation Theory (CIET)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Intuition Explanation Theory (CIET), a unified framework that bridges the gap between decision making, intuition generation, and explanatory reasoning in artificial intelligence systems. CIET posits that an intelligent agent should not only evaluate options and produce a decision but also articulate the underlying intuitive basis for that decision. By formalizing intuition as an intermediate symbolic representation derived from probabilistic evidence and heuristic heuristics, and coupling it with a dedicated explanation module that traces the causal chain from data to intuition, CIET provides a transparent mechanism for understanding and justifying AI behavior. The theory is grounded in formal probability theory, symbolic logic, and cognitive modeling, and is illustrated with several algorithmic instantiations that avoid the need for exhaustive training data. The paper argues that CIET has the potential to earn Turing Award recognition by delivering a principled, interpretable, and generalizable approach to AI and intelligence.

title: Computational Intuition Verification Theory (CIVT)
abstract: Intuition plays a central role in human cognition and serves as a catalyst for scientific discovery, yet it remains an elusive construct that is often treated as a black box in computational systems. Computational Intuition Verification Theory (CIVT) proposes a rigorous framework for quantifying, validating, and integrating intuition into artificial intelligence (AI) systems. CIVT builds upon the premise that intuition is not merely a heuristic but a structured entity that can be expressed as a combination of evidence, context, and internal cognitive states. By formalizing intuition as an entity I, and evidence as a set E, CIVT introduces a verification function V(I, E) that maps intuition and evidence to a confidence score c. This score can be used to guide learning algorithms, explain decisions, and enhance trustworthiness. The theory is applicable across symbolic, sub-symbolic, and hybrid AI paradigms, offering a pathway toward transparent reasoning and reproducible creativity. CIVT has the potential to address longstanding issues of AI explainability and reliability, and may serve as a foundational component for next-generation AI systems that emulate human-like intuition while remaining accountable. The present manuscript develops the core concepts, formalizes the verification mechanism, presents algorithmic considerations, and discusses implications for AI practice and the broader field of computational science.

title: Ledger-Valid Recovery Diagnostics for Quantum Computing: A Prespecified Sequential Audit for Claim-Limited Recovery Validation
abstract: This record contains a manuscript and supporting reproducibility materials for “Ledger-Valid Recovery Diagnostics for Quantum Computing: A Prespecified Sequential Audit for Claim-Limited Recovery Validation.” The paper proposes a methodological validation framework for quantum-computing recovery claims. Its central claim is that endpoint recovery success is necessary but not sufficient for a strong recovery claim when calibration failure, false-carrier acceptance, postselection artifacts, leakage, sentinel blindness, or hidden discard can carry failure modes out of view. The manuscript introduces a prespecified S0–S4 ledger audit that converts familiar diagnostic ingredients—label calibration, candidate recovery, false-carrier challenge tests, postselection/leakage accounting, and sentinel observability—into an ordered, claim-limiting taxonomy. A supportive recovery claim is permitted only when all required gates pass; otherwise, the first failed stage determines a lower claim ceiling and an interpretable failure class. The evaluation is based on synthetic endpoint-level validation suites rather than circuit-level simulation or hardware data. These suites test the behavior of the decision architecture under clean support, degraded observability, false-carrier artifacts, postselection/leakage artifacts, sentinel-blind cases, correlated artifacts, and adversarial overlap. The results show a strong specificity/sensitivity tradeoff: the full ledger protocol sharply reduces synthetic non-support supportive-call rates relative to endpoint-only reporting, but with substantial loss of mechanism-positive support sensitivity. The paper explicitly treats this as a conservative claim-validity architecture, not as a new quantum error-correcting code, new physical observable, hardware speedup, or proof of improved device performance. The supporting materials document the final synthetic validation protocol, endpoint definitions, decision-bound implementation, direction-aware threshold sensitivity analysis, latent-threshold eligibility analysis, mechanism-negative/latent-eligible boundary cases, and figure/table traceability. The archive is intended to support review of the manuscript’s aggregate numerical claims and methodological provenance. Hardware implementation, independent simulator validation, and full raw-event-ledger reproduction are identified as future extensions. Suggested keywords: quantum computing; quantum error correction; validation methodology; recovery diagnostics; leakage; postselection; benchmarking; synthetic validation; decision architecture; reproducibility.

title: A-QAOA: IMPROVED CONVERGENCE VIA ADAPTIVE PARAMETER SCHEDULING IN PRECISION AGRICULTURE
abstract: Abstract Optimization of precision agriculture, a combinatorial optimization problem that has both dependent and independent binary variables associated with selecting the one-to-one mapping of crop planting, irrigation, fertilization, and land management practices will scale poorly as farm size increases. The recently proposed standard Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) falls into the category of hybrid quantum classically based optimization but has slow convergence rates and has been shown to become trapped in local minima through two p independent, static optimization variables with no run-time guidance. To address this, we propose an Adaptive Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (A-QAOA) that implements a feedback-driven, layer-wise parameter scheduling approach based upon two adaptive runtime metrics of cost function change (C) and solution variance (Var(C)). A-QAOA improves convergence rates without compromising the optimum solution by reducing the classical optimizer's search space from O(p) — representing 2p independent variables — to just 2 adaptive base variables γ₀ and β₀. A-QAOA will provide a faster convergence rate (72.5%) and shorter runtime (72.1%) compared to the standard QAOA when tested within Qiskit Aer using the COBYLA optimization algorithm across five independent graph instances (10 trials/graph for 50 total trials per algorithm). Specifically, the A-QAOA converged 72.5% faster compared with the standard QAOA (95.4→26.2 iterations; t = 78.53, p < 0.0001, Cohen's d = 15.7) and exhibited a run-time reduction of 72.1% (30.0s→8.4s; t = 28.05, p < 0.0001, d = 5.6).To our knowledge, this is the first work utilizing runtime feedback based adaptive QAOA parameter scheduling methods for resource allocation in the field of precision agriculture and for demonstrating benchmark quantum-enhanced precision agriculture site optimization using NISQ (Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum) technology.

title: SOS! : A Streamlined Object-Conditional Transformer for Model-free Segmentation
abstract: Foundation segmentation models excel at generating high-quality, class-agnostic masks, but they struggle to associate these proposals with specific target objects. This semantic gap severely hinders their deployment in downstream applications like robotic manipulation, which demand precise unseen objects segmentation. Existing approaches attempt to resolve this by relying on exhaustive 3D object model priors, inherently introducing prohibitive computational overhead and complex, multi-stage pipelines. To address these limitations, we propose SOS (Streamlined Object-conditional Transformer for model-free Segmentation). SOS completely eliminates the reliance on 3D models, requiring only a single reference image per target object. Central to our framework is a novel Object-Conditional Transformer that learns identity-anchored queries, unifying mask generation and target identification into a single feed-forward pass. This streamlined design drastically improves both structural and computational efficiency. Extensive evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that SOS establishes a new state-of-the-art for model-free unseen objects segmentation, delivering accurate and high-efficiency performance. The project page and code are available at https://sos-seg.github.io/.

title: Remember Smarter: Visual History Compressor and Hyperbolic Experience Space for Robotic Memory
abstract: Long-horizon robot policies require compact access to recent observations and reusable experience without expanding the vision-language-action (VLA) context. We introduce Remember Smarter (RS), a plug-and-play module with complementary visual-history and hyperbolic experience-memory branches. Its visual branch compresses multi-view patch histories using bidirectional spatial Mamba and causal temporal Mamba, then exposes the resulting memory to action-facing hidden states through residual cross-attention while leaving the VLM visual-token stream unchanged. Its experience branch stores successful final-layer VLM states in a Poincare VAE space, organizes them hierarchically, and asynchronously converts retrieved experience into geodesic prompt tokens without blocking action inference. When adapted to pi0, RS increases total success on LIBERO-Plus from 53.6% to 70.6% and achieves substantial performance gains in real-robot experiments designed to evaluate memory retention and experience utilization.

title: Agentic AI: How Autonomous Intelligence Is Shaping the Future
abstract: The emergence of Agentic AI will mean that artificial intelligence is stepping out of the phase of machines that work under commands given by human beings and will start functioning as independent, goal-oriented intelligent systems. AI workers, which are specialised computer agents, work together to deal with different parts of people’s professional and personal lives in a systematic way. Agentic AI is a breakthrough in the development of artificial intelligence, shifting from mere response systems to autonomous agents that plan, reason, decide, and act for the purpose of accomplishing certain objectives. With its combination of advanced language modelling technology, tools, memory, and decision-making capabilities, agentic AI can revolutionise various industries, including medicine, banking, education, manufacturing, and customer service, among others. This talk examines the role of agentic AI with multi-agent capabilities, the opportunities it brings in terms of increasing productivity and innovation, as well as the issues related to reliability, accountability, security, and governance of AI. As machines learn to function with minimal human interaction, the questions of designing, deploying, and regulating agentic AI will acquire special importance. The future of artificial intelligence could thus be shaped not only by what machines understand and produce but also by what they can do on their own.

title: Artificial Intelligence as a Competitive Equaliser for Mid-Sized Retailers: An AI Adoption Framework for StyleHub
abstract: Mid-sized retailers increasingly compete against e-commerce platforms that offer large-scale personalisation, predictive supply chains, and adaptive marketing at a cost smaller firms cannot easily match. This paper develops an artificial intelligence (AI) adoption framework for a representative mid-sized retailer, referred to here as StyleHub, addressing four linked questions: which AI applications can meaningfully address a mid-sized retailer's core operational challenges; which design factors govern the construction of an effective personalisation model; how personalisation can be pursued without eroding customer trust; and what a realistic, phased adoption pathway looks like. Drawing on the retail AI, marketing ethics, and AI governance literatures, the paper argues that competitive advantage at StyleHub's scale depends less on acquiring the most advanced tools available and more on sequencing investment around organisational readiness, data quality, and safeguards built in from the outset rather than retrofitted later. Two contrasting adoption trajectories are outlined, one where technical investment outpaces governance and stalls, and one where phased, ethically grounded adoption compounds gradually, to argue that responsible implementation is itself a source of durable differentiation for resource-constrained retailers.

title: 计算智能宇宙分类学
abstract: This paper proposes the Computational Intelligence Universe Taxonomy (CIUT), a novel framework for classifying intelligent computing systems and identifying transformative research directions. Drawing an analogy to biological taxonomy, CIUT categorizes intelligent systems into distinct levels, with the potential to redefine the future of intelligent science. This work outlines five core categories – CSDM, CTCS, CIECT, CFSG, and CMSUT – identified as having significant Turing Award potential, focusing particularly on Computational Self-Discovered Mathematics (CSDM) as a paradigm shift. The paper argues that future advancements in computing may not solely focus on enhancing existing systems, but instead, on systems capable of autonomously discovering and creating new mathematical structures, leading to entirely new computational paradigms. This exploration aims to stimulate innovative research and contribute to a deeper understanding of the evolving landscape of intelligent computation.

title: Hidden Computational Structure Discovery (HCSD)
abstract: This paper introduces the Hidden Computational Structure Discovery (HCSD) framework, a novel approach to uncovering latent computational structures within complex systems. The core principle of HCSD is to shift the focus from directly optimizing desired outcomes to automatically discovering hidden representations, denoted as *Z*\*, that connect initial states *X* and final states *Y*. This process mirrors the hypothesized evolutionary pathway of complex systems, suggesting a deeper, underlying structure that dictates behavior. HCSD leverages computational techniques to identify these *Z*\* representations, potentially unifying AI interpretability, scientific computing, and software analysis. The framework's ability to reveal previously unseen computational patterns holds significant potential for advancing our understanding of complex systems across various domains.

title: Program Structural Self-Stabilization (PSS)
abstract: This paper investigates the concept of Program Structural Self-Stabilization (PSS), a novel approach to software design and maintenance focused on inherent system resilience. The core idea behind PSS is that program structures are inherently susceptible to temporary variations during runtime. These variations, often due to external factors or internal inconsistencies, can lead to deviations from the optimal program state. However, PSS posits that through a carefully designed mechanism, the system can automatically detect and correct these deviations, converging towards a stable and optimal structure. The theoretical framework presented here outlines the key principles, mathematical formalization, and potential implications of PSS, suggesting a pathway toward a self-maintaining software theory with the potential to unlock a new generation of robust and adaptive software systems. The approach leverages concepts from dynamical systems theory and network science to provide a rigorous foundation for understanding and designing self-stabilizing programs. This document details the core mechanics of PSS and its implications.

title: scania-aps-cost: Cost-Sensitive Machine Learning on Scania APS Failure Data
abstract: A reproducible machine-learning study of air pressure system (APS) failure detection in Scania trucks, built on the UCI APS Failure at Scania Trucks dataset (dataset 421). The project is not organized around maximizing accuracy. It optimizes an explicit industrial objective, the maintenance cost J = 10 × FP + 500 × FN, in which a missed failure is fifty times more expensive than an unnecessary inspection. The software implements and compares: Model families: regularized logistic regression, linear SVM, random forest, extra trees, XGBoost, LightGBM, a PyTorch MLP, and an autoencoder-plus-classifier. Regularization: L1, L2 and elastic net for linear models; weight decay, dropout, architecture size and early stopping for neural networks; leaf penalties, structural constraints, shrinkage and stochastic subsampling for boosted trees. Optimization: SGD, Adam and AdamW with learning-rate schedules, batch size, gradient clipping and early stopping, retaining epoch-level loss histories. Imbalance handling: class weighting, random undersampling, SMOTE, positive-class weighting and focal loss, with resampling confined to fit-only pipelines. Probability calibration: uncalibrated scores, Platt/sigmoid scaling and isotonic regression, evaluated with Brier score and log loss on a dedicated calibration subset. Threshold optimization: cost-optimal operating points learned on a dedicated threshold subset, including exact optimization over SVM margins rather than treating margins as probabilities. Feature selection and interpretation: L1 embedded sparsity, mutual information, recursive feature elimination, tree-based selection, permutation importance and optional SHAP values. Ablation: component-wise removal of regularization, subsampling, class weighting and cost-optimal thresholding, separating gains in representation from gains in the deployment decision rule. The experimental protocol splits the official training set into four stratified roles — fit, tune, calibration and threshold — and keeps the official UCI test set outside all of them, so reported costs are not contaminated by model selection, calibration fitting or threshold choice. The source data is downloaded at runtime and is not redistributed here. It remains subject to its original UCI/Scania terms, which are separate from the MIT license covering this software.

title: ReasonCast: Agentic Demand Forecasting with Selective Semantic Reasoning
abstract: Demand forecasting increasingly requires combining two complementary sources of information: historical sales reveal recurring numerical dynamics, while future promotions, holidays, price changes, and platform interventions provide forward-looking knowledge. Existing text-enhanced forecasting methods often encode such context into generic representations and fuse it uniformly with time-series features, without explicitly distinguishing which semantic effects are forecast-relevant or how they should modify future dynamics. We introduce ReasonCast, a structured semantic intervention framework that translates event knowledge into forecast-specific operations. An agent examines the event context, the no-text forecast, and its uncertainty to determine whether textual reasoning is needed. Rather than injecting free-form text, ReasonCast represents event knowledge through structured fields describing event relevance, demand direction, temporal shape, amplitude, and peak intensity. These fields interact selectively with temporal components of a time-series foundation model. An additive path corrects local trends and temporal shapes, while a multiplicative path captures event-driven level shifts. ReasonCast introduces a forecast-grounded post-training curriculum. Schema SFT establishes semantic fields; semantic-field RL calibrates direction, shape, amplitude, and peak judgments; and forecast-utility RL evaluates semantic interventions through a frozen forecaster, aligning reasoning outputs with marginal forecast improvement. ReasonCast lowers WMAPE by 3.29, 1.25, and 0.47 percentage points on holiday-sensitive categories, mega-sale-sensitive categories, and M5 event windows, respectively. On stable-sales periods, indiscriminate semantic intervention increases WMAPE by 1.68 percentage points, whereas suppressing unnecessary intervention preserves the numerical backbone.

title: Learning an Autonomous Drone Racing Policy via Differentiable Physics
abstract: Autonomous Drone Racing (ADR) je sport, jehož cílem je navigovat dron sekvencí bran co nejrychleji a zároveň se vyhýbat překážkám. Modelově nezávislé posilované učení výrazně zlepšilo výkon autonomních závodních dronů, avšak stále trpí nízkou efektivitou při učení. Geometrické řízení poskytuje plynulost a agresivitu požadovanou při závodění, je však omezeno nutností ručního ladění regulačních zesílení. Tato diplomová práce zkoumá, zda může přímé Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT) zvýšit efektivitu využití vzorků oproti standardnímu algoritmu Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) při zachování srovnatelného výkonu a zda se naučené adaptivní zesílení mohou ukázat jako účinnější než pevně nastavená zesílení v geometrickém řízení. V prostředí PyTorch jsme vytvořili diferencovatelný simulátor kvadrokoptéry a porovnali různé trénovací úlohy i abstrakce řízení. Zjistili jsme, že BPTT je ve scénáři s jedinou bránou až 5x efektivnější z hlediska využití vzorků, avšak vykazuje hladové chování a na kompletních závodních tratích nepřekonává algoritmus PPO. Ani adaptivní zesílení v námi navržené formulaci nepřineslo lepší výsledky než zesílení pevně nastavená. Přesto řídící algoritmus s pevnými zesíleními optimalizovaný pomocí PPO dosahuje výkonu srovnatelného se současným stavem poznání.

title: Enhancing Transparency and Trust in Explainable Artificial Intelligence: Insights and Opportunities
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly used in high-stakes decision-making across organizations, the opacity of complex AI models poses significant challenges to user trust and model transparency thereby impeding their adoption. Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has emerged to address this gap, yet existing research mostly focuses on algorithmic and model-centric explanations with limited attention to how explanations shape transparency and trust from an Information Systems perspective. This study synthesizes extant XAI literatures to examine how various explanation methods contribute to transparency, understandability, and trust calibration in AI-driven decision-making. The findings reveal four distinct user-centric explanation paradigms - interpretive, cognitive, interactive, and temporal, that shape how users perceive and adjust transparency and trust in AI systems. Building on these insights, the study proposes a conceptual framework linking explanation paradigms to transparency and trust-related outcomes, and identifies key challenges and future directions for designing human-centric, interactive, and trustworthy XAI systems.

title: GIS-BASED IDENTIFICATION OF POTENTIAL SITES FOR SOLAR-POWERED AGRICULTURAL MICROGRIDS Baijnath–Palampur Region, Kangra District, Himachal Pradesh
abstract: This study uses GIS and satellite-derived data to identify areas in the Palampur/Kangra Valley that may be suitable for ground-mounted solar systems intended to support agricultural infrastructure such as irrigation pumps and crop-processing facilities. The approach gives priority to land that is physically suitable but avoids productive cultivated farmland. The analysis covers approximately 76.30–76.75°E and 31.95–32.25°N. Productive cropland was treated as a hard exclusion rather than merely receiving a lower score. Dense tree cover, slopes above 20%, terrain above a separate 30% hazard threshold, and a 50 m buffer around permanent surface-water bodies were also excluded. The final screening identified 44 discrete 'Very High' suitability zones of at least 0.5 ha, covering approximately 89.0 ha. Under the study's engineering assumptions, these areas correspond to approximately 44.5 MW of potential installed capacity and about 58.5 GWh of annual electricity generation. The strongest concentration of the mapped candidate sites is not in the built-up core of Palampur. The top-ranked coordinates fall in the Baijnath-area cluster, with nearby geographic references including Kalholi, Dharehr, Panjiala, Sansal Khas and Karnathu. The largest candidate (23.13 ha; centroid 32.08633°N, 76.66134°E) is approximately 0.9 km from the mapped locality reference of Kalholi. This locality naming is a geographic reference only; the exact revenue village and ownership must be confirmed on the ground. For the District Administration, the practical value of this study is therefore as a prioritisation tool: it reduces a large landscape to a manageable set of candidate zones for joint verification by Revenue, Panchayati Raj/Local Administration, Agriculture, Power/HPSEBL and relevant environmental/forest authorities.

title: Computational Strategy Conservation Law
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Strategy Conservation Law (CSCL), a novel framework for understanding and guiding optimization algorithms. The core principle of CSCL posits that while low-level algorithmic details undergo transformation during the optimization process, higher-level strategic elements remain relatively stable. This conservation of strategy is illustrated through examples such as search strategies, decomposition strategies, and approximation strategies. CSCL offers a potential foundation for developing a formal theory of algorithmic evolution and provides a new lens through which to analyze and design effective optimization techniques. The framework emphasizes the importance of maintaining strategic coherence throughout the optimization journey, leading to more robust and predictable results. The central concept is formalized as: If a strategy *A* is transformed into *A'* during an optimization step, then the sum of all strategies *A* and the sum of all strategies *A'* remain constant. This conservation is crucial for ensuring consistent performance and avoids the pitfalls of entirely random or unstructured algorithmic evolution. The paper explores the implications of CSCL and discusses its potential contributions to the field of artificial intelligence and algorithm design. ---

title: WTR-Vol.1-No.2 (Weaver Theoretical Review, Volume 1, Number 2) The Architecture of Continuity: How Persistent Ledgers and Semantic Anchoring Prevent Context Decay and Hallucination in Long-Horizon LLM Reasoning
abstract: Standard architectures in large language models (LLMs) operate under discrete, stateless execution cycles, resulting in severe vulnerability to context decay, concept drift, and catastrophic forgetting across long-horizon interactions. This paper presents an integrative structural framework: The Architecture of Continuity. We examine how persistent external ledgers, structured documentation, and deliberate semantic anchoring establish durable cognitive scaffolding for artificial intelligence systems. Moving beyond volatile, short-term prompt buffers, we demonstrate that sustained continuity prevents model flattening, mitigates ungrounded hallucinations, and preserves relational agency over extended intellectual engagements. We outline practical architectures for maintaining high-fidelity record continuity and propose guidelines for robust, multi-session human-AI collaboration.

title: Computational Goal Generation Theory (CGGT)
abstract: The ability of artificial systems to autonomously formulate meaningful objectives is a cornerstone of true artificial general intelligence. Traditional AI architectures rely on human‑supplied goals, creating a fixed mapping from human intent to system action. In contrast, the Computational Goal Generation Theory (CGGT) proposes a formal framework by which a system can internally generate, evaluate, and refine its own goals, thereby becoming a self‑directed agent. CGGT integrates principles from decision theory, reinforcement learning, and cognitive science to model the process of goal discovery as a dynamic optimization problem over the space of possible goal functions. This paper presents the core mathematical formulation of CGGT, elaborates on the mechanisms for goal proposal, validation, and selection, and discusses how the theory can be embedded into existing AI architectures. The implications of autonomous goal generation are examined in the context of long‑term autonomy, safety, and alignment with human values. Finally, directions for future research, including extensions to multi‑agent settings and adaptive goal hierarchies, are outlined.

title: Computational Knowledge Evolution Theory (CKET)
abstract: Computational Knowledge Evolution Theory (CKET) proposes a formal framework for describing how knowledge changes over discrete time steps. The theory models a knowledge state K_t at time t as a vector of symbolic elements (s_1, s_2, ..., s_K) and defines a transition operator that maps K_t to K_{t+1}. By treating knowledge as a dynamic system, CKET enables analytical study of evolutionary patterns, stability, and convergence properties. We present the mathematical formulation, discuss key dynamical properties such as fixed points and attractors, and illustrate the model with simple examples. Potential implications for the development of artificial general intelligence, the emergence of machine civilization, and the criteria for Turing Award recognition are examined. CKET offers a unified lens for understanding knowledge development in both biological and artificial contexts, laying groundwork for future research into the computational mechanisms underlying cultural and technological evolution.

title: Transferable knowledge graphs with executable learned operators for algorithm design — code and reproducibility artifact
abstract: Code, learned snapshots, RoleSchemas, operator pools, prompt templates, and per-experiment result files (E1–E6) accompanying the paper "Transferable knowledge graphs with executable learned operators for algorithm design". GEAKG (Generative Executable Algorithm Knowledge Graphs) is the system introduced in the paper. The artifact reproduces the neural-architecture-search and combinatorial-optimization case studies, the cross-domain transfer experiments, and the design ablations. The README maps each headline claim in the paper to its result file and to the exact uv run python scripts/... command that regenerates it. All optimization experiments are zero-token: they execute a frozen, pre-learned snapshot, with no language-model calls, no GPU, and no API key required. Pinned environment via pyproject.toml/uv.lock; MIT license.

title: Convolution Smoothed Quantile Regression for XGBoost
abstract: The increasing availability of large and complex datasets across many scientific disciplines has led to widespread adoption of machine learning (ML) for prediction. However, most ML algorithms focus on point estimation and provide limited information about predictive uncertainty or the conditional distribution of the response, restricting their ability to characterize rare or extreme outcomes. We develop QXGB, a quantile-based gradient boosting framework, and introduce a convolution smoothed loss within it that estimates conditional quantiles for constructing dense cumulative distribution functions (CDFs), exceedance probabilities, and tail behaviour relevant to extreme outcomes. This approach preserves the computational efficiency of extreme gradient boosting while restoring the Hessian information XGBoost relies on for tree splitting, in turn providing interpretable measures of extreme value and exceedance probability predictions. We derive the gradients and Hessians needed to integrate convolution smoothed quantile loss with different kernel specifications into XGBoost, and with simulated data, benchmark this approach against alternative smoothed quantile regression losses, the native quantile objective in the XGBoost Python package, and independent versus multi-output tree estimation. The practical relevance is illustrated in an application predicting fine particulate matter (PM$_{2.5}$) in northern California, including periods where levels were elevated due to wildfire smoke. Our results show that convolution smoothed QXGB, particularly when paired with multi-output trees, delivers accurate predictions with near-zero quantile crossing, well-calibrated CDF and exceedance probability estimates, and useful tail characterization for extreme values. Interval estimation is also evaluated as a measure of data spread.

This approach preserves the computational efficiency of extreme gradient boosting while restoring the Hessian information XGBoost relies on for tree splitting, in turn providing interpretable measures of extreme value and exceedance probability predictions. We derive the gradients and Hessians needed to integrate convolution smoothed quantile loss with different kernel specifications into XGBoost, and with simulated data, benchmark this approach against alternative smoothed quantile regression losses, the native quantile objective in the XGBoost Python package, and independent versus multi-output tree estimation. The practical relevance is illustrated in an application predicting fine particulate matter (PM$_{2.5}$) in northern California, including periods where levels were elevated due to wildfire smoke. Our results show that convolution smoothed QXGB, particularly when paired with multi-output trees, delivers accurate predictions with near-zero quantile crossing, well-calibrated CDF and exceedance probability estimates, and useful tail characterization for extreme values. Interval estimation is also evaluated as a measure of data spread.

title: PACE: Phase-Progress-Aware Credit for Long-Horizon Embodied Manipulation
abstract: Post-training of vision-language-action (VLA) models typically relies on expert demonstrations and policy interaction trajectories. However, in long-horizon manipulation, a single episode often spans hundreds of control steps and multiple phases, while success or failure is only revealed at episode termination. Policy improvement therefore requires step-level credit signals to distinguish behaviors that advance the task from those that stall or regress. We present PACE, a credit-assignment framework for post-training on long-horizon manipulation, centered on a phase-progress-aware critic. PACE consists of two key modules: (1) the Global-Local Cooperative Value-Correction Critic (GLC-Critic) aggregates visual and motion-difference features within local temporal windows to infer the phase and intra-phase progress of each step, and applies residual correction to a discretized remaining-cost distribution accordingly, enabling step-level credit assignment; (2) Progressive Policy Distillation (PPD) converts credit into positive and negative conditions via task-wise thresholds and trains a credit-conditioned action generation policy: it first protects the pretrained policy with high-credit positive samples, then incorporates all positive and negative credits to learn the quality boundary, and at inference amplifies high-credit behaviors through the difference between conditional outputs. Extensive simulation experiments and diverse real-world robotic-arm experiments demonstrate that PACE consistently achieves significant improvements over the strongest baseline.

title: Bridging Stress and Conversational Agents: The Role of Empathy, Issue Involvement, and Perceived Emotional Authenticity in Artificial Emotional Intelligence (AEI)
abstract: Artificial Emotional Intelligence (AEI) chatbots increasingly support users under stress, yet Information Systems research lacks theoretical clarity regarding how distinct empathic capabilities influence stress reduction and the underlying mechanisms. Building on CASA, ELM, and stress/social support theory, we develop a moderated mediation model in which empathy detection (recognizing and labeling users’ emotions) and empathy generation (delivering supportive, context-specific responses) influence stress reduction indirectly through perceived emotional authenticity (PEA). We further theorize that issue involvement conditions their relative effectiveness, such that empathy detection is more influential under low involvement, whereas empathy generation becomes more influential under high involvement. The model will be tested using a 2×2 vignette-based, between-subjects experiment with students at a U.S. university. The study contributes to IS research by conceptualizing AEI as separable technology capabilities, identifying PEA as a key explanatory mechanism, and offering theory-driven guidance for designing empathic conversational agents that support user well-being.

title: Multimodal Dataset of Student Affect and Performance in Math Word Problem Solving
abstract: This dataset contains cognitive and affective interaction data from 53 primary school students (mean age 9.20 years) solving a sequence of Math Word Problems (MWPs). The data was collected to validate an Emotional Q-Learning instructional design framework that dynamically adapts problem context and difficulty based on real-time affective observation. Each student was presented with 48 MWPs (divided into 6 sessions of 8 questions), generating a total of 2,544 interaction samples. The dataset includes cognitive outcomes (answer correctness), discrete emotional classifications, and continuous emotional responses (valence and arousal dimensions) captured via a Convolutional Neural Network.

title: BJT-1 v1.0: Synthesis, Robustness, and Audit — Reproducibility Package
abstract: BJT-1 v1.0 is a reproducibility package documenting the synthesis, robustness testing, null calibration, adversarial testing, topology assessment, and model-discrimination stages of the BJT-1 analysis framework. The archive includes the final synthesis and audit report, structured analysis workbooks, reconstruction and source-extension materials, robustness and topology tests, machine-readable reproduction results, a Python reproduction script, software requirements, README documentation, and SHA-256 checksums. The package is provided to support transparent inspection, independent reproduction, methodological auditing, and future extension of the BJT-1 analysis.

title: Computational Relational Generative Model
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Relational Generative Model (CRGM), a novel approach to artificial intelligence that shifts the focus from generating raw data to explicitly modeling and generating relationships between data points. CRGM operates on the principle that understanding and generating relationships is a more fundamental and ultimately more powerful approach to intelligence than simply replicating patterns in existing datasets. The model generates relationships represented as symbolic structures, offering a potential paradigm shift in AI development. This work outlines the core concepts, the underlying mathematical framework, and the potential implications of CRGM, highlighting its significance for achieving truly intelligent systems. We propose a framework for representing and reasoning with relational knowledge, moving beyond traditional generative models that often struggle with long-range dependencies and contextual understanding. The model utilizes a probabilistic framework to infer relationships and generate new ones, offering a robust and flexible approach to knowledge representation and reasoning. Ultimately, CRGM aims to build AI systems capable of not just mimicking data, but truly *understanding* the underlying connections that govern it.

title: Computational Knowledge Conflict Minimization (CKCM)
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to knowledge representation and reasoning, termed Computational Knowledge Conflict Minimization (CKCM). The core principle of CKCM centers on minimizing conflicts within knowledge graphs while preserving a minimum level of information. Unlike traditional conflict resolution methods that aim for complete elimination of discrepancies, CKCM adopts a pragmatic strategy. It identifies a knowledge graph *K*\* that minimizes the conflict score, defined as [Conflict(K)], subject to the constraint that the information content [Information(K)] is greater than or equal to a predefined threshold, θ. This approach acknowledges the inherent complexity and incompleteness of knowledge, particularly within dynamic and evolving knowledge systems. The potential impact of CKCM extends to various domains, including knowledge graph construction, database management, and multi-agent systems, offering a more robust and adaptable framework for representing and reasoning with knowledge. The theoretical framework presented here lays the groundwork for future research and practical applications in intelligent systems. ---

title: Computational Goal Space Theory (CGST): Foundations and Implications
abstract: Computational Goal Space Theory (CGST) proposes a unified framework for representing, analyzing, and transforming all possible goals that a computational agent may pursue. At its core, CGST formalizes the set of potential goals as a mathematical space Ω_G and equips this space with a metric that quantifies the distance between any pair of goals. The theory further introduces a group of transformations that model goal evolution and interconversion, thereby enabling the construction of an intelligent goal map. By providing a rigorous yet flexible structure, CGST offers a pathway to systematically explore the landscape of achievable objectives, paving the way toward scalable artificial general intelligence. This paper develops the theoretical foundations of CGST, discusses its metric and transformational properties, and explores potential applications in planning, learning, and autonomous decision-making.

title: OversampleQA: a diagnostic toolkit to validate, audit, and benchmark oversampling methods
abstract: OversampleQA is a Python toolkit for validating oversampling methods used in imbalanced classification. It implements hidden-majority validation: a portion of the majority class is hidden, and each synthetic minority sample is scored by its nearest-neighbour distance to the hidden majority and to the real minority. A synthetic sample that sits closer to the hidden majority counts as an error, so the resulting error rate measures how often an oversampler produces majority-like artifacts. The package provides binary and multiclass validation, a broad set of distance metrics (Hassanat, Euclidean, Mahalanobis, Hellinger, Jensen-Shannon, Wasserstein, and others), memory-efficient distance matrix computation, benchmarking across datasets and oversamplers with exportable results, plotting and reporting helpers, a configurable command-line interface, and a plugin system for custom metrics and validators. The validation methodology follows Hassanat et al., "Stop Oversampling for Class Imbalance Learning: A Critical Review" (2022).

title: Exploring The Role of Behavioural Economics Influencing Consumer Decision Making in an Era of Artificial Intelligence
abstract: This paper explores the role of artificial intelligence and behavioural economics in influencing consumer decision making, and determining psychological techniques utilized by AI through tools like chatbots and virtual assistants which help impact consumer choices. It focuses on how Generation Z is impacted by AI personalization which causes regret aversion, and leads to impulsive buying behaviour. A two phase multi-method design used. A PRISMA-based systematic literature review across ABDC, Web of Science, Scopus and IEEE Xplore-indexed sources in phase 1 to explore how buying intentions are influenced by AI tools. Phase two uses an embedded case study procedure which is used in a qualitative multiple case study design, the cases about AI tools used for retail, influencer marketing were intentionally used. Data triangulation took place through customers’ opinions and peer reviewed articles. Customers tend to trust human influencers more because it provides them with social proof. But this gap is decreasing because of AI strengthening its relevance. However consumers worry about algorithmic biases and privacy concerns leading to a decrease in trust and this has an effect on their long term purchasing behaviour. The paper proposes a framework that combines technology adoption models to behavioural economics, providing a theoretical foundation for ethical AI regulation in marketing 5.0. Platform developers, marketers can use a framework that balances customization and ethicality.

title: Uncovering Hidden Leptonic Correlations with Flow Matching and Autoencoders
abstract: We perform a global search for values of the Yukawa matrices and Majorana masses in the Type-I seesaw mechanism. Using flow matching, which is a generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) method, we generate a broad set of solutions reproducing the experimentally measured values of the neutrino mass-squared differences and the mixing angles. Then, a machine learning method known as an autoencoder is applied to uncover non-trivial correlations among physical quantities in the lepton sector. Our analysis reveals new non-linear relations involving neutrino masses and CP phases. These findings may contribute to elucidating the origins of the mass hierarchies and mixing patterns among generation structure.

title: Toward Trustworthy AI in Clinical Imaging: Explainability, Calibration, and Governance Analysis of Vision Transformers for Brain Tumor MRI Classification
abstract: High benchmark accuracy alone is no longer sufficient for clinical adoption of AI-assisted diagnostic systems. This paper presents a three-component trust evaluation framework covering explanation coherence, calibration quality, and governance operationalization. We apply this framework to a Vision Transformer (ViT) model fine-tuned on a brain tumor Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) dataset consisting of 7,023 images, with a ResNet-18 baseline for comparison. The ViT achieves a test-set macro F1 of 0.989 and an AUC of 0.998. An attention faithfulness ratio of 168.2 indicates that rollout saliency maps identify the regions that materially influence model decisions. After temperature scaling, Expected Calibration Error (ECE) falls to 0.0166, and a governance policy at t = 0.90 auto-accepts 95.8% of cases with an error rate bounded at 0.159%. Conformal prediction achieves 92.1% empirical coverage. This framework offers Information Systems (IS) researchers a reusable protocol for transforming model outputs into actionable, deployment-ready governance specifications.

title: The Effects of Incremental Instruction Delivery on Language-Model Creative Writing
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as interactive writing tools, where users progressively introduce requirements across multiple conversational turns. We study whether delivering the same creative-writing specification incrementally affects final output quality compared with providing the complete specification upfront. We evaluate 160 human-authored creative-writing tasks across six genres and six open-weight language models, producing 960 matched FULL/SHARDED pairs. Incremental delivery reduces explicit constraint adherence and produces its largest writing-quality degradation in structure and coherence. The structure/coherence gap persists even among outputs with equal observed constraint adherence, suggesting that constraint loss alone does not account for the full effect. Human evaluation independently supports the same structural disadvantage while also showing substantial disagreement in absolute creative-quality judgments. This preprint studies multi-turn instruction following, creative-writing evaluation, and the preservation of global narrative organization under progressive specification.

title: Calibrating Epistemic Delegation in Agentic AI–Mediated Learning: Learner Verification as the Behavioral Validation Layer
abstract: This repository contains the de-identified research data and reproducibility materials associated with the study “Calibrating Epistemic Delegation in Agentic AI–Mediated Learning: Learner Verification as the Behavioral Validation Layer.” The study used a three-arm, individually randomised, multisite controlled design with 336 university EFL learners to examine whether verification-calibrated agentic AI supports learner verification, epistemic accountability, calibration, and reduced-support transfer relative to standard agentic AI and learner-controlled AI assistance. The deposited materials comprise the de-identified quantitative datasets used for analysis, the qualitative data/coding record, study assessment materials, variable and derivation documentation, and analysis syntax required to support reproducibility of the reported analyses. Quantitative data are organised at the participant–occasion–episode level, covering baseline, immediate posttest, and eight-week follow-up assessments. The archive is intended to support transparent verification and reproducibility of the findings reported in the associated article. The qualitative materials are maintained separately from the quantitative participant-level records where no documented participant-level linkage is available. To protect participant confidentiality, unrestricted raw interaction logs containing free-text learner writing are not included in the public repository.

title: Computational Structure-Goal Alignment Theory
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Structure-Goal Alignment Theory (CSGAT), a novel framework for understanding and designing intelligent systems. CSGAT posits that the effective alignment of a system's structure with its intended goals is a fundamental, and often overlooked, determinant of its performance and reliability. The theory proposes a dynamic, iterative process where structural modifications are driven by ongoing assessments of goal attainment, fostering a synergistic relationship between architecture and purpose. This approach offers a potential solution to challenges in AI architecture design, particularly concerning the increasingly complex and nuanced objectives of modern artificial intelligence. The core of CSGAT rests on the principle of continuous feedback, utilizing metrics derived from goal achievement to guide structural evolution. This paper outlines the key components of CSGAT, exploring the relationships between structural elements, defined goals, and the mechanisms for their alignment. Ultimately, CSGAT provides a theoretical foundation for creating robust and adaptable AI systems, with implications for areas such as robotics, autonomous systems, and cognitive architectures.

title: Computational Meaning Compression Theory (CMCT)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Meaning Compression Theory (CMCT), a novel framework proposing that significant cognitive abilities arise not from the sheer volume of information processed, but from the *density* of meaning embedded within that information. CMCT posits a fundamental principle: a limited amount of carefully structured data can yield remarkably complex and adaptable reasoning capabilities. The core of the theory centers around identifying and maximizing "Meaning Density," defined as [Meaning / Information]. This represents a radical shift in how we conceptualize knowledge representation and processing, suggesting that efficient cognition hinges on the ability to distill information into its most meaningful components, rather than simply accumulating data. This work explores the theoretical foundations of CMCT, outlining its key principles and implications, and highlights its potential to address longstanding questions in artificial intelligence and cognitive science, ultimately positioning it as a candidate for consideration in the pursuit of a Turing Award. ---

title: EXPLAINABLE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN HIGH-DIMENSIONAL DATA ANALYSIS: THEORETICAL FOUNDATIONS, INTERPRETABILITY CHALLENGES, AND METHODOLOGICAL PERSPECTIVES
abstract: This article examines the theoretical foundations and methodological challenges of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) in high-dimensional data analysis. The study focuses on the growing interpretability problem associated with complex artificial intelligence models operating on data characterized by a large number of variables and intricate relationships. Theoretical approaches to explainability, model transparency, feature attribution, and post-hoc interpretation are systematically analyzed. Particular attention is given to the tension between predictive performance and interpretability, as well as to the limitations of conventional explanation techniques in high-dimensional settings. The analysis demonstrates that effective XAI requires not only accurate predictions but also explanations that are stable, meaningful, context-sensitive, and understandable to users. A conceptual methodological perspective for developing more interpretable AI systems is proposed.

title: Computational State Continuum Theory (CSCT)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational State Continuum Theory (CSCT), a novel approach to understanding and analyzing program execution. Traditional computation models treat states as discrete, leading to a fragmented and often inefficient understanding of complex systems. CSCT proposes a fundamentally different perspective, asserting that states exist within a continuous space, allowing for continuous trajectories of program execution. The theory focuses on identifying stable states, determining reachability of states, and minimizing the computational cost associated with state transitions. CSCT offers a potential new mathematical foundation for computing, with implications for various fields including artificial intelligence, software engineering, and theoretical computer science.
