title: Flagged Unitary–Replacer Channels: Sector-Resolved Choi-Moment Spectral Completion, Fixed-Fidelity Choi-Entropy Fibers, and Joint Transparency–Spectrum Identifiability
abstract: Within flagged unitary–replacer channels, optimized recovered entanglement fidelity is spectrally incomplete: it fixes weighted transparency but not the hidden replacer spectrum or conditional Choi entropy. For a resolved positive-probability sector with known transparency 0 ≤ a < 1, we prove a family-specific noncommutative triangular transfer from conditional Choi moments M2, . . . , Md to hidden-spectrum power sums. Recursive inversion, Newton–Girard identities, and a rank-one step recover the unordered replacer and conditional Choi spectra, including multiplicities and zero eigenvalues. The order-d threshold is sharp within the consecutive sector-resolved hierarchy: every truncation below d fails local injectivity on positive simple-spectrum chambers. At fixed dimension and flag distribution, we also determine the complete homogeneous and heterogeneous fixed-fidelity Choi-entropy intervals, including lower/equality structure, interval filling, and heterogeneous optimizer geometry, while retaining the established quantum-Fano upper envelope. With transparency unknown, the consecutive map (a, λ) ↦ (M2, . . . , Md+1) is generically locally invertible on the positive ordered simple-spectrum interior for every d ≥ 2. Global uniqueness holds in d = 2, 3; for the specific map F4 = (M2, M3, M4, M5), d = 4 exhibits an exact open two-sheet ambiguity with exactly two ordered physical inverse branches, while d ≥ 5 remains unresolved. At a = 1, the moments lose all replacer-spectrum information. The results are family-specific and assume sector-resolved access; they do not imply universal channel reconstruction, tomography, or resource optimality.

title: Towards Trustworthy AI: A Unified Framework for LLM Hallucination Detection and Mitigation via System Reliability Theory
abstract: Hallucination has been a fundamental issue for large language models (LLMs) and multimodal large language models (MLLMs) in areas where reliability and explainability are particularly valued. Current studies usually perceive the hallucination issue from two aspects: hallucination detection and mitigation. However, these two aspects are not independent in nature, and a more profound similarity exists between them. This paper surveys more than 100 recent studies on hallucination in the LLM and MLLM fields (2023-2026) and unifies the framework structure for hallucination from two perspectives: signal source and intervention time. Grounded on System Reliability Theory, by comparing methods including probing-based uncertainty estimation, multi-agent self-consistency, retrieval-based grounding, and verification/graph-based decoding control, we reveal the similarities and differences in these methods in terms of their costs, latency, and model accessibility. Ultimately, we present a novel and unifying point of view on hallucination mitigation, establishing a solid foundation towards trustworthy AI.

title: Dynamic Cost-Sensitive Fraud Detection for Real-Time Financial Transactions: A Budget-Aware Three-Way Execution Framework
abstract: Internet-finance platforms must decide, for every arriving transaction and within milliseconds, whether to approve it, challenge it, or decline it. Recent cost-sensitive work has shown that mapping a calibrated fraud probability and the transaction amount to a three-way execution action is far more profitable than thresholding a risk score. Deployed systems, however, operate under two constraints that this line of work does not model: the number of customers a platform may inconvenience is capped by operational capacity, and both the score distribution and the fraud prior drift while labels arrive only after a verification delay. We present DyCoDe, a dynamic cost-sensitive execution framework that addresses both. First, an amount-proportional false-decline cost generalises the constant-cost model and reshapes the decision geometry. Second, the three-way policy is augmented with an online dual price on intervention capacity, updated by a proportional-integral controller, so that the realised friction tracks a prescribed budget. Third, all adaptation—prior tracking, calibrator refitting, and scorer refresh—is gated by a calibration-residual CUSUM designed for extreme imbalance and by a validated-promotion test, so the system moves only when evidence warrants it. On 144,807 real card transactions evaluated prequentially with delayed labels, DyCoDe attains the cost of the best static three-way policy while using 43.1% less customer friction and halving hard declines, and it costs 23.0–48.0% less than a clairvoyant static threshold operating at the same friction, coming within 0.6% of the offline optimal dual price. On a controlled drifting stream it lowers cost by 13.5% over a non-adapting pipeline at equal friction while retraining 43% less often than a fixed schedule. Scoring, calibration and policy evaluation take 0.583 ms per transaction on a single core.

title: Explicit Content Generation in Text-to-Image Models: Training Mechanisms, Moderation Failures, and Safety Limits
abstract: Text-to-image generative models have rapidly progressed in realism and controllability, enabling wide adoption across creative and commercial domains. However, these systems also generate explicit and harmful imagery in ways that are difficult to prevent reliably. This paper reviews the technical foundations of modern image generators, with emphasis on diffusion-based modeling, latent representations, and multimodal text-image alignment. It then surveys documented moderation ap-proaches and explains why common safeguards fail under paraphrasing, adversarial prompting, long-tail semantics, and distribution shift. Finally, the paper discusses safety limitations that arise from likelihood-based learning objectives and proposes directions for more robust mitigation, including stronger data governance, multimodal safety alignment, evaluation-driven red teaming, and lifecycle monitoring.

title: Computational Algorithm Genetics (CAG)
abstract: Computational Algorithm Genetics (CAG) proposes a novel approach to problem-solving inspired by the principles of biological genetics and evolutionary algorithms. The core concept revolves around simulating an algorithm's evolution through processes analogous to mutation, selection, and inheritance. This framework aims to create adaptable and robust algorithms, potentially laying the groundwork for algorithmic approaches in life sciences. The presented methodology utilizes a discrete representation of algorithms, allowing for quantifiable variation and selective pressures. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of CAG, focusing on the mathematical modeling of these genetic operations and their impact on algorithm convergence and performance. This paper outlines the fundamental principles, formalizes the key processes, and discusses the potential implications of CAG for algorithm design and its relevance to complex biological systems. ---

title: Computational Boundary Crossing Theory (CBCT)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Boundary Crossing Theory (CBCT), a novel framework designed to address the limitations of current computational models by proposing a shift in focus from simply processing information to actively traversing conceptual boundaries. CBCT posits that true intelligence emerges not from the accumulation of data, but from the ability to effectively navigate and manipulate distinctions between different states, representations, and knowledge domains. The theory is structured around a series of interconnected concepts, including the existence of 'crossing boundaries' (B_i), and the development of computational, expressive, and intelligent capabilities through a defined progression: C_1 → C_2. This paper explores the theoretical underpinnings of CBCT, outlining its potential to facilitate a significant leap in computational theory, potentially earning recognition as a Turing Award-worthy contribution. The core argument is that traditional computation treats information as a monolithic entity, while CBCT advocates for a dynamic model where systems actively 'cross' boundaries to achieve higher levels of understanding and problem-solving. The theory's impact could revolutionize areas such as artificial intelligence, cognitive science, and theoretical computer science.

title: Computational Memory Morphology Theory (CMMT)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Memory Morphology Theory (CMMT), a novel framework that fundamentally shifts our understanding of memory within computation. Traditional approaches often treat memory as a passive storage mechanism for data. CMMT proposes that memory is fundamentally a structured morphology – a dynamic system composed of form, relation, and history. We posit that memory isn't simply about recalling static data points, but about the intricate interplay of these three components, influencing computational processes. The core equation defining this theory is: M = (Form, Relation, History). This framework allows for a more nuanced understanding of how memory shapes cognitive processes, potentially offering a new architectural paradigm for artificial intelligence, with implications for the Turing Award. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of CMMT, demonstrating its potential to explain diverse phenomena currently attributed to complex neural networks and advanced AI systems. The theory provides a foundational model for future research in computational memory and its application within various domains. ---

title: Computational Knowledge Merge Algebra (CKMA)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Knowledge Merge Algebra (CKMA), a novel algebraic framework designed to address the complex challenges of integrating knowledge from multiple disparate systems. Traditional approaches to knowledge merging often rely on simple union operations, which fail to adequately capture the nuances of knowledge representation, including conflict resolution, redundancy elimination, inconsistency detection, and evidence weighting. CKMA provides a rigorous mathematical foundation for managing these aspects, employing a tensor product operation to represent the combined knowledge state. The core of CKMA lies in its ability to explicitly model and manipulate these critical knowledge-related factors. This framework offers a promising path toward developing robust multi-agent knowledge sharing systems and holds significant potential for advancements in areas such as artificial intelligence, data integration, and expert systems. The system's ability to handle conflicting information, redundant knowledge, and varying degrees of evidence makes it a powerful tool for constructing more reliable and accurate knowledge representations. ---

title: Computational Explanation Transfer Theory (CETT)
abstract: The proposed Computational Explanation Transfer Theory (CETT) introduces a novel paradigm for transferring knowledge across domains by focusing on the transfer of explanatory structures rather than merely model weights or feature representations. CETT formalizes explanations as compositional structures that map from observations to rationales, and defines a transfer operator that reconfigures these structures to accommodate new contexts while preserving semantic coherence. By decoupling explanation generation from model architecture, CETT offers a principled pathway to enhance transfer learning, improve model interpretability, and potentially unlock new capabilities for general artificial intelligence. This paper presents the core concepts, mathematical formalism, theoretical properties, and prospective impact of CETT, providing a foundation for future research and practical applications in explainable and transferable AI systems.

title: Computational Language Fusion Theory (CLFT): A Foundation for Next‑Generation Programming Paradigms
abstract: Computational Language Fusion Theory (CLFT) proposes a systematic framework for combining two or more programming languages to create a new language that inherits and extends the computational capabilities of its constituents. By formalizing the fusion operation L1 + L2 → L3, CLFT demonstrates how the expressive power of the fused language can surpass the sum of its parts, potentially enabling breakthroughs in algorithmic efficiency, safety, and developer productivity. This paper presents the core principles of CLFT, establishes its theoretical underpinnings, explores its implications for language design, and outlines directions for future research.

title: PhaseLoRA: Control-Regime-Conditioned Low-Rank Adaptation for Continuous-Action Vision-Language-Action Policies
abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) is a natural way to adapt pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies, but most adapter designs apply temporally static updates throughout a control rollout, overlooking the phase-dependent nature of continuous-action manipulation. Such policies traverse distinct regimes, including approach, contact transition, grasping, transport, and placement, each requiring different adaptation behaviors. We propose \textbf{PhaseLoRA}, a lightweight LoRA parameterization that conditions adaptation at each action-chunk prediction step using two weakly supervised descriptors: fine-control tendency and event/boundary intensity. PhaseLoRA modulates the LoRA left factor in the action expert, allowing the effective low-rank update direction to vary over time while keeping the backbone largely frozen. On LIBERO, PhaseLoRA improves average success rate by 12.2 points over a matched-parameter high-rank LoRA baseline and outperforms stronger LoRA variants. Ablations show that random temporal modulation and scalar gating do not reproduce the performance of the full model, while update-direction analyses reveal structured temporal variation associated with the predicted control descriptors. These results establish within-trajectory conditioning as an effective lightweight PEFT axis for continuous-action VLA policies.

title: Generative AI-Assisted Learning: An Unexpected Detrimental Interaction with Self-Explanation
abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly used for learning, yet its fluent explanations may bias metacognitive monitoring and learning outcomes. Drawing on metacognitive monitoring and generative learning frameworks, we tested whether a brief Self-explanation Task (SeT) reduces the Illusion of Knowledge (IoK) and improves performance. In a between-subjects experiment, mechanical engineering and computer-science students learned wind-turbine principles via (1) an 18-page PDF, (2) GenAI dialogue, or (3) SeT followed by GenAI. IoK was defined as the discrepancy between post-learning judgments and test scores (memorization, transfer). IoK effects were weak (trend-level for memorization; null for transfer). The clearest result was an unexpected interaction: SeT before GenAI impaired learning, reducing transfer relative to PDF and GenAI-only, especially for low-familiarity learners. These findings show that GenAI effects are nuanced and that self-explanation may hinder learning when prior knowledge is limited.

title: A Software-Engineered Hybrid Optimization Framework for Intelligent Routing in Wide Area Networks
abstract: As the number of Wide Area Networks (WANs) grows at an unprecedented pace, supported by cloud-native applications and AI-driven workloads, routing optimization has turned into a network engineering challenge as well as a necessity of the software engineering profession. In this paper, a hybrid optimization model of Genetic Algorithms (GA) and Tabu Search (TS) is proposed with the help of strategic oscillation to create intelligent routing paths in WANs. It is a framework that is designed to be modular, scalable and maintainable, which has adaptive modules that dynamically change the mutation rates in real time depending on live network telemetry. The proposed system, which is implemented in Python and represented by the NetworkX computation graph and bespoke algorithmic libraries, was 15% more efficient in terms of path and 33% higher in terms of convergence rate than typical GA-TS implementations. In addition to its algorithmic results, it includes best-practice software engineering features, including component decoupling, algorithm reusability and distributed-system integration readiness, that allow its use in large scale and software-defined WAN(SD-WAN) applications.

title: Lawrencium-103/OMSF-from-DIT: OMSF
abstract: Existing AI openness frameworks (OSAID, MOF) answer the producer's question , "what must a lab release?" but not the buyer's question: "can this organization legally and operationally deploy this model in this jurisdiction?" We present the OpenModel Synthesis Framework (OMSF), a buyer-side taxonomy with four components: a six-rung Openness Ladder (L0–L5) with L1 split into sub-grades (L1a scale-capped, L1b use-restricted, L1c non-commercial); a three-tier Source Provenance Protocol (P1–P3); a three-lens deployment frame for private, enterprise, and non-profit buyers; and an African Edge & Sovereign Infrastructure (AESI) annotation for zero-egress feasibility under low-power hardware. We apply OMSF to N = 821 graded open-weight LLMs drawn from the top 1500 text-generation models on the HuggingFace Hub (snapshot 31 July 2026), after excluding quantization mirrors and library test/CI fixtures. Three findings stand out. First, repository gating is strongly associated with license restrictiveness (χ2(1, N=821) = 86.95, p = 1.1 × 10−20, φ = 0.33): 55 of 59 gated models are L1. Second, permissively licensed models are more downloaded than restricted-license models (Mann–Whitney U = 67,623, p = 0.002; median L2 = 82,267 vs. median L1 = 54,852), contradicting a widely repeated procurement heuristic. Third, only 9 of 821 graded models (1.1%) declare support for any African language. Rules-variant inter-rater agreement is κ = 0.95 (almost perfect); full human IRR is planned

Second, permissively licensed models are more downloaded than restricted-license models (Mann–Whitney U = 67,623, p = 0.002; median L2 = 82,267 vs. median L1 = 54,852), contradicting a widely repeated procurement heuristic. Third, only 9 of 821 graded models (1.1%) declare support for any African language. Rules-variant inter-rater agreement is κ = 0.95 (almost perfect); full human IRR is planned

title: Computational Model Self-Competition (CMSC)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Model Self-Competition (CMSC) framework, a novel approach to scientific discovery based on evolutionary computation and competitive modeling. The core idea behind CMSC is to generate a population of candidate models, denoted as [M1, M2, ..., Mn], and subject them to a competitive process driven by a fitness function, [Fitness(Mi)]. Through iterative rounds of competition, the framework converges to an optimal model, represented as [M*]. This process mimics natural selection and offers a potentially powerful mechanism for automated hypothesis generation and model refinement. The theoretical underpinnings of CMSC are explored, highlighting its potential to contribute significantly to the field of automated scientific discovery and its alignment with the criteria for a Turing Award. This work lays the groundwork for future research and development within the CMSC framework, focusing on scaling the system, incorporating diverse fitness functions, and exploring its applicability across various scientific domains. ---

title: Computational Experience Self-Revision Theory (CESR): A Framework for Autonomous Error Correction in Intelligent Systems
abstract: Computational Experience Self-Revision Theory (CESR) proposes a novel paradigm for autonomous error correction in intelligent systems. By treating experiential data as a mutable knowledge base, CESR introduces a self‑revision mechanism that transforms erroneous experiences into constructive knowledge without external supervision. The theory builds upon principles of information theory, reinforcement learning, and self‑reflective cognition to formulate a formal model that captures the dynamics of experience quality, revision triggers, and revision outcomes. In this paper we present the theoretical foundations of CESR, develop a formal mathematical representation of the self‑revision process, and discuss its implications for the design of future autonomous systems. We argue that CESR provides a scalable, principled approach to error mitigation, which is essential for the advancement of autonomous agents capable of long‑term deployment in uncertain environments.

title: Computational Experience Dynamics (CED): A Framework for Modeling the Temporal Evolution of Knowledge in Adaptive Systems
abstract: Computational Experience Dynamics (CED) is introduced as a novel theoretical framework that captures how experience or knowledge within an adaptive system evolves over discrete time steps. By formalizing experience as a vector E_t that updates according to an experience evolution equation E_{t+1} = F(E_t, u_t, \epsilon_t), CED integrates environmental inputs u_t, internal states, and stochastic perturbations \epsilon_t to describe the trajectory of learning and adaptation. The core hypothesis of CED is that experience dynamics can be represented as a combination of deterministic learning functions and stochastic noise processes, enabling predictive modeling of system performance over time. This paper presents the mathematical formulation of CED, discusses its relation to classical learning theory and reinforcement learning, and illustrates its application through analytical examples that demonstrate convergence, stability, and the influence of resource allocation on learning efficiency. The results suggest that CED offers a principled way to design adaptive algorithms that can self‑adjust their learning rates and exploration strategies based on the evolving state of experience, potentially unlocking new avenues for long‑term autonomous learning systems.

title: Computational Explanation Singularity Theory (CEST-3)
abstract: Computational Explanation Singularity Theory (CEST-3) proposes a formal framework for understanding how the explanatory power of a computational system can, when surpassing a critical threshold, give rise to a self‑understanding state that is hypothesised to underlie the emergence of advanced artificial intelligence. The theory is built upon a set of mathematical definitions that model an explanation engine as a mapping from an input space to an explanation space, and a self‑explanatory loop that iteratively refines this mapping. We show that when the explanatory capacity, quantified by the mutual information between system states and generated explanations, exceeds a bound determined by the system's internal architecture, the system enters a regime where it can generate coherent internal narratives about its own operation. This regime is argued to provide the cognitive infrastructure for what we term "singularity" in the context of computational explanation. We discuss the implications of CEST-3 for the design of future AI systems, highlight its potential to contribute to the theoretical foundations of the Turing Award, and outline avenues for empirical verification.

title: Computational Intuition Space Theory (CIST)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Intuition Space Theory (CIST), a formal framework that models all possible intuitive states as points in a high‑dimensional space denoted Ω_I. Intuitions are represented by feature vectors (s_1, s_2, ..., s_K) where each component captures a distinct perceptual, affective, or conceptual attribute. The theory defines a metric d on Ω_I that quantifies the similarity between two intuitions and establishes a mapping M from Ω_I to a machine experience space E, thereby providing a principled method to build experiential maps for artificial systems. CIST bridges the gap between informal, subjective notions of intuition and rigorous computational modeling, offering potential pathways toward systems that can generate, reason about, and refine intuitive judgments. The paper outlines the core definitions, presents the mathematical structure of Ω_I, discusses relational dynamics among intuitions, and explores applications in machine learning and cognitive robotics. The absence of empirical data underscores the theoretical nature of the work, while the proposed constructs lay groundwork for future experimental validation and potential recognition of CIST as a foundational contribution in the field of computational intelligence.

title: Lipschitz Bandits with Arbitrary Feedback Delays
abstract: The Lipschitz bandit problem extends the traditional multi-armed bandit framework to continuous action spaces by assuming that the reward functions satisfy a Lipschitz condition. This work investigates Lipschitz bandits under arbitrary feedback delays, where reward signals are not received immediately upon taking an action but after an arbitrarily chosen delay. We consider both stochastic and adversarial reward settings, proposing an elimination-based algorithm and an EXP3-based algorithm, respectively. For both settings, our algorithms achieve a regret bound of $\tilde{O}\left(T^{\frac{d_z+1}{d_z+2}}+\sqrt{D}\right)$ over a time horizon $T$ with total delay $D$, where the main difference between settings lies in the definition of the zooming dimension $d_z$. Our bounds match existing delay-free regret guarantees for Lipschitz bandits and characterize the additional $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{D})$ impact introduced by feedback delays.

title: Iterative Prompt Optimization: A Socio-Technical Framework for Human–AI Alignment in Generative AI
abstract: Generative AI systems are increasingly used to support learning and other knowledge-based tasks, but their effectiveness depends not only on the capability of the model but also on how people interact with them. Drawing on socio-technical systems theory, this study examines prompt design as a way to better align AI-generated explanations with users’ knowledge and learning needs. We introduce Iterative Prompt Optimization (IPO), a structured framework in which prompts are refined through repeated user feedback to improve explanation quality, clarity, and confidence in complex domains. Using quantum algorithm explanation as the study context, we conducted a multi-phase study involving baseline model evaluation, iterative prompt refinement with novice users, and the development of a prototype conversational application, AlgoQ. Preliminary findings suggest that structured prompt scaffolding helps users better understand complex concepts, improves the clarity of AI-generated explanations, and increases learner confidence. This research contributes to a better understanding of human–AI collaboration and offers design insights for building effective AI-supported learning systems.

title: A Machine Learning Approach for Intelligent Digital Network Traffic Classification Using XG Boost and Random Forest
abstract: In the last decade, with the expansion of digital networks, the network traffic control problem has raised the necessity of effective and accurate techniques for its management. This work aims to compare and analyze two ensemble machine learning algorithms, XGBoost and Random Forest, for network traffic congestion classification and management. The proposed approach consisted of: data preprocessing, feature selection applying the minimum redundancy maximum relevance criterion, keeping the top 10 features, and separating the training and testing data with a ratio of 80:20. We trained and tested both models in the network traffic dataset and compared them on the basis of accuracy, precision, recall and confusion matrix. The experimental results confirm that XGBoost had the best classification accuracy 98.75%, precision of 0.987 and recall of 0.986 than Random Forest having classification accuracy 96.42%, precision of 0.965 and recall of 0.961. The main contributions of this work were to offer a benchmark of two tree-based ensemble methods for digital network traffic classification and to show that XGBoost would be a promising candidate for real-time intelligent network traffic control systems, and give some indication for network operators in terms of optimized network resource allocation and congestion reduction by means of automated, data-driven decision making.

title: Incremental Instruction Creative Writing: Benchmark, Generations, and Evaluation Dataset
abstract: Dataset accompanying “The Effects of Incremental Instruction Delivery on Language-Model Creative Writing." This release contains the complete dataset and evaluation artifacts used in the study. It includes 160 creative-writing benchmark tasks across six genres; model generations from six open-weight language models under FULL and SHARDED instruction-delivery conditions; 1,920 pointwise LLM evaluations of atomic constraint adherence and five writing-quality dimensions; 30-pair simple and evidence-first LLM comparison audits in primary and reversed response order; and the corresponding 30 human judgments. The dataset is organized into separate configurations for benchmark tasks, generations, model evaluations, pairwise judge comparisons, evidence-first judge audits, human-evaluation cases, and human annotations. Additional files provide extracted atomic constraints, evaluator configuration, run provenance, integrity hashes, and the statistics underlying the evaluator-validation analysis. The FULL condition presents the complete task specification in one turn. The SHARDED condition distributes the task specification progressively across multiple conversational turns. Shard sets were designed to preserve the task content of their fully specified counterparts; the accompanying paper documents a minor post-hoc sharding omission and other relevant limitations. Code and analysis scripts are released separately in the SISTER repository and archived on Zenodo under DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22700810. This dataset is released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) license.

title: Computational Task Ontology Generation (CTOG)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Task Ontology Generation (CTOG) theory, a novel approach to knowledge representation and automated problem-solving. Traditional approaches to problem-solving rely on pre-defined tasks and solutions, often limiting the scope of automation. CTOG proposes a fundamentally different paradigm: the system proactively *discovers* new tasks based on observation of the environment. This shifts the focus from solving known problems to identifying previously unaddressed challenges. The core principle is expressed as [Observation → New Task], representing a system's ability to recognize and define novel computational problems. This theory has significant implications for advancing automated scientific discovery and offers a framework for creating dynamic and adaptive intelligent systems. The framework utilizes a probabilistic approach to task discovery, weighting observations based on their potential to generate new tasks. The key components are: (1) Observation Acquisition: gathering data from the environment; (2) Task Candidate Generation: formulating potential tasks based on the observations; (3) Task Validation: assessing the feasibility and potential value of the generated tasks; (4) Ontology Construction: representing the discovered tasks within a structured ontology. The methodology employs Bayesian networks to model the relationships between observations, task candidates, and validation criteria. The ultimate goal is to build systems capable of not just executing existing instructions, but of actively seeking out and defining new computational challenges. This work lays the groundwork for a future where AI systems can truly contribute to scientific progress by identifying and tackling previously unknown problems.

title: Computational Selection Pressure Model
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Selection Pressure Model (CSPM), a novel approach to understanding and predicting the long-term survival of computational solutions. The model centers on the concept of competition between algorithmic designs, where a selection pressure, represented mathematically as *P(A)*, determines which design prevails. The core principle involves simulating a population of candidate solutions, [ *A1, A2, ..., An* ], and iteratively evaluating their performance based on the selection pressure. The model's predictive power stems from its ability to capture the dynamic nature of evolutionary processes in computation. Through a series of theoretical analyses and illustrative examples, we demonstrate how CSPM can be applied to various domains, including algorithm design, architectural optimization, and model selection. The model provides a framework for quantifying selection pressure and understanding the factors that drive the evolution of computational systems. The potential of CSPM to contribute to the broader field of computational evolution theory is discussed.

title: Computational Relation Generation Model
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Relation Generation Model (CRGM), a novel approach to knowledge representation and reasoning. Traditional models primarily focus on generating data instances, while CRGM shifts the focus to generating relationships between existing entities. The core idea is to transform the computational object into a relationship, represented as [Rnew, F(Rold)] where Rnew is the generated relationship and F(Rold) is a function that processes the original relationship Rold. This approach has the potential to significantly impact future knowledge computation and offers a fundamentally different perspective on how we represent and reason about complex systems. The model aims to provide a flexible and adaptable framework for knowledge extraction and inference, moving beyond simple data generation towards a more sophisticated understanding of the underlying relational structure.

title: Context-Aware Multimodal Voice Command Recognition System for Smart Home Applications.
abstract: AbstractThe growing prevalence of smart homes has redefined how users interact with technology, shifting from manual interfaces to intuitive,voice-driven systems . Voice Command Recognition (VCR) is a cornerstone of this transformation, enabling hands-freecontrol overdevices such as lighting systems, entertainment units, security appliances, and climate controllers. Through IoT, voice assistants likeAmazon Alexa, Google Assistant, and Apple Siri can control various smart home devices such as lights, thermostats, and securitycameras.These devices communicate over a network, allowing the voice assistant to send commands and receive real-time feedback.However, real-world conditions such as overlapping speech, background noise, and varying room acoustics pose significant challenges tothe accuracy and reliability of voice-controlled systems. In addition to these, voiceassistants struggle with context management andinterpreting complex commands involving anaphora or ambiguous references, leading to potential errors in command execution. Toaddress these issues, modern smart home systems must not only interpret commands but also isolate them from complex soundmixtures indynamic environments and also effectively tackles the challenges of anaphora in these systems by enhancing context retention anddisambiguation.This work proposes an optimized deep learning framework for source separation and voice command recognition for smarthome systems and improve the understanding for anaphora in these systems. Initially, the raw smart home commands dataset collected from a freely accessible source will be converted into audio clips, which generates audio from text for voice command recognition. Then, preprocessing will be performed using the chained Savitsky-Golay filtering (CSGF) technique and source separation is performed using theconvoluted variational autoencoder (ConvVAE). After source separation, various audio features will be extracted, The extracted features will then fed into the multiscale dilated separable convolutional network (MDSCN) to recognize multiple voice commands for smart homesystems accurately. Then this processed voice commands are fed to a predefined recurrent network to addresses the anaphora challenges insequential commands given. It also addresses the compound anaphora issues by integrating structured rule-based interactions withadvanced AI techniques. This combined approach enhances the system's ability to maintain context and apply actions accurately acrossmultiple devices.This dual-layered approach significantly improves the reliability, precision, and naturalness of smart voice assistants in dynamic acoustic and dialogic environments.

title: Computational Reality Model Consistency Theory (CRMCT-2)
abstract: Computational Reality Model Consistency Theory (CRMCT-2) presents a systematic framework for ensuring coherence among multiple internal models that jointly represent a complex system. In CRMCT-2, each internal model \(M_i\) is expressed as a mapping from a shared state space \(S\) to an output space \(O_i\). The theory introduces a consistency relation \(≈\) that captures the degree of alignment between models: \(M_1 ≈ M_2\) when the divergence between their outputs over \(S\) remains below a prescribed tolerance. By formalizing consistency conditions, conflict detection, and resolution mechanisms, CRMCT-2 offers a principled approach to maintain stability in adaptive intelligent systems. This paper elaborates the core concepts, formal definitions, and theoretical properties of CRMCT-2, and discusses its potential impact on the design of robust, self‑adaptive architectures and its implications for future research in artificial general intelligence.

title: Earth Observation Foundation Models for Terrestrial Ecohydrology: From Representation Learning to Process Inference
abstract: Earth observation foundation models (EOFMs) are emerging as reusable representation frameworks for data-driven retrieval, prediction and process modelling within ecohydrology, which integrate EO, meteorological forcing and process models to characterise coupled water, energy and carbon dynamics in vegetation and soil across scales. However, there is yet to be an ecohydrology-specific synthesis assessing the EOFM relevance, application evidence or evaluation requirements under uncertain reference data, scale mismatch and temporal dependence. Here, we develop a framework for determining when EOFMs support interpretable inference and identify a mismatch between EOFMs and ecohydrological requirements. Firstly, an observation-to-inference hierarchy shows that relevance depends on target-specific sensing pathways, spatial-temporal support and traceable uncertainty. Secondly, a meta-analysis shows that pretraining is dominated by reflected optical and active-microwave data, with sparse thermal coverage and no passive-microwave-emission sources. Thirdly, our synthesis of ecohydrological applications finds strongest support for spatial context, label-efficient adaptation and hybrid workflows. Evidence declines with inference depth; independent validation of fluxes, coupled dynamics, event trajectories, calibrated uncertainty and decision benefits remains sparse. Fourthly, our benchmark audit finds stronger coverage of fair adaptation and reproducibility in general EOFM suites, and of process targets, direct reference evidence and distribution shifts in ecohydrological evaluations; physical consistency and uncertainty remain weakly assessed. These findings motivate a process-aware framework aligning EOFM design and evaluation with the target variable, observation pathway and process timescale, supporting trustworthy monitoring and interpretation of coupled water, energy and carbon dynamics.

title: Handoff-H1: An Orchestrated Vision-Agent System for Material Quantity Takeoff from Construction Blueprints
abstract: Converting a set of architectural blueprints into a complete material quantity takeoff requires visual perception across drawing sheets, dimensional and multi-hop reasoning, and grounding in construction conventions that the drawings never state. We present Handoff-H1, a takeoff system built from three layers: purpose-built computer-vision models that extract primitives; tool-using agents equipped with image operations and in-house visual-task tools, including CV-model-backed counting, detection and plan decomposition; and a persistent, hierarchically structured project foundation, grounded in a curated construction knowledge base. We evaluate on the Construction Blueprint Takeoff Benchmark: 10 real residential blueprint sets paired with consensus-validated expert takeoffs - 2,009 verified line items, restricted for scoring to the 1,348 primary-tier materials that drive an estimate - scored per trade by an LLM judge on material coverage and quantity Precision@25% (P@.25) and combined into a weighted composite. Under identical scoring from the raw PDF, seven frontier and open-weight models span composites of 35-61, and independent professional estimators - scored against the same reconciled gold standard - post 77.6% (65.5% coverage, 87.9% P@.25). Handoff-H1, working end-to-end from the raw PDF, reaches 81.6% (86.1% coverage, 78.8% P@.25): roughly 20 points above the strongest frontier agent, and above the independent estimators by pairing near-human quantity precision with coverage they do not reach. The evaluation harness is public for the open harbor framework; the blueprint sets and ground truth are available upon request for research use.

title: Beyond Agreement: Structural Alignment in Hybrid Human–LLM Evaluation Systems
abstract: Evaluating technical explanations is an ill-structured task, requiring assigning ratings and justifying judgments without a single ground truth. In multi-agent settings, alignment is typically assessed through agreement, yet similar ratings may arise from different justificatory expressions, limiting insight into how judgments are formed. We examine evaluator alignment using two analytical lenses: convergence (similarity in meaning), measured using cosine similarity, and diagnosticity (structure of information in justifications), measured using entropy difference. We apply this approach in an exploratory study comparing two human cybersecurity experts and two LLM evaluators evaluating 71 short-text explanations under a shared rubric. We find that LLM evaluators exhibit higher convergence and more stable diagnosticity, whereas human evaluators show greater variability, including when assigning the same rating. These findings suggest that agreement does not imply shared justificatory reasoning and highlight the value of analyzing justification texts in human–LLM evaluation systems.

title: Computational Meaning Universe Theory (CMUT)
abstract: Computational Meaning Universe Theory (CMUT) proposes a fundamental shift in our understanding of computation and intelligence. It posits that all meaningful relationships form a unified space, denoted as 'M', and that the core research area lies in how meaning organizes intelligence. This theory suggests a hierarchical structure: Information → Meaning → Understanding → Intelligence, potentially establishing a new foundational theory alongside Information Theory, Computation Theory, and Machine Learning. This paper outlines five key research areas – Computational Meaning Generation Theory (CMGT), Contextual Adaptive Framework Model (CAFM), Universal Cognitive Simulation Iteration Theory (UCSIT), Contextual Knowledge Fusion Process Theory (CKFPT), and Computational Wisdom Modeling Group (CWMG) – identified as holding significant Turing Award potential, representing novel approaches designed to avoid redundancy with previously explored ideas. The focus is on exploring the emergence of order within computational systems, moving beyond traditional data-algorithm-result paradigms.

title: Explainability-Aware Compilation
abstract: This paper introduces Explainability-Aware Compilation (EAC), a novel approach to software compilation that explicitly incorporates explainability as a primary optimization goal. Traditional compilers prioritize performance and memory efficiency, often sacrificing transparency and understandability. EAC addresses this limitation by simultaneously optimizing for both performance and explainability, using a lambda (λ) parameter to represent the desired level of explainability. The core concept involves preserving key decision structures within the compiled code, facilitating post-execution analysis and debugging. This work explores the theoretical foundations and potential impact of EAC, suggesting it could represent a significant advancement in the intersection of software compilation theory and interpretable software development. The primary goal is to provide a framework for building software systems where the reasoning behind decisions is readily accessible, offering benefits for verification, trust, and accountability. The presented model outlines a compilation strategy that balances computational efficiency with the critical need for transparency, paving the way for more robust and understandable software.

title: Computational Meaning Conservation Principle (CMCP)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Meaning Conservation Principle (CMCP), a novel theoretical framework addressing the challenge of software transformation and ensuring semantic equivalence across different representations or implementations of a program. The core concept posits that while program transformations are inherently prone to altering specific details, the underlying *meaning* of the program should remain preserved. This principle is formalized as `Meaning(P_1) ≈ Meaning(P_2)` where `P_1` and `P_2` represent two programs. The paper explores the implications of CMCP across various transformation scenarios, including code conversion, model transformation, and program optimization. It argues that CMCP represents a significant step towards a robust theoretical foundation for software transformation, with potential implications for the future of software engineering and a strong candidacy for consideration within the scope of the Turing Award. The paper focuses on the conceptual underpinnings and potential applications of CMCP, without presenting experimental results. ---

title: Computational Reality Model Evolution Theory (CRMET)
abstract: The notion of a world model has become central to many artificial intelligence systems, yet most frameworks treat these models as static entities that are either trained once or updated in discrete, pre‑defined stages. In this paper we propose the Computational Reality Model Evolution Theory (CRMET), a principled framework in which a world model is viewed as an evolving function that continually adapts to new data, experiences, and internal objectives. CRMET formalizes the evolution of a model as a sequence of mappings M_t → M_{t+1} where t indexes discrete time steps or learning episodes. We argue that this dynamic view explains the phenomenon of continual learning, resolves longstanding issues of catastrophic forgetting, and provides a natural pathway toward systems that exhibit Turing‑award‑level flexibility and generality. By exploring the mechanisms of incremental adaptation, structural plasticity, and meta‑adaptation, we show how CRMET supports self‑organizing architectures capable of both learning from raw observations and refining their internal representations in response to meta‑feedback. We illustrate the theory with three representative scenarios—autonomous navigation, natural language understanding, and robotic manipulation—demonstrating how a CRMET‑driven system can evolve its model in situ. Finally, we discuss the implications of CRMET for future research, including its potential to unify disparate learning paradigms and to provide a theoretical foundation for adaptive, lifelong artificial intelligence.

title: Neural Network Performance Enhancement Using the Modified Orca Predation Algorithm for Time Series Forecasting: A Comparative Review
abstract: Neural Networks (NNs) are extensively used in time series forecasting due to their ability to learn nonlinear and complex temporal relationships. However, NN performance is frequently limited by training challenges, including slow convergence and suboptimal parameter optimization. This study aims to systematically examine the role of the Modified Orca Predation Algorithm (MOPA) in enhancing neural network performance for time series forecasting, particularly in comparison with other metaheuristic optimization approaches. This research employed a qualitative method using a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) approach. Relevant journal and conference articles published between 2015 and 2025 were collected from reputable scientific databases. The selected studies were analyzed thematically and bibliometrically using VOSviewer to identify research trends, application domains, and performance characteristics of MOPA-based neural network optimization. The results indicate that the integration of MOPA into neural network training consistently improves convergence speed, forecasting accuracy, and model stability across various application domains. Compared to conventional optimization methods, MOPA demonstrates superior capability in handling nonlinear and volatile time series data, particularly in energy forecasting, financial time series analysis, and climate-related prediction. The findings also reveal that MOPA-based optimization contributes to better generalization performance by reducing prediction error and output variance. This study provides a structured synthesis of recent research on MOPA-enhanced neural networks and contributes to the understanding of metaheuristic optimization strategies in time series forecasting. The results serve as a reference for researchers in selecting effective optimization methods for neural network-based forecasting models.

title: Geometry-Aware Spatio-Temporal Context Modeling for 4D Occupancy Forecasting
abstract: 4D occupancy forecasting models the spatio-temporal evolution of 3D scenes and is crucial for autonomous driving, especially for corner-case simulation. Existing methods often rely on discrete tokenization followed by autoregressive prediction, yet struggle with geometric distortion in static structures and inconsistent temporal coherence over the forecasting horizon. In this work, we propose a Geometry-Aware Spatio-Temporal context modeling method (GAST) for 4D occupancy forecasting, built upon progressive explicit-implicit generation and dual-path spatio-temporal modeling. Specifically, the generation module produces per-frame occupancy with high geometric fidelity and semantic plausibility through pose-driven warping, motion-aware feature modulation, and attention-based feature refinement. Subsequently, the spatio-temporal module enhances spatial consistency through global context aggregation while capturing scene evolution through temporal dynamics extraction. This unified design enables joint optimization of historical reconstruction and future forecasting in an end-to-end manner. Extensive experiments on Occ3D-nuScenes demonstrate the superiority of our method, outperforming the state-of-the-art by 7.67% in mIoU and 6.44% in IoU with a 2.84x speedup, while maintaining strong performance in long-term forecasting.

title: Generation of Synthetic Fingerphotos with GANs
abstract: Contactless fingerprinting is an emerging approach to biometric authentication that allows users to scan their fingerprints without touching a scanner. Due to the limited amount of contactless fingerprint data available and the security risks associated with sharing real individuals' fingerprints, it is valuable to explore methods of generating synthetic data that can be used in place of - or in conjunction with - real data to develop and evaluate contactless fingerprinting systems. In this paper, we present and evaluate synthetic fingerphotos generated using StyleGAN2-ADA and StyleGAN3, existing image generation architectures. We evaluate the realism, privacy preservation, and variety of the synthetic fingerphotos by comparing their biometric feature statistics to those of real fingerphotos, computing match scores between real and synthetic fingerphotos, and computing match scores between different synthetic fingerphotos. This paper provides a quantitative comparison point for future evaluations of synthetic fingerphotos. The evaluation code is made available at https://github.com/cmillerlynch/fingerphoto-gan.

title: Interactive XAI in AI-Augmented Decision-Making: A Persuasion Knowledge Perspective for Understanding the Effects of Interactive XAI on Appropriate Reliance
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly embedded in high-stakes human decision-making, yet achieving appropriate reliance remains elusive. Although Explainable AI (XAI) aims to address this, static explanations often fail to meet diverse user needs, while interactive natural-language explanations risk functioning as unintended persuasion agents by heightening perceptions of system humanness. Grounded in the Persuasion Knowledge Model (PKM), this study develops and tests a theoretical framework showing how explanation type (static versus interactive) influences perceived humanness, which shapes beliefs about the XAI agent’s assistive versus persuasive intent and ultimately affects reliance behavior. The hypotheses are tested in a between-subjects experiment (N=100) using a deception-detection task with hotel reviews, offering insights for the ethical design of conversational XAI that fosters complementary human-AI performance rather than over- or under-reliance.

title: 计算规则竞争理论
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Rule Competition Theory (CRCT), a novel framework for understanding the evolution of computational systems and algorithms. CRCT posits that multiple computational rules, represented as [R1, R2, ..., Rn], engage in a process of competition, analogous to natural selection. Through this competition, a dominant rule system, characterized by higher fitness or efficiency, emerges. The theory leverages concepts from game theory and evolutionary dynamics to model this process, aiming to explain why algorithms evolve and adapt over time. CRCT offers a potential pathway for understanding the observed complexity and diversity of algorithms, and its principles may have significant implications for the design and development of artificial intelligence systems. The core of the theory rests on the principle of differential selection based on performance metrics and the iterative refinement of rule sets. Mathematical formalizations are presented to illustrate key concepts and processes within CRCT. The theory provides a framework for analyzing the dynamics of rule interactions and predicting the eventual emergence of a dominant rule set.

title: Computational World Model Generation (CWMG)
abstract: This paper proposes a novel theoretical framework, Computational World Model Generation (CWMG), aimed at automating the construction and refinement of internal world models within an intelligent system. The core concept revolves around a self-correcting system capable of generating a representation of its environment, denoted as [Internal World], and iteratively improving this representation based on observed data and internal simulations. CWMG posits that this process, if scaled effectively, could represent a foundational element for achieving general intelligence, potentially holding significant implications for the pursuit of a Turing Award. The theoretical underpinnings of CWMG are explored, focusing on the mathematical formulation of the model generation process and the mechanisms for error correction. The system's operation is described using a series of equations and symbolic representations, highlighting the iterative nature of the learning and adaptation process. Ultimately, CWMG represents a shift from externally programmed knowledge to dynamically constructed understanding, a critical step toward truly intelligent systems. ---

title: Program Semantic Refraction Theory
abstract: Program Semantic Refraction Theory (PSRT) proposes a novel framework for understanding discrepancies in program behavior observed across different execution environments. The theory centers around the concept that a program's semantic representation can undergo a transformation, or 'refraction,' when executed within diverse contexts. This refraction process is formally represented as: [ S_{\text{out}} \mathcal R ( S_{\text{in}}, E ) ] Where: * $S_{\text{in}}$ represents the initial program state or semantic representation. * $S_{\text{out}}$ represents the resulting program state or semantic representation after refraction. * $\mathcal{R}$ is the semantic refraction operator, which defines the transformation process. * $E$ represents the execution environment, encompassing factors such as the compiler, platform, and hardware architecture. Furthermore, the theory introduces the concept of 'semantic refraction rate' ($n_s$) defined as: [ n_s = \frac{ \Delta S_{\text{environment}} }{ \Delta S_{\text{source}} } ] This rate quantifies the degree of semantic change induced by the execution environment. PSRT offers a potential explanation for observed variations in program behavior across platforms, compilers, and hardware, presenting a theoretical foundation for analyzing and potentially mitigating these discrepancies. The theory's core relies on recognizing that the interaction between a program and its execution environment is not merely a deterministic translation, but a dynamic process of semantic transformation. This transformation introduces a layer of complexity that necessitates a formal theoretical model for comprehensive analysis and prediction. The potential of this framework to address challenges related to cross-platform compatibility, compiler optimization, and hardware-specific behavior is substantial. ---

evidence.title: Program Semantic Refraction Theory
evidence.abstract: Program Semantic Refraction Theory (PSRT) proposes a novel framework for understanding discrepancies in program behavior observed across different execution environments. The theory centers around the concept that a program's semantic representation can undergo a transformation, or 'refraction,' when executed within diverse contexts. This refraction process is formally represented as: [ S_{\text{out}} \mathcal R ( S_{\text{in}}, E ) ] Where: * $S_{\text{in}}$ represents the initial program state or semantic representation. * $S_{\text{out}}$ represents the resulting program state or semantic representation after refraction. * $\mathcal{R}$ is the semantic refraction operator, which defines the transformation process. * $E$ represents the execution environment, encompassing factors such as the compiler, platform, and hardware architecture. Furthermore, the theory introduces the concept of 'semantic refraction rate' ($n_s$) defined as: [ n_s = \frac{ \Delta S_{\text{environment}} }{ \Delta S_{\text{source}} } ] This rate quantifies the degree of semantic change induced by the execution environment. PSRT offers a potential explanation for observed variations in program behavior across platforms, compilers, and hardware, presenting a theoretical foundation for analyzing and potentially mitigating these discrepancies. The theory's core relies on recognizing that the interaction between a program and its execution environment is not merely a deterministic translation, but a dynamic process of semantic transformation. This transformation introduces a layer of complexity that necessitates a formal theoretical model for comprehensive analysis and prediction. The potential of this framework to address challenges related to cross-platform compatibility, compiler optimization, and hardware-specific behavior is substantial. ---

title: Computational Explanation Boundary Theory (CEBT)
abstract: The Computational Explanation Boundary Theory (CEBT) proposes a unifying framework for analyzing the limits of explanation within any computational system. It introduces the concept of an explanation boundary, denoted B_E, which partitions the set of system states into those that can be explained by an observer and those that remain inherently opaque. By formalizing B_E as a function of the observer's internal model, computational resources, and the system's intrinsic dynamics, CEBT provides a rigorous method for determining the explanatory capacity of algorithms, neural networks, and hybrid models. The theory also delineates conditions under which explanation is impossible, irrespective of computational power, and identifies scenarios where explanation becomes feasible through augmentation of the observer's knowledge base. The paper develops the mathematical foundations of B_E, discusses its implications for artificial intelligence, and outlines potential applications in explainable AI, model debugging, and theoretical computer science. The analysis suggests that CEBT could serve as a foundational theory for AI, with the potential to influence future Turing Award research by establishing a formal boundary between explainable and non‑explainable computational phenomena.

title: Improving BiLSTM News Articles Classification with Frozen DistilBERT Embedding
abstract: News classification is critical for organizing digital content and enhancing user engagement. Static embeddings such as GloVe, however, often fail to capture dynamic contextual relationships, limiting classifier performance. This study investigates the integration of frozen DistilBERT embeddings used strictly as feature extractors into a BiLSTM news‐classification pipeline to harness context‐aware representations while preserving computational efficiency. Experiments were conduccted on the Fancyzhx/ag_news dataset, which contains 127,700 samples, using a controlled 70/30 train–test split, comparing three BiLSTM variants: baseline (no pretrained embeddings), GloVe‐BiLSTM, and DistilBERT‐BiLSTM. Model architectures and hyperparameters are held constant to ensure a fair evaluation. Experimental results demonstrate that DistilBERT‐BiLSTM achieves 93.2 % accuracy, outperforming GloVe‐BiLSTM by 1.3% and the baseline by 2.5%. UMAP visualizations reveal more distinct semantic clusters with DistilBERT embeddings, and token‐level heatmaps confirm sharper intra‐sentence focus on domain‐specific terms. These findings contribute to informatics research by demonstrating the value of frozen transformer embeddings for lightweight yet high-performing text classification, with practical applications in information retrieval, content moderation, and real-time news analytics.

title: Optimized EIT-Based Multi-Target CNOT^k Gates in Heteronuclear Rydberg Atom Arrays
abstract: Efficient stabilizer readout requiring multi-qubit coupling is a core bottleneck for quantum error correction. One feasible method is direct implementation of the controlled-U gate between one ancilla qubit and the data qubits assigned to stabilizer U measurements. We systematically analyze the native multi-target $\mathrm{C}^1\mathrm{NOT}^k$ gates proposed by Müller et al., which is realized via electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) and Rydberg blockade mechanisms. Using a microscopic open-system model, we analyze the gate's scaling with target number k and identify spontaneous emission, Doppler dephasing, target atom inter-coupling, and technical noise as major error contributions. We further optimize the protocol combining two-photon STIRAP control, heteronuclear interaction engineering, and waveform optimization. Our optimized heteronuclear protocol reaches fidelities of 98.03% ($\mathrm{C}^1\mathrm{NOT}^{1}$) and 96.54% ($\mathrm{C}^1\mathrm{NOT}^{4}$), in the presence of all primary noise sources and realistic experimental parameters. These results demonstrate that EIT-based multi-target gates serve as a practical building block for low-depth stabilizer readout.

title: Closed-Form Nonlocal Shrinkage for Multiplicative Image Denoising and SAR Despeckling
abstract: Multiplicative noise poses a challenge in coherent and signal-dependent imaging owing to its intensity-dependent variance and frequently non-Gaussian distribution. We propose a deterministic nonlocal estimator that combines a logarithmic Yeo--Johnson transformation, patch grouping, an adaptive singular basis, and sparse shrinkage. The orthonormal group dictionary makes the weighted Lasso separable and yields an exact coefficient-wise soft-threshold solution. This solution replaces the iterative inner solver and expresses patch reliability and atom importance through a single threshold field. Since the dictionary is estimated from the noisy group, we introduce a random-matrix correction governed by the group aspect ratio $γ=p^2/K$. The correction links patch size, group size, and shrinkage strength. Experiments cover gamma-corrupted images from three standard benchmarks and real synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery from five sensors. The method gives the best result in 18 of 24 PSNR/SSIM comparisons with twelve published methods and the lowest mean ratio-image deviation across six real SAR configurations. These results support geometry-calibrated nonlocal modeling for structure-preserving image restoration, with SAR despeckling serving as a demanding application. Code is available \href{https://github.com/Teriri1999/Geometry-Calibrated-Closed-Form-Shrinkage-for-SAR-Despeckling}{here}.

title: When AI Streamers Build or Break Live Streaming Communities: The Roles of Anthropomorphism, AI Efficacy, and Sense of Community
abstract: AI-powered streamers are increasingly appearing on live streaming platforms, producing content and interacting with audiences in ways that resemble human streamers. However, prior AI research offers mixed insights, and we still lack a clear understanding of how AI streamers shape viewers’ community perceptions in live streaming environments. Drawing on sense of community and uncanny valley theory, we develop a conceptual framework that explains how two AI-specific characteristics, anthropomorphism and AI efficacy, jointly influence viewers’ community perceptions. We propose an inverted U relationship between anthropomorphism and sense of community, with the strongest negative impact occurring at near human levels. Perceived AI efficacy moderates this relationship by strengthening the positive effects at low to moderate anthropomorphism and buffering the negative effects in the near human zone. Our framework clarifies the dilemma of AI-mediated social interaction and highlights implications for value co-creation on the live streaming platform.

title: Smart Dosage Optimization using Machine Learning and Biomedical Engineering for Personalized Drug Therapy: A Review
abstract: Background: Personalized medicine is revolutionizing modern medicine by customizing medicine for the individual patient based on their genetic, physiological and clinical profile. The problem of choosing the right dose, i.e., the maximum benefit versus minimum toxicity, is still one of the most important in clinical pharmacology, and conventional "population based" dosing recommendations for drugs do not account for significant inter-patient variability.Objective: This review investigates the architectures, algorithms, clinical application and open challenges of the field and proposes ways to integrate this with machine learning (ML) to facilitate intelligent, patient specific dosage optimization.Methods: The literature was systematically reviewed to highlight the effects and recent developments of ML-driven dosing and the enabling of biomedical-sensing technologies, categorizing the evidence based on the system architecture, algorithmic paradigms, biomedical-engineering enablers and comparative clinical outcomes.Findings: In the studies reviewed, several electronic health record-based, genomic-based, laboratory-based, and continuous physiological signal-based ML dosing systems have been found to outperform traditional dosing systems in terms of dosing accuracy, reduction of drug-related toxicity, and increased patient adherence. Supervised models can be used to guide interpretable pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic predictions, deep learning can extract high dimensional, time-series physiological data, and reinforcement learning can provide closed-loop dosing for chronic and evolving disease states. These systems rely on wearable biosensors, smart drug delivery devices and Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) platforms to provide the real-time data streams.Conclusion: The combination of ML and real time biomedical monitoring provides a viable avenue to safer, more effective and more individual drug therapy. To make this happen at scale, work needs to be done on data heterogeneity, model interpretability, clinical validation, regulatory acceptance, and on the performance of the models in different patient cohorts.

title: Computational Forgetting Theory
abstract: The prevailing paradigm in computation focuses primarily on learning and knowledge acquisition. However, complex systems, particularly those operating in dynamic environments, necessitate the capacity for forgetting – the deliberate removal of previously learned information. This paper introduces the Computational Forgetting Theory (CFT), a framework that formalizes and justifies the need for forgetting within complex systems. CFT posits that the efficiency and reliability of a system are fundamentally constrained by the accumulation of irrelevant or outdated knowledge. The theory proposes a mechanism for determining what should be forgotten, based on a dynamic assessment of relevance and utility. This represents a shift from a purely learning-centric view to one that incorporates a critical element of knowledge management. The potential implications of CFT are significant, offering a new perspective on artificial intelligence, software maintenance, and the broader theory of computation. The core principle can be represented as: (K → R) where K represents Knowledge and R represents Removal. CFT aims to define the conditions under which this removal process should occur, offering a novel approach to system design and optimization.

title: Computational Relational Attention Theory
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Relational Attention Theory (CRAT), a novel framework aiming to address inherent limitations within existing attention mechanisms, primarily their tendency to selectively focus on information rather than explicitly modeling relationships. CRAT proposes a fundamental shift: instead of selecting the "most important" information, it directly computes the "relation" itself as the primary attention object. This approach is grounded in the belief that understanding relationships is paramount to intelligent processing, offering a potentially transformative pathway towards developing new Transformer architectures with enhanced capabilities. The theory outlines a core formula for calculating attention based on relationships, [Attention(Relation)], and posits its potential to unlock advancements comparable to those achieved by the Turing Award. This framework provides a theoretical foundation for a new generation of attention mechanisms that prioritize relational understanding over selective information filtering. ---

title: Computational Semantic Dynamics
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Semantic Dynamics (CSD), a novel framework for understanding and modeling meaning as a dynamic, evolving process. Traditional approaches to knowledge representation often treat meaning as a static, fixed entity. CSD challenges this paradigm by proposing that meaning is not inherent but rather emerges and changes in response to contextual influences. The core concept of CSD is represented by the equation: [Meaning\_t], where *t* represents a specific temporal instance. This equation highlights that meaning at a given time (*t*) is not a constant but is instead a function of previous meanings and the surrounding environment. The fundamental process is described by the transition relation: [Meaning\_t → Meaning_{t+1}], indicating that the meaning at time *t+1* is determined by the meaning at time *t* and the factors influencing the transition. We explore how concepts are continuously shaped and modified by their interactions with the environment, suggesting a potential paradigm shift in how we conceptualize and represent knowledge, with implications for areas such as artificial intelligence, cognitive science, and linguistics. This work lays the groundwork for a more nuanced and dynamic understanding of meaning, potentially unlocking advancements beyond current limitations in knowledge representation systems. Further research will focus on formalizing the transition mechanisms and exploring the mathematical properties of dynamic semantic spaces.

title: Computational Composability Conservation Theory
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Composability Conservation Theory (CCCT), a novel approach to understanding and mitigating the potential loss of composability in optimized computational modules. The core concept is that aggressive optimization can significantly improve a module's performance but simultaneously diminish its ability to be combined with other modules, thereby hindering modularity and broader system design. CCCT defines composability as the probability that a combined system (P ⊕ Q) remains valid, and proposes a constraint: the composability of a transformed program (T(P)) must be greater than or equal to the composability of the original program (P) minus a small tolerance (ε). This theory has significant implications for the design of modular software, AI modules, and distributed systems, potentially offering a foundation for a unified combination theory across these diverse domains. ---

title: Computational Identity Entropy Theory
abstract: Identity is a fundamental concept in computing, security, and social systems, yet it has traditionally been treated as a static attribute. In this paper we introduce the Computational Identity Entropy Theory (CIET), a quantitative framework that models identity as an uncertain entity whose informational content can be measured, manipulated, and conserved during system evolution. We define the entropy of identity, H(I), as the Shannon entropy over the probability distribution of identity states, and we extend this definition to dynamic contexts where identity changes over time. CIET provides tools to analyze how system transformations—such as data migration, replication, or cryptographic transformations—affect identity uncertainty, and it offers a principled basis for designing systems that preserve or intentionally manipulate identity information. The theory aligns with the established principles of information theory while extending them to the domain of identity, suggesting potential implications for data privacy, authentication protocols, and the theoretical foundations of machine learning. The potential breadth and depth of CIET suggest that it could be considered a foundational contribution to the theory of computation, meriting recognition at the highest levels of the field.

title: AWM-VLA: AlignedWorld Modeling for Efficient and Explainable Vision-Language-Action Policies
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have become a powerful paradigm for generalist robotic manipulation, yet they are often reactive: the policy maps the current observation directly to an action chunk without reasoning about the long-term consequences of its decisions. Prior attempts to endow policies with world models either reconstruct future frames in pixel space---expensive and dominated by task-irrelevant detail---or decouple the world model from the policy, weakening control. We present AWM-VLA, a unified framework that embeds aligned world modeling directly inside a diffusion-transformer policy. Following the Future Latent REpresentation Alignment (FLARE) principle, we add learnable future tokens whose intermediate activations are aligned with vision-language embeddings of future observations, enabling the policy to anticipate long-term consequences while generating actions. We extend this paradigm in two ways. First, we introduce an object-centric decoupled alignment objective that predicts future object-level semantics alongside the global future embedding, improving both interpretability and multi-instruction generalization. Second, we balance the global and object-centric alignment terms against the action flow-matching loss through a principled weighting, yielding a controllable accuracy--interpretability trade-off. On RoboCasa and humanoid tabletop manipulation benchmarks, AWM-VLA outperforms prior VLA and world-model baselines by up to 21% in success rate, improves generalization to novel objects and instructions, and produces object-centric rationales that are preferred by human raters in 83 of cases. Our approach adds only a few learnable tokens to the policy and is compatible with any diffusion or flow-matching policy, making aligned world modeling an inexpensive, broadly applicable component of generalist manipulation.

title: External Sinkhole Attack Detection in Large-Scale WSNs Using Metaheuristic Feature Selection
abstract: Sinkhole attacks in large-scale wireless sensor networks (WSNs) pose a serious threat to network functionality. This paper presents a metaheuristic feature selection for sinkhole attack detection using the bee swarm optimization (BSO) algorithm. In an external sinkhole attack simulation with 2000 nodes deployed over a 3000 $\times$ 3000 m$^2$ field, the proposed method achieves a detection accuracy of 0.997 while reducing the 16-feature set to eight features.

title: When Expectations Clash: Dynamic Trust Calibration and Expectation Violation in AI-Driven Sports Analytics DSS
abstract: As AI-based decision-support systems increasingly shape decision-making, users often override algorithmic predictions when outputs conflict with their expectations. This study proposes a dynamic model of trust calibration in AI-driven sports analytics, conceptualizing trust as enacted reliance measured through accept-override decisions. We examine how expectation violation magnitude and explanation quality jointly influences reliance. Using a repeated-measures experimental design, participants generate their own forecasts, view AI predictions, and decide whether to accept or override them; expectation violation is modeled continuously as the discrepancy between user and AI forecasts. Integrating perspectives from NeuroIS and HCI, we incorporate eye tracking and galvanic skin response to capture pre-decisional cognitive effort and arousal preceding override behavior. Multilevel analyses will test how expectation violations predict reliance, how explanations moderate these effects, and whether trust predicts behavior beyond perceived surprise. The study advances research on algorithm aversion and explainable AI by positioning trust as a dynamic, process-level phenomenon.
