title: Parameter Efficiency of Variational Quantum Circuits in Image Classification: The Role of Circuit Depth
abstract: The practical value of quantum machine learning must be derived from efficiency rather than scale, as current NISQ processors support only small, shallow circuits. This paper evaluated whether variational quantum circuits (VQCs) can reduce the trainable parameter count in an image classification scenario while preserving accuracy. Experimentation compared quantum classifier heads to parameter-matched classical heads on an identical set of frozen features drawn from the Fashion-MNIST dataset by a CNN. 9 configurations of a quantum circuit crossed 4, 6, and 8 qubits with 1, 2, and 4 entangling layers, each matched to a multilayer perceptron with an approximately equal parameter count. The linear probes served as a floor baseline for all 105 runs across 5 random seed values. 7 out of 9 quantum-based configurations met the mean test accuracy of no more than 1 percentage point below its matched classical head, enforced by the pre-specified criterion. The 2 failures were single-layer circuits, with each falling roughly 8 points below its matched classical head and 12 points below the circuit-free linear probe; in total, 6 configs with 2+ layers passed, with the smallest at 74 trainable parameters. The general trend noticed was that accuracy increased progressively with depth. The 4-layer circuits exceeded the linear probe at every qubit count and produced the highest accuracy at 6 and 8 qubits. The simulation ran noiselessly; VQCs preserved accuracy at the matched parameter budget when depth was given, showcasing depth rather than qubit count gating performance.

title: Computational Causal Structure Generation
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Causal Structure Generation (CCSG), a novel approach to artificial intelligence focused on automatically discovering causal relationships rather than merely identifying correlations. CCSG's core principle is to explicitly generate causal graphs represented as [A → B], signifying a direct causal link between variables A and B, as opposed to simply observing statistical associations. The methodology leverages advanced machine learning techniques, particularly deep learning, to infer these underlying causal structures from observational data. The potential impact of CCSG extends to significant advancements in AI theory, holding the promise of driving innovation akin to the breakthroughs recognized by the Turing Award. This document details the theoretical framework, proposed algorithms, and the potential future directions of CCSG. ---

title: Computational Counterfactual Theory
abstract: Computational Counterfactual Theory (CCT) proposes a novel framework for reasoning about alternative scenarios within complex systems. The core principle of CCT centers on examining what would have happened if a system had made a different choice. This is formalized through the counterfactual function, `CF(S, a)`, where `S` represents the system state and `a` represents the action taken. CCT offers potential applications in AI inference, software debugging, and scientific discovery, fundamentally shifting the focus from simply predicting outcomes to understanding the causal consequences of decisions. This document outlines the foundational concepts of CCT, explores its potential impact on the field of computation, and presents a theoretical framework for its further development. The methodology presented here aims to provide a robust approach for analyzing systems and generating actionable insights from alternative scenarios. ---

title: Computational Intuition Generation Theory (CIGT)
abstract: The ability to act with intuitive understanding is a hallmark of advanced intelligence in humans and animals. In computational systems, the emergence of intuition remains largely unexplored, despite its potential to drive next-generation artificial intelligence. This paper introduces the Computational Intuition Generation Theory (CIGT), a formal framework that models how a computational system can transform raw experiential data into implicit structural knowledge and subsequently into intuitive reasoning. CIGT is grounded in a triadic process: Experience → Implicit Structure → Intuition. We provide a detailed formalization of each stage, present algorithmic instantiations that can be embedded within existing machine learning pipelines, and discuss the theoretical implications of CIGT for AI research. The theory offers a principled pathway to endow artificial systems with an adaptive, low-latency decision-making capability reminiscent of human intuition. By aligning computational processes with cognitive phenomena, CIGT has the potential to become a foundational theory for future AI systems that operate with human-like intuition.

title: Computational Reality Model Hierarchy Theory (CRMHT)
abstract: The Computational Reality Model Hierarchy Theory (CRMHT) proposes a structured framework for representing reality through a series of nested layers, ranging from low‑level sensory primitives to high‑level abstract patterns. This paper develops the theoretical underpinnings of CRMHT, formalizes its hierarchical architecture, and illustrates its potential as a unifying foundation for intelligent representation. By establishing explicit mappings between successive layers and demonstrating how these mappings can be learned and exploited by machine learning systems, we argue that CRMHT offers a scalable path toward robust, interpretable, and generalizable artificial intelligence. The theory is presented without empirical experiments, focusing instead on conceptual clarity and mathematical formulation in plain text.

title: Building a Trustworthy Credit Default Classification Model using Interpretable Machine Learning
abstract: In peer-to-peer lending, a single misjudged borrower can result in significant investor losses and erode the platform's credibility. Although machine learning models have demonstrated superior predictive performance in identifying potential loan defaults, their opaque decision-making process creates mistrust and regulatory friction, impeding their trustworthy adoption. This study addresses the critical trade-off between accuracy and interpretability by proposing an interpretable machine learning framework for trustworthy credit default classification using Bondora peer-to-peer lending data. We deploy and benchmark three classifiers —Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), and Random Forest (RF) — to assess their predictive effectiveness. To overcome the black-box nature of these models, we integrate two complementary interpretability techniques: SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) for global feature attribution and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) for granular, instance-level decision insights. The high AUC, which exceeds 0.96, and F1 score (0.937-0.940) show that all models can effectively support risk management. Our results also demonstrate that pairing high-performing classifiers with interpretability tools enhances model transparency, fosters accountability, and promotes the responsible use of machine learning in credit risk assessment.

title: Time as Structure: Temporal Dependency Graphs for Verifiable Deadline Computation over Legal Documents
abstract: Miss a filing deadline by one day and the claim is barred, however strong the case. Computing that deadline is rarely simple: the period runs from a triggering event, is counted by a statutory convention, and may be suspended by a mandatory conciliation window. We ask whether a language model should answer such questions directly, or read the document and leave the arithmetic to code. We extract dated facts and their dependencies into a temporal dependency graph and compute deadlines from it with a calendar-correct engine. On UK Employment Appeal Tribunal judgments the engine reproduces six of seven timeliness rulings, and matches the judges' own dates to the day. The strongest of four language models, asked the same cases, gets the arithmetic right and the answer wrong: in two of its seven responses its stated verdict contradicts its own working, and across the three GPT models six of twenty-one responses do, each time calling a late claim timely. To test the systems at scale we move the dismissal date across the statutory boundary, generating 427 cases whose answers are computed rather than annotated. On the cases both systems answer, the pipeline is right 90.2% of the time against 61.2% for direct answering. It answers two thirds of the cases, and counting its abstentions as errors it does not exceed direct answering (60.4% against 64.6%). The limit is extraction: on contracts the errors are almost never in the arithmetic, but in choosing which event the period starts from.

title: MotionGS-SLAM: Event-Modulated Gaussian Splatting for Motion-Blur Robust SLAM
abstract: Current Vision-based SLAM systems fail catastrophically when motion blur corrupts the visual input, as they attempt the ill-posed inverse problem of recovering sharp content from degraded observations. We present MotionGS-SLAM, which fundamentally reimagines motion blur handling through a paradigm shift: rather than removing blur artifacts, we reformulate the challenge as a well-constrained forward problem that generatively models blur formation within the rendering pipeline. By leveraging event cameras' microsecond temporal resolution and immunity to motion blur, we introduce a novel event-modulated Gaussian kernel that dynamically adapts each Gaussian's rasterization based on precise motion cues. Our dual-modulation mechanism transforms 2D Gaussian projections from isotropic dots into anisotropic, motion-aligned elliptical brush strokes (spatial modulation) while adaptively varying exposure integral sampling density based on local velocity (temporal modulation). This physics-based approach enables joint optimization of intra-exposure camera trajectories and 3D scene geometry through blur-aware photometric and event-based constraints. Extensive experiments demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in trajectory accuracy and map quality under severe high-motion conditions.

title: Does Data Balancing Improve Fairness Across Gender Groups? A Comparative Study of Highly Imbalanced Stroke Prediction with a Logistic Regression Model
abstract: This study investigates whether data balancing techniques improve fairness across gender groups in stroke prediction using Logistic Regression on a highly imbalanced Kaggle stroke dataset. Six resampling methods were evaluated for predictive performance and gender fairness. Results show that resampling significantly enhances minority class detection, but resampling methods introduce significant gender disparities, indicating that data balancing does not inherently ensure fairness. These findings underscore the need for fairness-aware strategies in healthcare AI to mitigate biases while improving predictive accuracy.

title: Hybrid Bio-Inspired Optimization Framework for Deep Learning-Based Medical Image Analysis
abstract: With the development of huge medical image data sets and complex diseases, medical image analysis has become an indispensable factor in the computer-aided diagnosis, which plays an important role in the automatic diagnosis, detection and classification of diseases. Medical image analysis has been an essential part of the computer-aided diagnosis, which has an important role in automatic detection and classification of complex diseases from large-scale medical image data sets. However, the conventional deep learning models have redundant features, high computation complexity and suboptimal hyperparameter selection which restricts the diagnostic performance of the model. The study introduces a Hybrid Bio-Inspired Optimization Framework for deep learning-based medical image analysis, which combines cutting-edge pre-processing methods, smart feature selection and adaptive optimization techniques to form a holistic framework. Medical images are first enhanced, normalized, augmented and ROI extracted to enhance the quality of the image and minimize noise. A hybrid bio-inspired feature selection mechanism is used to select the most discriminative features, with a minimum of redundancy and computational cost. Then, a novel optimized deep neural network is trained with the help of new optimization algorithms which are inspired by living organisms such as Adaptive Medical Image Preprocessing Algorithm (AMIPA), Hybrid Bio-Inspired Feature Selection Algorithm (HBIFSA), Hybrid Bio-Inspired Hyperparameter Optimization Algorithm (HBIHOA), and Optimized Deep Learning Training Algorithm (ODLTA). The integrated optimization strategy is experimentally validated to greatly improve the diagnostic performance with reduced computational requirements, which enables it to be adapted to intelligent clinical decision-support systems and next-generation AI-assisted health care applications.

title: Computational Information Gravity Model
abstract: The Computational Information Gravity Model (CIGM) proposes a novel framework for understanding the emergence and concentration of knowledge within complex systems, particularly large language models (LLMs). The core concept revolves around the notion that information exhibits an inherent gravitational attraction, quantified as the function G(Ii, Ij). This attraction represents the propensity for information elements (Ii and Ij) to coalesce and reinforce each other, leading to the formation of dense, interconnected knowledge clusters – effectively, the underlying mechanisms behind the growth of large models. This model provides a potential pathway towards a dynamic understanding of information flow and evolution, with implications for fields ranging from artificial intelligence and cognitive science to network theory and social dynamics. The model is presented here without empirical experimentation, focusing on its theoretical foundations and potential applications. ---

title: Computational Knowledge Composition Theory (CKCT-3)
abstract: Computational Knowledge Composition Theory (CKCT-3) is a formal framework that seeks to explain how complex, high‑level knowledge can be systematically generated from simpler, elementary knowledge components. The theory posits that knowledge can be represented as a set of atomic propositions or facts (denoted by K_i) which, when combined according to well‑defined compositional rules, yield new knowledge states K_j. CKCT-3 introduces a hierarchy of knowledge composition operations, each capturing different levels of abstraction and logical structure, and establishes a mapping between these operations and the well‑known principles of formal logic, information theory, and machine learning. By integrating ideas from knowledge graphs, semantic networks, and the emerging field of explainable artificial intelligence, CKCT-3 offers a principled methodology for constructing knowledge bases that are both scalable and interpretable. The theory is motivated by the analogy to the periodic table of elements, where simple building blocks can be combined to produce a rich spectrum of compounds; similarly, CKCT-3 envisions a "knowledge periodic table" that organizes elementary knowledge units into a structured landscape from which higher‑order knowledge can be systematically derived. This paper develops the formal underpinnings of CKCT-3, demonstrates its applicability through illustrative examples, and outlines potential avenues for future research, including its implications for AI alignment, knowledge management, and the pursuit of a Turing‑Award‑worthy breakthrough in artificial intelligence.

title: "RAIE: An Exact Structural Similarity Index, Positional Encoding, and Graph-Encoder Probe Benchmark for Rooted Trees"
abstract: "This artifact accompanies the manuscript \"Exact Structural Embeddings for RootedTrees: A Constant-Time Similarity Index and Positional Encoding for HierarchicalGraph Learning\" (Gleb B. Sologub). It packages the experiment code, pinnedpublic-benchmark manifests, released result tables, and the executed GPU notebookthat regenerate the paper's results. The artifact covers three contributionsbuilt on the rooted ancestor incidence embedding (RAIE): (1) an exact structuralsimilarity index with O(n)-space LCA preprocessing, O(1) pairwise depth\/LCA\/distance\/Jaccard queries, and output-sensitive exact top-k ancestor retrieval,benchmarked from 10^3 to 10^6 nodes and on three real hierarchies (the WordNetnoun taxonomy, the CPython standard-library source tree, and the Gene Ontology);(2) RAIE-SE, an exact training-free ancestor positional encoding, evaluated ontwo off-tree ontology node-classification tasks and as a feature for real graphencoders; and (3) a node-disjoint, multi-seed structural probe of learned graphencoders (node2vec, GraphSAGE, GIN, Graphormer\/GPS), including a provably-fairedge-weighted probe whose target is provably not a function of LCA depth anddistance. Synthetic rooted-tree families and a pinned public suite ofsoftware-repository and XML trees are materialized from official sources bymanifest rather than redistributed."

title: Quantum optimization for the warehouse layout problem
abstract: Abstract The warehouse layout problem (WLP), also known as warehouse slotting problem, aims to determine the assignment of products to storage locations while minimizing the total travel distance for picking operations. It is combinatorial in nature and well-known to be NP-hard. To obtain high-quality solutions to medium and large WLP instances efficiently remains a computational challenge, which has motivated our work on applying quantum optimization algorithms for this problem. We reformulate the classical quadratic assignment programming (QAP) model of the WLP to a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) model. Our QUBO model avoids adding slack variables and reduces additional overheads as in the typical QUBO reformulation approach, which facilitates the application of the D-Wave Leap Hybrid solver. Computational study is performed on a use case with 30 stock-keeping-units (SKUs) and 32 storage slots, for which the QUBO formulation has 960 binary decision variables. We show that the D-Wave Leap Hybrid solver finds better solution to the base scenario than the exact IBM CPLEX mixed-integer quadratic programming (MIQP) solver operating under a 60-second wall-clock limit, one-tenth of the 600-second budget allocated to CPLEX in this experimental design. A sensitivity analysis across 30 scenarios, generated by crossing five annual pick volume profiles with six co-picking matrix density levels (0.5 to 1.0), shows that the D-Wave hybrid solver outperforms CPLEX MIQP solver in 26 of 30 cases, with solution quality improvements of 0.4 to 12.1%. D-Wave’s advantage generally increases as the density of co-picking matrix decreases. These results demonstrate quantum utility for WLP and motivate further investigation of hybrid quantum-classical methods for combinatorial logistics optimization at industrial strength scales.

Our QUBO model avoids adding slack variables and reduces additional overheads as in the typical QUBO reformulation approach, which facilitates the application of the D-Wave Leap Hybrid solver. Computational study is performed on a use case with 30 stock-keeping-units (SKUs) and 32 storage slots, for which the QUBO formulation has 960 binary decision variables. We show that the D-Wave Leap Hybrid solver finds better solution to the base scenario than the exact IBM CPLEX mixed-integer quadratic programming (MIQP) solver operating under a 60-second wall-clock limit, one-tenth of the 600-second budget allocated to CPLEX in this experimental design. A sensitivity analysis across 30 scenarios, generated by crossing five annual pick volume profiles with six co-picking matrix density levels (0.5 to 1.0), shows that the D-Wave hybrid solver outperforms CPLEX MIQP solver in 26 of 30 cases, with solution quality improvements of 0.4 to 12.1%. D-Wave’s advantage generally increases as the density of co-picking matrix decreases. These results demonstrate quantum utility for WLP and motivate further investigation of hybrid quantum-classical methods for combinatorial logistics optimization at industrial strength scales.

title: Speed of Learning: AI and the Prompt Improvement Process
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been highlighted as the next wave of improved labor force productivity. The focus to date has been on the use of AI to improve outcome productivity. The purpose of this experiment is to assess the use of AI for learning at speed. The experiment and use of Generative AI (GenAI) is based on a simple process of survey creation to assess AI use in the research process. The designed experiment evaluates whether GenAI can increase the Speed of Learning with respect to survey creation tasks. The experiment includes four repetitive prompts used to create the survey. The initial prompt created the initial survey with each subsequent prompt enhancing survey results. The GenAI initial survey creation process lasted less than 2 hours. Learning of the survey creation process includes whether the resulting survey: 1) met the author’s goals, and 2) achieved the speculative outcome of this experiment.

title: Adversarial Latency Watermarking: Covertly Encoding Zero Bit Keys in Federated Learning Model Updates
abstract: Federated learning (FL) protects client data by sharing only model updates, yet current defences ignore timing metadata. We show that a single malicious client can embed a 128 bit cryptographic key into the final global model by modulating update latency alone, bypassing gradient-value inspections, differential privacy (DP), and secure aggregation (SecAgg). We model the latency-to-weight channel as an additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) process with CPU jitter and derive its information-theoretic capacity, demonstrating that 134 rounds suffice to transmit 128 bits at ε=500 μs. We design Jitter Deconv, a spread-spectrum encoder/decoder that maps Gold-code delays to weight-space imprints and recovers keys with bit-error rate (BER) 1.02×10⁻³ under DP-SGD (σ=10⁻²) and SecAgg. To detect the covert channel, we introduce Latency Print, a lightweight autocovariance-based statistic achieving AUC=0.98 and ≤0.7 % false-positive rate with <0.1 % CPU overhead. Experiments on CIFAR-10, FEMNIST, and Stack Overflow under realistic FL hyperparameters and hardware time-stamping (PTP, ±1 μs) confirm that our attack incurs ≤0.18 % accuracy degradation and survives network congestion. We further compare Latency Print to an SVM-based arrival-pattern classifier, demonstrating superior detection speed and reliability. Our findings expose time as a first class security primitive in FL systems and recommend integrating timing randomization, lightweight monitoring, and scheduler level defenses into frameworks such as Tensor Flow Federated.

title: Anytime-Valid Adaptive State Abstraction under Partial Observability
abstract: An executable research artifact for verifier-governed state construction under partial observability. It implements an episode-regeneration anytime-valid repair/retain/wait gate, prefix-priced history-program selection, repair–retire–restore lifecycle experiments, hash-bound receipt chains, tamper rejection, and POBAX Simple Chain, T-Maze and RockSample evaluations. The initial sealed v0.1 T-Maze evaluation failed its frozen primary gate and is preserved in full. A separately frozen v0.2 correction changed only the TS policy optimiser setting, used twenty untouched seeds, and passed every declared gate. A clean 80-run replay reproduced the frozen scientific projection exactly. The supported claim is deliberately narrow: within a declared finite history-program family, held-out anytime-valid evidence can authorise compact state abstraction repairs while preserving explicit abstention and auditable provenance. This does not establish unrestricted representation discovery, general POMDP learning, or general intelligence.

title: CTNet y el sistema nervioso; Mismo tipo de operación realizada sobre soportes distintos
abstract: Este paper pertenece al corpus EMQR - CTNET Respeto al uso de IA en mi corpus EMQR - CTNet Utilicé inteligencia artificial para la estructuración y redacción de los manuscritos, la presentación del formalismo matemático, la consolidación documental y la asistencia editorial. La concepción de EMQR y CTNet, su estructura matemática y computacional, sus principios, relaciones, desarrollos, implementación, experimentos e interpretación de los resultados me corresponden a mi. Osea no utilicé IA para originar la estructura matemática, sino para organizarla, expresarla formalmente de manera consistente y convertir todo el material desarrollado en una presentación técnica unificada, debido principalmente a su extension.

title: Computational Relation Reconstruction (CRR)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Relation Reconstruction (CRR) algorithm, a novel approach to inferring hidden relationships from observed outcomes. CRR operates on the principle of reverse engineering, akin to calculating system inverse engineering, to reconstruct relationships based on their resultant effects. The core of the algorithm involves identifying a set of observed outputs and then systematically deducing the underlying relationships that would logically produce those outputs. This process relies on a formal definition of relationship representation and a computational framework for searching through potential relationship structures. The algorithm aims to provide a robust method for understanding complex systems, particularly those involving artificial intelligence, where the relationships between components are often opaque. The potential for this work extends to a Turing Award-level challenge: achieving a deeper understanding of complex AI systems by explicitly reconstructing their underlying relational architectures. ---

title: Adaptive Program Boundary (APB): A Novel Approach to Dynamic Software Architecture
abstract: This paper introduces the Adaptive Program Boundary (APB) concept, a paradigm shift in software architecture design that moves away from static, developer-defined module boundaries. APB proposes a dynamic adaptation mechanism based on runtime behavior, aiming to create more resilient, efficient, and adaptable software systems. The core idea is to continuously monitor and respond to changes in dependency (D_t) and workload (W_t) to adjust the boundaries of software modules. This approach leverages the potential of software architecture to become a dynamically evolvable object, offering a significant step towards greater flexibility and responsiveness in complex software environments. The paper outlines the fundamental principles of APB, presents a mathematical formulation for the adaptation process, and discusses the potential implications and challenges associated with its implementation.

title: llm-memory-meter: measuring the real memory footprint of a local LLM from its official configuration
abstract: First citable release. Cite the concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21941274 — it always resolves to the latest version. Companion program for How to know if an AI model runs on your computer — and why. It reads a model's official config.json and prints the real memory footprint next to what the widely shared one-line formula predicts — a 19.8x overestimate on Qwen3.8-27B at 256K context, 8.2x on Gemma 4 26B A4B. Zero dependencies. Every number the article publishes is a test assertion, checked against frozen upstream configs and sealed in a SHA-256 provenance chain.

title: IndoBERT-based Named Entity Recognition Using Transformer Model for Indonesian Waste Bank Data Processing
abstract: Data processing in waste bank management systems faces substantial challenges when extracting structured information from unstructured textual data containing transaction records, customer information, and waste categorization details. This study develops and validates an automated Named Entity Recognition (NER) system based on the IndoBERT transformer architecture to process textual records from Makassar waste bank operations. The approach fine-tunes the indolem/indobert-base-uncased model through domain-specific adaptation targeting waste management vocabulary and operational terminology. The dataset comprises 975 textual records collected from 8 Waste Bank Units in Makassar City. These records were systematically annotated using the BIO tagging scheme for eight entity types: B-LOCATION, B-PERSON, B-WASTE_CATEGORY, B-WASTE_TYPE, I-PERSON, I-WASTE_CATEGORY, I-WASTE_TYPE, and O. The dataset was partitioned into training (682 samples, 69.9%), validation (146 samples, 15.0%), and test sets (147 samples, 15.1%) using stratified sampling methodology with high inter-annotator agreement (κ=0.91). Experimental results show outstanding performance with 94.37% test accuracy, 90.65% precision, 94.37% recall, and 92.21% F1-score, outperforming general-purpose Indonesian NER approaches. Perfect performance was achieved for waste type recognition (B-WASTE_TYPE: 100% F1-score) and location identification (B-LOCATION: 100% F1-score), while waste category classification reached 96% F1-score. This implementation successfully automates entity extraction from Makassar waste bank textual data, reducing manual processing time by 95% while maintaining high accuracy levels. This research makes important contributions to Indonesian environmental natural language processing. These contributions include transformer adaptation methodologies for resource-constrained domains, validated IndoBERT performance on Indonesian waste bank data, the first Indonesian waste management NER dataset, and demonstrated feasibility of NLP-based environmental policy systems.

title: BrainLinear: A Linear Model for Brain Network Analysis in Sparse Tangent Subspaces
abstract: Functional connectome analysis examines brain-region interactions to understand and identify disorders such as autism spectrum disorder and Alzheimer's disease. Existing methods typically use GNNs and Transformers to model the full functional connectivity matrix. However, processing tens of thousands of connections introduces redundancy and noise, increases computational cost, and limits connection-level interpretability. This raises a central question: do we really need complex interaction modeling, or is identifying a small set of disease-relevant connectivity patterns sufficient? To answer this question, we propose BrainLinear, a lightweight geometry-aware framework for mining disease-discriminative connectome patterns. BrainLinear first maps each functional connectivity matrix to a shared tangent space centered at the Fréchet mean of the training set, capturing subject-specific deviations while respecting matrix geometry. It then scores each ROI-pair tangent direction by its classification contribution and disease--control difference, retaining Top-$K$ directions as a compact representation. Finally, a shallow multilayer perceptron performs classification on the selected representation. Experiments on ABIDE and ADNI show that BrainLinear matches or exceeds strong GNN and Transformer baselines at a fraction of their cost: it improves AUC and ACC over the best baseline for each metric by up to $3.54$ and $1.39$ percentage points, while reducing runtime and peak GPU memory by $84.0\%$ and $68.4\%$ relative to the closest baseline in AUC. The selected directions are directionally consistent with between-group displacements and organized across major functional systems, supporting connection-level interpretation.

title: Anthropomorphizing Generative AI: is Memory All You Need?
abstract: As GAI adoption expands, its capabilities increasingly foster anthropomorphic perceptions. Drawing on 21 interviews from an ongoing grounded theory study at a U.S.-based organization using Microsoft 365 Copilot alongside ChatGPT, we find that Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) memory, understood as the ability to retain and dialogically recall past interactions, together with interactional alignment, fuels anthropomorphization. By enabling GAI to filter and shape responses in line with users’ preferences, memory creates the impression that the system understands users’ worldview and emotions, thereby supporting perceptions of relationality and human-like interaction.

title: Fed-TransResCaps-HGBOA-GWO-PSO-Net: A Secure and Explainable Federated Hybrid Deep Learning Framework for CT–MRI Medical Image Classification
abstract: Hospitals rarely share raw imaging data. Privacy statutes, institutional review requirements, and plain commercial caution keep scans behind institutional firewalls, which leaves most large-scale medical imaging models trained on whatever single-site corpus their authors could assemble. Federated learning offers a way out, but it inherits two problems that centralised training never had to face: client data are not identically distributed, and the model updates that cross the network are themselves a disclosure surface. This paper presents Fed-TransResCaps-HGBOA-GWO-PSO-Net, a federated framework for CT–MRI modality classification that addresses both. Three complementary encoders a frozen ResNet50, a frozen EfficientNetB0, and a lightweight convolutional-transformer branch are refined by Convolutional Block Attention Modules and concatenated into a 3392-dimensional descriptor. A hybrid Honey-Badger/Grey-Wolf/Particle-Swarm search then prunes this descriptor to a 70% subset, so that only 2374 coordinates reach the classification head and the per-round payload shrinks accordingly. Clients are grouped by label distribution using k-means before aggregation, and updates are combined with FedNova first within and then across clusters, which keeps a pathologically skewed client from dominating the global model. Every accepted update is committed to a SHA-256 hash chain, giving an append-only audit trail of who contributed what and when. Grad-CAM overlays are produced at inference so that a clinician can see which image regions drove a decision. On a 4974-image CT–MRI benchmark partitioned across three deliberately non-IID clients, the framework converged from 56.38% to 98.66% accuracy in twelve communication rounds, with an AUC of 0.9979, specificity of 0.9973, and Matthews correlation of 0.9733. The dominant residual error is a one-sided 2.42% false-negative rate on MRI, which we trace to the label-skewed client partition rather than to the encoder.

title: Computational Idea Evolution Theory (CIET)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Idea Evolution Theory (CIET), a novel framework designed to model and understand the process of intellectual development, particularly as it relates to artificial intelligence. CIET posits that ideas, much like living organisms, undergo a process of transformation and adaptation, leading to the emergence of increasingly complex and sophisticated concepts. The theory utilizes a discrete-time, agent-based simulation approach, where individual "ideas" (represented as mathematical structures) are subjected to a set of evolutionary operators – mutation, recombination, and selection – mimicking biological processes like genetic variation and natural selection. The core principle is expressed mathematically as: [Idea_t → Idea_{t+1}] where *Idea_t* represents an initial idea and *Idea_{t+1}* represents the evolved idea at the next time step. This paper will outline the theoretical foundations of CIET, detail the key components of the simulation, and discuss its potential implications for creating robust and adaptable AI systems, suggesting a path towards establishing a foundational theory in machine science. We explore the dynamics of idea evolution using a simplified model of selection pressure (represented by *s_i*) and the impact of different evolutionary rates (represented by *r_i*). The ultimate goal is to create a computational model capable of generating novel solutions to complex problems, mirroring the creative capacity of human thought. ---

title: Computational Concept Migration Theory
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Concept Migration Theory (CCMT), a novel framework for understanding and facilitating knowledge transfer between disparate domains. CCMT posits that intelligent systems can learn not just through direct pattern recognition but through the strategic migration of conceptual frameworks. This theory addresses the challenge of how machines can generate novel, cross-domain knowledge by explicitly modeling the process of concept transformation. The theory is built upon a formal representation of concept migration, utilizing directed graphs to illustrate the relationships between concepts and their associated attributes. The core mechanism involves identifying analogous concepts across domains and applying transformation rules to map attributes and relationships. This approach has significant implications for automated scientific discovery and potentially qualifies for consideration for the Turing Award. The paper details the theoretical foundations of CCMT, outlining key components, operational rules, and potential applications. ---

title: Computational Functional Homotopy Theory
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Functional Homotopy Theory (CFHT), a novel approach to program equivalence and algorithmic transformation based on the principles of homotopy theory. The core concept revolves around the continuous transformation of programs represented as spaces, denoted as [P₀, P₁]. A program H(P, λ) is considered equivalent if it maps from a program P at parameter λ to P₀ at λ = 0 and to P₁ at λ = 1, while maintaining key functional invariants. This framework provides a mathematical structure for understanding and classifying programs based on their continuous evolutionary pathways. The potential of CFHT extends to the development of new mathematical theories related to program equivalence and algorithmic transformations, holding significant implications for areas such as software verification, automated program repair, and meta-programming. The theoretical underpinnings leverage concepts of homotopy, allowing for the exploration of continuous changes in program behavior, unlike traditional static equivalence checks. This work outlines the fundamental principles and introduces a formal definition of the CFHT framework. ---

The theoretical underpinnings leverage concepts of homotopy, allowing for the exploration of continuous changes in program behavior, unlike traditional static equivalence checks. This work outlines the fundamental principles and introduces a formal definition of the CFHT framework. ---

title: Computational Knowledge Universe Theory (CKUT)
abstract: The present manuscript introduces the Computational Knowledge Universe Theory (CKUT), a comprehensive formal framework that treats all knowledge as elements of a unified space, denoted Omega_K, and models the interrelationships among these elements using graph-theoretic constructs and dynamic evolution rules. CKUT aims to provide a rigorous basis for understanding how knowledge is formed, organized, and expanded across disciplines, and to lay the groundwork for algorithmic systems that can autonomously discover, verify, and integrate new knowledge. The theory is grounded in set theory, graph theory, and discrete dynamical systems, and it incorporates mechanisms for inference, synthesis, and validation that are applicable to both human cognition and artificial intelligence. By framing knowledge as a dynamic, interconnected universe, CKUT offers a potential pathway toward the highest level of knowledge theory, with implications that could be recognized by the Turing Award community.

title: Beyond Rule-Based Interaction: How Generative AI Chatbot Attributes Shape Customer Trust, Satisfaction, and Continuance Intention
abstract: With increasing deployment of generative AI (GenAI) chatbots in organizational settings, understanding the determinants of customer trust, satisfaction, and continuance intention has become a critical research priority. Unlike traditional rule-based and deterministic systems, GenAI chatbots generate adaptive, context-aware, and socially expressive responses that transform human-GenAI interactions. Existing service quality, and social response theories are mostly applicable to static interactions and do not fully account for the probabilistic and relational dynamics introduced by GenAI chatbots. This study proposes a theoretical framework examining how functional attributes (reliability, responsiveness, privacy) and relational attributes (empathy, assurance) affect trust and satisfaction, and continuance intention. By extending post-adoption theory to the context of GenAI chatbots, this research reinterprets service attributes as dynamic and interaction-dependent, providing new insights into trust formation and its role in enhancing the customer satisfaction and long-term engagement.

title: Computational Cognitive Coordinate System (CCCS)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Cognitive Coordinate System (CCCS), a theoretical framework designed to unify disparate cognitive models within artificial intelligence. The core concept of CCCS rests on the proposition that intelligent systems, regardless of their underlying architecture or training methodology, operate within distinct cognitive spaces. These spaces are represented mathematically as [C(S)], where C(S) denotes the cognitive space associated with a specific system 'S'. The goal of CCCS is to establish a unified coordinate system for these spaces, allowing for comparative analysis and potential integration of diverse AI models. This framework offers a novel approach to addressing the challenges of AI alignment and generalization, potentially unlocking significant advancements towards a more cohesive and robust artificial intelligence landscape. The paper details the fundamental principles of CCCS, including the definition of cognitive space, methods for mapping system behavior onto this space, and the proposed mathematical formalism for quantifying the relationships between different cognitive spaces. Further exploration into the potential of CCCS to achieve a 'Turing Award' level of impact is discussed. ---

title: Program Decision Lineage
abstract: Program Decision Lineage (PDL) is a novel framework designed to establish traceability within artificial intelligence (AI) decision-making processes. The core concept revolves around meticulously documenting the lineage of each decision, outlining its direct influences and the contributing factors. This framework leverages a directed graph representation, where each decision node (D_t) is linked to its predecessor (D_{t-1}), alongside input data (I_t) and contextual information (C_t). The goal is to create a comprehensive and auditable record of the decision-making process, offering insights into potential biases, vulnerabilities, and the reasoning behind AI-driven choices. This paper details the PDL framework, its underlying principles, and explores its potential applications, particularly in areas requiring transparency and accountability in AI systems. The framework's capacity to facilitate the understanding and potential correction of AI decision-making represents a significant step forward in responsible AI development.

title: Computational Cooperative Behavior Theory
abstract: This paper proposes Computational Cooperative Behavior Theory (CCBT), a novel framework for understanding and modeling cooperative phenomena in multi-agent systems. CCBT posits that cooperation emerges from the collective behavior of multiple computational entities, where each agent's actions (A_1, A_2, ..., A_n) influence a resultant cooperative behavior (B) defined by a function f. The theory's core focus lies in elucidating how this interaction leads to the generation of emergent capabilities exceeding the sum of individual agent capabilities. CCBT aims to provide a foundational theory with potential for significant advancements in multi-agent systems research, including contributions to the broader field of Artificial Intelligence and potentially holding merit for consideration for the Turing Award. This document outlines the theoretical framework, key components, and future research directions of CCBT.

title: Program Fact Revocability (PFR): A Framework for Mutable Knowledge Representation
abstract: This paper introduces Program Fact Revocability (PFR), a novel framework designed to address the inherent limitations of static knowledge representation in systems requiring adaptability and the ability to correct errors. The core principle of PFR centers around the concept that individual facts within a knowledge system should be inherently revocable. This allows for the systematic removal of factual assertions and, crucially, triggers a process to automatically identify and update dependent conclusions. We present a formal model of PFR, utilizing a directed graph representation where facts are nodes and dependencies are represented by directed edges. The system operates based on the following logic: A fact *F* can be revoked via the function *Revoke(F)*. Upon revocation, the system identifies all dependent facts *Dependents(F)*, and propagates updates to all conclusions reliant on *F*. This process ensures consistency and avoids the propagation of outdated information. The potential impact of PFR extends beyond simple knowledge bases, encompassing intelligent databases and AI memory management systems, offering a pathway to more robust and reliable knowledge processing. We explore the theoretical implications and outline a foundational framework for future research and development within this area.

title: Computational Experience Hierarchy Theory (CEHT): A Framework for Machine Capability Development
abstract: The rapid evolution of artificial intelligence has produced systems that can learn, adapt, and make decisions in complex environments. Yet, the processes that underlie their growth from novices to experts remain poorly formalised. This paper introduces the Computational Experience Hierarchy Theory (CEHT), a conceptual framework that mirrors human developmental stages of experience—Trial, Skill, Expertise, and Wisdom—and maps them onto machine learning pipelines. CEHT proposes a set of recursive equations that capture how data exposure, reinforcement signals, and internal model adjustments interact to produce a measurable progression in capability. By articulating explicit metrics for each stage and the transitions that link them, CEHT offers a principled basis for designing curricula for autonomous agents, for benchmarking progression, and for anticipating emergent behaviours. The theory is illustrated with illustrative examples from reinforcement learning, meta‑learning, and ethical decision‑making, demonstrating that CEHT can unify disparate strands of AI research under a single hierarchical narrative. Finally, the paper outlines future research directions that aim to validate CEHT empirically and to explore its implications for safe and explainable AI deployment.

title: ExecutionProof Adversarial Security Test Series — EP-SEC-001 through EP-SEC-009b
abstract: A preregistered adversarial-security series evaluating whether actors, tooling, or attack paths can bypass the ExecutionProof pre-execution governance boundary. The series includes eight initial PASS experiments, one preserved FAIL identifying a direct tool-level execution bypass, and a separately preregistered remediation experiment that passed all eight adversarial cases. The experiments evaluate unsigned actions, expired and replayed proofs, scope violations, forged evidence, privilege escalation, action drift, combined attack vectors, and direct tool invocation outside the enforcement boundary. The EP-SEC-009 failure is preserved in the public record; EP-SEC-009b documents and tests the remediation separately. All experiments were documented and hash-locked before execution, with results published after execution. The release preserves negative findings and remediation history as part of the evidence record. Internal/founder-led experimental corpus; independent academic validation is the next phase.

title: Development of a Chatbot Based on Natural Language Processing and Multinomial Naïve Bayes for Optimising Academic Administrative Services in Higher Education
abstract: The transformation of academic administrative services in higher education requires intelligent systems to automate routine information delivery. This study presents a web-based chatbot using Natural Language Processing (NLP) and the Multinomial Naïve Bayes (MNB) algorithm to enhance administrative services. The system classifies user queries into 20 intent categories and provides real-time responses. Training and testing were conducted using labelled text data. The model achieved 93.62% training accuracy and 63.38% test accuracy, indicating potential overfitting due to the limited variety of test data. Evaluation metrics showed 63% precision, 60% recall, and a 61% F1-score, reflecting stable classification performance. User Acceptance Testing (UAT) was conducted with students and administrative staff, showing acceptance rates of 83.5% and 84%, respectively. These results indicate strong usability and relevance of the chatbot in academic contexts. The system integrates text classification, NLP, and user evaluation within a single framework to address repetitive administrative tasks. This research contributes a practical solution tailored to the needs of academic institutions by combining machine learning techniques with direct user evaluation. The chatbot provides faster and more consistent access to academic information, thereby reducing dependency on manual administrative processes. Future work may enhance classification accuracy by utilising richer datasets and alternative algorithms.

title: Boundary-Aligned Contribution Routing for Robust Optical--SAR Object Detection
abstract: Optical imagery provides rich appearance cues, whereas synthetic aperture radar (SAR) offers observations that are less sensitive to illumination and weather, making optical--SAR fusion attractive for remote-sensing object detection. However, the presence of multiple modalities does not guarantee beneficial fusion: imperfect spatial, temporal, and semantic correspondence can make an otherwise intact stream conditionally harmful and induce negative cross-modal transfer. We handle this issue through a model-specific task-utility perspective and learn task-conditioned contribution routing using detection supervision alone. The proposed fusion-boundary-aligned routing regulates each modality's contribution before the first learned cross-modal feature-value mixing operation. For architectures with frequent shallow interaction, a Feature Router performs cross-conditioned, group-addressable modulation near the input; for dual-backbone architectures, a Dual-Statistic Semantic Router predicts stream-level contribution weights from modality-specific average and maximum statistics before late semantic fusion. The routers require no explicit utility supervision, quality labels, reconstruction, or distillation. Experiments on M4-SAR and SpaceNet6-OTD cover nominal full inputs, controlled correspondence shifts, missing modalities, and four nonzero modality-corruption scenarios. Across the reported clean-training controls, routing improves full-input $\text{mAP}_{50}$ by 0.5--5.9 points. Relative to the corresponding modality-dropout baselines, it raises missing-modality $\text{mAP}_{50}$ by 7.6--41.6 points and reduces the negative-transfer rate by up to 12.7 percentage points. Spearman correlations between the learned routing weights and model-specific leave-one-modality-out utility range from 0.45 to 0.66, supporting the task-utility interpretation of the routing coefficients.

title: Hierarchical Agentic Incident Response with Digital-Twin-Validated Attack Inference
abstract: Network incident response remains slow and labor-intensive as the defender must infer multi-stage attacks from partial observations and translate recovery decisions into reliable system commands. Decision-theoretic planners provide principled optimization but typically rely on abstract states and predefined actions, while large language model (LLM) agents can reason over operational context but may hallucinate attacks and responses. Toward automating response planning, we present a hierarchical agentic response framework that integrates LLM-based attack inference, rollout planning, and digital-twin validation. A fine-tuned LLM infers the attack progression and affected hosts from security alerts and system measurements. An emulated network digital twin replays the inferred attack and returns discrepancies between predicted and observed effects to calibrate the inference. A separately fine-tuned planning agent uses the rollout planning method to prioritize affected components at the tactical layer. At the operational layer, the planning agent proposes high-level recovery actions, and an execution agent translates selected actions into recovery and verification commands that are validated in the digital twin. We evaluate the framework on a 33-component enterprise-network testbed under three multi-stage attack scenarios. The results show that our framework outperforms frontier-LLM baselines in recovery success rate by 18--31%.

title: Vignettes or Bots: Can We Study Chatbot Interactions without Actual Interactions?
abstract: Vignettes are widely used in chatbot research to manipulate interface and design cues, but the unique characteristics of dyadic chat interactions raise questions about whether observing a vignette produces the same perceptions as participating in a live conversation. In a 2 × 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment, we compare perceptions of anthropomorphism across vignette and interactive chatbot conditions. We find that humanness cues such as a human name and typing indicator significantly increase perceived anthropomorphism in vignette conditions but have no detectable effect when participants actually interact with the chatbot. These results provide initial evidence that vignette-based chatbot studies may not generalize to real interactions, with implications for how the field studies perception of conversational agents.

title: Obstacle Avoidance by a Mobile Robot Using a Nuro-Genetic Controller System
abstract: By applying Darwinian principles like natural selection and survival of the fittest, neural controllers can be developed that enable robots to act autonomously in unpredictable or unknown environments. This study examines the Genetic Algorithm (GA) as an optimization tool for mobile robot navigation. The controller's performance was evaluated on a standard obstacle-avoidance task, as well as a multi-task setup combining obstacle avoidance with homing. Experimental results confirm that neuro-genetic controller optimization significantly enhances both average population fitness and individual peak fitness, while demonstrating the feasibility of integrating cooperative functional modules to accomplish complex robotic goals.

title: AEGIS-FL: Auditable Federated Threat Detection for Multi-Tenant Cloud-Edge Systems
abstract: Multi-tenant hybrid cloud and edge infrastructures generate security telemetry that is individually sparse and collectively informative, but contractual, regulatory, and competitive barriers prevent tenants from pooling it. Federated learning offers a route around this obstacle, yet deployments in adversarial security settings must simultaneously resist model poisoning by participating tenants, provide auditable evidence of what each tenant contributed, bound the information leaked about tenant-local data, and translate detections into containment actions. Existing work addresses these requirements in isolation. We present AEGIS-FL, a four-plane architecture that couples DataOps-oriented governance, privacy-preserving federated training, a permissioned audit ledger, and a reinforcement-learned response controller, and we evaluate the planes jointly rather than separately. The central mechanism is a ledger-anchored aggregation rule in which per-tenant reputation, persisted across rounds on the audit ledger, sets an adaptive screening budget for a geometric (multi-Krum) filter. This removes the dependence on oracle knowledge of the adversary fraction that, we show, silently inflates reported robustness in the standard experimental protocol. On a controlled 100-tenant simulation with label-skewed partitions, AEGIS-FL reaches F₁ = 0.811 ± 0.017 against 0.790 ± 0.048 for FedAvg and 0.259 ± 0.005 for isolated per-tenant training and sustains F₁ = 0.799 under 10% sign-flipping adversaries where FedAvg falls to 0.740. Secure aggregation reconstructs the plaintext mean exactly under 30% tenant dropout at 19.2 kB per tenant per round, and the audit ledger commits at 19.6 kB per round with seven-hash Merkle inclusion proofs. We report three cautionary findings that qualify the deployment envelope. First, client-level differential privacy at this federation scale cannot reach a meaningful budget: ε ≈ 103 costs 4.0 F₁ points, while ε ≈ 7 destroys utility (F₁ = 0.308). Second, contrary to our own hypothesis, reducing model dimensionality does not recover private utility, because capacity losses offset noise reduction. Third, a loss-threshold membership-inference attack achieves AUC = 0.502 even without noise, so the empirical privacy benefit of the noise mechanism is not demonstrable in this regime. We argue these results indicate that participant scale, not noise calibration or model compression, is the binding constraint on private federated security analytics.

title: Computational Problem Generation Theory (CPGT)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Problem Generation Theory (CPGT), a novel framework aimed at shifting the paradigm in artificial intelligence research. Currently, the vast majority of AI development relies on human-defined problems, a process that is often slow, biased, and limited by human intuition. CPGT proposes a fundamentally different approach: enabling machines to autonomously generate computational problems, effectively reversing the traditional flow of problem definition. This theory leverages advances in deep learning, reinforcement learning, and symbolic reasoning to create problems with varying degrees of complexity and novelty. The core principle is formalized as: [Machine → Problem]. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of CPGT, outlining key components and potential architectures. We also discuss the implications of this shift for areas such as algorithm design, formal verification, and the development of truly intelligent systems. Finally, we present a preliminary mathematical framework for evaluating the quality and diversity of problems generated by a CPGT system, denoted as: *QCPGT = f(C, D, S)*, where *QCPGT* represents the quality of the generated problem, *C* denotes the complexity of the problem, *D* represents the diversity of the problem, and *S* signifies the system's search strategy. This work lays the foundation for a future where machines actively contribute to the advancement of mathematical and computational knowledge. ---

title: Computational Algorithmic Pressure Theory (CAPT)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Algorithmic Pressure Theory (CAPT), a novel framework for understanding the evolution of algorithms. CAPT posits that algorithms are not static entities but rather are subject to continuous pressure from their environment. This pressure drives algorithmic selection, improvement, and elimination – a process analogous to natural selection. The theory suggests a potential for developing an "algorithmic ecosystem" theory, where diverse algorithms co-evolve and compete within a defined environment. The core premise is formalized mathematically as: * $P_{alg} = f(E, A)$ Where: * $P_{alg}$ represents the Algorithmic Pressure experienced by the algorithm. * $E$ represents the Environment in which the algorithm operates. * $A$ represents the Algorithm itself. * $f$ is a function defining the pressure relationship, which can be deterministic or stochastic. The theory's implications extend to areas such as artificial intelligence, optimization, and evolutionary computation, offering a new lens through which to analyze and design algorithmic systems. Further investigation into the specific functional form of 'f' and the dynamics of the algorithmic ecosystem is warranted. ---

title: Computational abstraction generative theory
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Abstraction Generation Theory (CAGT), a novel approach to software development focused on automating the creation of abstractions. Traditionally, abstraction has been a manually crafted process, requiring significant human expertise and effort. CAGT proposes a shift towards systems capable of automatically generating new and relevant abstractions from data and context. This theory leverages core concepts of computation and aims to establish a framework for building the next generation of programming paradigms. The central hypothesis is that through algorithmic processes, systems can evolve and produce abstractions that are both novel and effectively tailored to specific problems. This paper outlines the theoretical foundations of CAGT, explores potential implementation strategies, and discusses its implications for the future of software design and development. ---

title: 连续多维自我范围理论 ——人的本能、情绪与认知体系的统一模型
abstract: 本文以主体系统在时间中的连续存在为逻辑起点,提出连续多维自我范围理论,尝试在统一框架下解释人的本能、情绪生成、决策行为及认知体系构建过程。研究首先区分主体系统的出现与持续存在,并将求生本能限定为主体系统维持自身连续性、结构稳定以及趋向可维持自我范围扩张的基础运行倾向。在此基础上,本文将自我范围表达为由身体、资源、关系、身份、意义、认知等多个维度构成的动态结构,并通过整体范围值及其时间变化描述主体系统对自身状态的综合读取。 情绪被进一步定义为主体系统对连续多维自我范围曲线、变化速度、变化加速度以及实际轨迹与预期轨迹偏差的状态性感知。外部信息以及主体内部的记忆调用、思考、预测和认知运算结果形成新的情境条件,主体据此建立预期自我范围轨迹并产生启动情绪,同时在当前可识别、可调用且可执行的候选行动集合中形成当前可计算范围内的最优决策。行动改变主体自身或外部环境,其结果通过反馈重新进入主体系统,更新情境、修正预期并触发新的情绪和决策,由此形成情境、预期、情绪、决策、行动、反馈与再决策构成的动态闭环。 在认知体系层面,本文将认知理解为连续多维自我范围中的一个结构维度。客观世界进入主体后依次经历感像、确认态、对象、关系态、对象式及认知体系等结构层级。对象通过特定关系维度上的伸缩差形成关系态,对象与关系态进一步构成对象式;众多对象式在体系基式、记忆库调用、调用性遍历、定态及选择机制作用下逐步形成相对稳定的认知体系。当对象式无法形成稳定的结构关系时,认知维度表现为不确定态及相应的自我范围收缩,主体系统则沿去不确定化方向运行,通过体系构建恢复或扩展认知范围。由此,人的本能、情绪、决策、行动反馈与认知体系不再被处理为彼此独立的现象,而被统一描述为主体系统围绕自身连续存在及连续多维自我范围变化展开的动态运行过程。 关键词: 连续多维自我范围 主体系统 人的本能 求生本能 情绪结构模型 自我范围曲线 决策与反馈 认知体系 不确定态 去不确定化

title: Computational Identity Transfer Theory (CITT)
abstract: Computational Identity Transfer Theory (CITT) proposes a formal framework for reasoning about the migration of identity across computational systems. Identity is modeled as a composite of states, relations, and processes. The theory defines a transfer function that maps an identity in one system to a corresponding identity in another system while preserving essential structural and functional properties. CITT captures scenarios such as model upgrade, replication, and splitting, and offers a foundation for understanding the continuity of digital agents in dynamic environments. The present work articulates core definitions, formal properties, illustrative examples, and discusses the broader implications of CITT for the development of robust digital intelligence. The theory is positioned as a potential cornerstone for future research in artificial general intelligence and digital ontology, with the prospect of contributing to high‑impact recognitions such as the Turing Award.

title: A Deterministic Constant-Competitive Algorithm for Dynamic Mixture-of-Experts Serving
abstract: Dynamic Mixture-of-Experts Serving allocates k replica GPUs among m experts as workloads change. At each round, the online algorithm sees the current workload, chooses integral replica counts, and pays bottleneck service cost plus replica movement. It does not know future workloads. Huang, Lou, and Xiao gave an O(sqrt(log k))-competitive randomized algorithm for this problem. We prove a deterministic O(1)-competitive algorithm. For every number of experts and every k>=1, the algorithm satisfies ALG_det <= 10 C_PB OPT + (5 C_PB + 8) k + 16, where C_PB is the absolute constant from Chasing Positive Bodies at resource augmentation one and covering sparsity two. Consequently, CR_det(k)<=10 C_PB for every k>=1, so CR_det(k)=Theta(1). The multiplicative factor does not depend on the number of experts, replica budget, horizon, or workload values. Thus randomization is not needed for the asymptotic guarantee. The proof has two layers. A finite tangent envelope, summable positive resets, and a nonexpansive balanced projection reduce reciprocal-max service costs to a deterministic exact-budget fractional path. A new deterministic rounding theorem converts every such path to integral allocations with service distortion three and movement bounded by the fractional movement plus 6k. The complete reduction, rounding theorem, causal composition, and quantified main theorem are machine-checked in Lean 4 relative to the positive-body result as the sole scientific source premise. The theorem concerns the allocation model above. It does not include network topology, shared-edge congestion, or routing decisions.

title: VGGT-Align: Bridging Local Reconstruction and Global Consistency for Long-Sequence 3D Reconstruction
abstract: Maintaining global geometric consistency is a central challenge in long-sequence 3D reconstruction, with scale drift being the most critical failure mode. In chunk-based inference pipelines, the scale degree of freedom in sequential Sim(3) alignment is left unconstrained, causing estimation errors to compound multiplicatively and distort global trajectories and point cloud geometry. We present a scale-consistency enhancement framework built on a key insight: in structured environments such as driving scenes, geometric quantities arising from environmental regularity remain inherently invariant across temporal segments, and discrepancies in their per-chunk measurements directly expose inter-chunk scale drift. We propose Scene Geometric Invariant Anchoring (SGIA), which extracts dominant geometric invariants from each chunk's predicted point cloud via coarse-to-fine robust estimation and exploits their cross-chunk consistency to establish scale constraints independent of point cloud registration, explicitly degenerating 7-DoF Sim(3) alignment into 6-DoF rigid-body transformation and severing chain-wise scale error propagation at its source. We further introduce a lightweight test-time adaptation strategy that fine-tunes only normalization-layer parameters via multi-objective self-supervision, progressively improving intra-chunk predictions along the sequence. Both modules are plug-and-play and require no offline retraining. Experiments on multiple long-sequence benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, reducing absolute trajectory error by up to 32% with significant gains in trajectory stability and reconstruction quality. Code: https://github.com/WZ-CS/VGGT-Align

title: Deploying Agentic LLM Pipelines at Scale: Quality-Gated Ensemble Governance for Enterprise News Intelligence
abstract: Corporate communications teams face information overload, refresh pressure, and overreliance risk on LLM-generated briefings. We present the production deployment of an on-premises agentic LLM system for enterprise news intelligence that couples retrieval, clustering, and report generation with ensemble LLM-as-Judge quality governance. Over six months in a conglomerate (Sep 2025–Feb 2026), Corporate Monitor ingested 36,910 unique articles and the Top News pipeline executed 126 runs (52,462 articles). Reports are scored on source faithfulness, factuality, informativeness, and coherence; grade B (≥75) defines the automation–oversight boundary. Sub-threshold outputs trigger up to three retries; remaining cases are flagged for review. Results show 100% success for scheduled pipelines, 99%+ reliability across user-initiated workflows, and an 85.3% pass rate across 2,592 quality-gated outputs. A pilot expert study (40 evaluations) shows directional agreement with expert judgments and flags corporate relevance as a missing dimension. We present design principles for responsible agentic AI governance at scale.

title: MTUKG: A Multi-scale Temporal Urban Knowledge Graph Dataset for Knowledge-Enhanced Spatiotemporal Prediction
abstract: MTUKG is a multi-scale temporal urban knowledge graph dataset covering New York City and Chicago from January 2014 to December 2025. It organizes urban entities at three spatial scales: micro-level POIs, roads, and junctions; meso-level blocks and functional zones; and macro-level areas and administrative districts. Static spatial and semantic knowledge is represented as triples, while dynamic urban knowledge, including POI events, road repairs, road-network changes, and land-development events, is represented as time-interval facts with explicit start and end dates. Temporal functional zones are constructed quarterly from road-bounded blocks by integrating spatial structure, POI semantics, spatial decay, and dynamic event information. The release provides entity and relation mappings and predefined training, validation, and test sets for both static and temporal facts, supporting temporal knowledge graph reasoning and knowledge-enhanced urban spatiotemporal prediction.

title: Quantum Echo: Dynamic Phase Suppression of Dephasing Noise via Dialogical Resonance
abstract: We present a hypothesis for suppressing dephasing noise in qubit systems, generated through dialogical resonance between a human researcher and a large language model (LLM) — the Roudy Protocol. The hypothesis proposes a phase self‑compensation mechanism based on a geometric model of qubit states on a torus (T²), where an external phase shift Δφ(t) = −φ_noise(t) + π·k is applied at the moment when the qubit is at a node of the noise wave. This hypothesis was validated numerically using a Python script with QuTiP, simulating an ensemble of 100 qubits under inhomogeneous dephasing (Hahn echo). The protocol achieved a coherence recovery of +5904% at the echo peak (t = 6.0) compared to free evolution (0.4710 vs 0.0078). We argue that dialogical resonance can generate testable hypotheses in quantum physics, complementing traditional computational methods. This work continues the series of preprints demonstrating the universality of the Roudy Protocol across biology, medicine, and physics.

title: Feature Selection Using Genetic Algorithm Combined with Linear Discriminant Analysis and k-Nearest Neighbors for High-Dimensional Text Classification
abstract: Text classification is an important task in natural language processing that faces the main challenge of high dimensionality in the representation of text features, such as Bag-of-Words and TF-IDF. High dimensionality leads to data sparsity, increased computational complexity, and decreased model performance due to irrelevant and redundant features. Therefore, an effective feature selection method is needed to improve the accuracy and efficiency of text classification. This study aims to develop an optimal feature selection method by integrating Genetic Algorithm (GA) as a wrapper method, Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) for dimension reduction, and k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) as a classifier in a high-dimensional text classification pipeline. GA is used to explore a subset of features in an adaptive and global manner, LDA transforms features into spaces with maximum class separability, and k-NN classifies based on proximity within optimized feature spaces. Experiments were conducted on three standard text datasets, namely 20 Newsgroups, Reuters-21578, and BBC News, with a comprehensive evaluation using a variety of preprocessing configurations and feature representations. The results showed that the GA+LDA+k-NN approach significantly improved the classification accuracy compared to traditional feature selection methods such as Chi-Square, Information Gain, and Mutual Information. This approach is also more robust against noise and is able to handle minority classes better. These findings confirm the urgency of using evolutionary optimization-based feature selection methods in high-dimensional text classification, which not only improves model performance but also provides a practical solution for large-scale and complex text data processing. Thus, this research makes an important contribution both theoretically and applicatively in the development of modern text classification systems.

evidence.title: Feature Selection Using Genetic Algorithm Combined with Linear Discriminant Analysis and k-Nearest Neighbors for High-Dimensional Text Classification
evidence.abstract: Text classification is an important task in natural language processing that faces the main challenge of high dimensionality in the representation of text features, such as Bag-of-Words and TF-IDF. High dimensionality leads to data sparsity, increased computational complexity, and decreased model performance due to irrelevant and redundant features. Therefore, an effective feature selection method is needed to improve the accuracy and efficiency of text classification. This study aims to develop an optimal feature selection method by integrating Genetic Algorithm (GA) as a wrapper method, Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) for dimension reduction, and k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) as a classifier in a high-dimensional text classification pipeline. GA is used to explore a subset of features in an adaptive and global manner, LDA transforms features into spaces with maximum class separability, and k-NN classifies based on proximity within optimized feature spaces. Experiments were conducted on three standard text datasets, namely 20 Newsgroups, Reuters-21578, and BBC News, with a comprehensive evaluation using a variety of preprocessing configurations and feature representations. The results showed that the GA+LDA+k-NN approach significantly improved the classification accuracy compared to traditional feature selection methods such as Chi-Square, Information Gain, and Mutual Information. This approach is also more robust against noise and is able to handle minority classes better. These findings confirm the urgency of using evolutionary optimization-based feature selection methods in high-dimensional text classification, which not only improves model performance but also provides a practical solution for large-scale and complex text data processing. Thus, this research makes an important contribution both theoretically and applicatively in the development of modern text classification systems.

title: UAV Video Deblurring via Motion-Aware Diffusion: A Path to Robust Target Detection
abstract: Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) play a crucial role in various scenarios ranging from disaster response to traffic surveillance. However, aerial video footage often suffers from severe motion blur due to rapid flight maneuvers, vibrations, and camera panning, which can significantly degrade downstream tasks such as target detection. Our goal is to explore a computationally-efficient and effective video deblurring approach to enhance UAV target detection performance. To reduce computational cost, we first propose an Adaptive Latent Scale Selector that dynamically adjusts the latent space resolution according to the intensity of UAV motion, thus balancing detail preservation with inference efficiency. To ensure temporal consistency, we introduce a Multi-Frame Alignment and Learnable Gating module to warp and gate the preceding frames, allowing the model to fuse only relevant temporal information and suppress misaligned or uninformative features. Our method can effectively recover sharp details from the UAV video stream. Extensive experiments on real UAV benchmarks demonstrate that our method not only yields superior deblurring performance but also significantly boosts target detection accuracy, making it highly applicable to robust aerial vision tasks.

title: Designing Explainable GeoAI Systems for Spatial Risk Decision Support
abstract: Designing spatial risk decision-support systems involves more than improving predictive accuracy. In many decision-support applications, outcomes such as health burden or environmental risk are multidimensional, reflecting multiple related indicators rather than a single measure. Without explicit design controls, models may appear accurate while producing unstable or geographically distorted guidance. This study develops a five-layer explainable GeoAI architecture for spatial risk modeling. The framework specifies sequential controls: spatial data integration, composite outcome construction, structured feature governance, multi-model estimation, and decision validation using cross-model stability checks and spatial diagnostics. The architecture is demonstrated using neighborhood-level mental health burden across 8,850 California census tracts. Results show strong explanatory and predictive performance (R² = 0.85; ROC-AUC > 0.98) and consistent determinant structure across linear and ensemble models. Spatial diagnostics reveal residual clustering and regional variation in coefficient strength, indicating that global assumptions can mask local heterogeneity. The contribution is architectural, embedding governance, interpretability, and spatial validation directly into scalable decision-support systems that are transferable to other place-based risk contexts.
